items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: an egg laid on Yom Tov, the measures for leaven, and covering blood after slaughter. Beit Shammai permits the egg, while Beit Hillel prohibits it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with three disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding an egg laid on Yom Tov, the measures for leaven, and covering blood after slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which case of a hen is being discussed. If it is a hen designated for eating, the egg is merely food that became separated, so why would Beit Hillel prohibit it? It concludes the hen is designated for laying eggs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which case of a hen is being discussed, and if it is a hen designated for eating, why would Beit Hillel prohibit the egg, since it is merely food that became separated.
The Gemara resolves that the hen is designated for laying eggs, not for eating.

items.text: Objection regarding מוקצה
items.text_en: Objection regarding מוקצה
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the hen is for eggs, it is מוקצה (set aside), so why would Beit Shammai permit it? It then reframes: perhaps Beit Shammai rejects מוקצה, but even those who permit מוקצה forbid נולד (a newly created item). So what is Beit Shammai's reasoning?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the hen is for eggs, it is מוקצה (set aside), so why would Beit Shammai permit it?
The Gemara reframes: perhaps Beit Shammai rejects מוקצה, but even those who permit מוקצה forbid נולד (a newly created item), so what is Beit Shammai's reasoning?

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the dispute is about a hen designated for eggs. Those who accept מוקצה also accept נולד, and those who reject מוקצה reject נולד. Thus, Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Shimon (who rejects מוקצה), and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Yehuda (who accepts it).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the dispute by explaining that the hen is designated for eggs, and the positions on מוקצה (set-aside) and נולד (newly born) are linked: Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Shimon (who rejects מוקצה), and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Yehuda (who accepts it).

items.text: Contradiction from another Mishnah
items.text_en: Contradiction from another Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai permits handling bones and peels on Shabbat, and Beit Hillel requires removing the entire table. Rav Nachman had previously stated there that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Yehuda (who is stringent) and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Shimon (who is lenient), contradicting his current alignment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's alignment by citing a Mishnah where he previously assigned Beit Shammai to Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel to Rabbi Shimon, contradicting his current statement.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that regarding Shabbat, the Tanna's anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon (lenient), so he aligns Beit Hillel with Rabbi Shimon there. But regarding Yom Tov, the anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, so he aligns Beit Hillel with Rabbi Yehuda here.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by explaining that regarding Shabbat, the anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon (lenient), so he aligns Beit Hillel with Rabbi Shimon there, but regarding Yom Tov, the anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, so he aligns Beit Hillel with Rabbi Yehuda here.

items.text: Gemara's question about conflicting anonymous Mishnayot
items.text_en: Gemara's question about conflicting anonymous Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the anonymous Mishnah on Yom Tov follows Rabbi Yehudah (who is stringent), while the anonymous Mishnah on Shabbat follows Rabbi Shimon (who is lenient). It asks why the same Tanna (Rabbi) would adopt different opinions for Shabbat vs. Yom Tov, and answers that Shabbat's severity prevents leniency, whereas Yom Tov's lightness might lead to disrespect, so a stringent view is adopted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the anonymous Mishnah on Yom Tov follows Rabbi Yehudah's stringent view.
The Gemara asks why the same Tanna (Rabbi) adopts Rabbi Shimon's lenient view for Shabbat but Rabbi Yehudah's stringent view for Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that Shabbat's severity prevents leniency, while Yom Tov's lightness might lead to disrespect, so a stringent view is adopted.

items.text: Rejecting the מוקצה explanation and proposing a compromise
items.text_en: Rejecting the מוקצה explanation and proposing a compromise
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the Mishnah deals with a hen set aside for laying eggs, and the dispute is about מוקצה. It asks why the Mishnah focused on the egg rather than the hen. Initially it suggests that the Mishnah wanted to show Beit Shammai's leniency, but then notes it would have been better to show Beit Hillel's stringency as well. The Gemara proposes a compromise: a joint dispute about both the hen and its egg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah is about a hen set aside for laying eggs and the dispute is about מוקצה (set-aside), why did the Mishnah focus on the egg rather than the hen itself?
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah chose the egg to demonstrate Beit Shammai's lenient position that a newly laid egg is permitted.
The Gemara objects: if so, the Mishnah should also have stated the dispute about the hen itself, to show Beit Hillel's stringency regarding מוקצה (set-aside).
The Gemara proposes a compromise: the Mishnah could have stated a joint dispute about both the hen and its egg, with Beit Shammai permitting both and Beit Hillel forbidding both.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation: the case is a hen designated for eating, and the prohibition stems from הכנה
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation: the case is a hen designated for eating, and the prohibition stems from הכנה
items.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that the Mishnah discusses a hen designated for eating, on a Yom Tov that follows Shabbat. The dispute is about הכנה (preparation). Rabbah holds that eggs laid now were already completed yesterday, and no preparation can cross from Yom Tov to Shabbat or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that the Mishnah discusses a hen designated for eating on a Yom Tov that follows Shabbat, and the dispute is about הכנה (preparation).
Rabbah holds that every egg laid now was already completed yesterday, so no new preparation occurs today.
Rabbah cites the verse 'וְהָיָה בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי וְהֵכִינוּ' to prove that חול (weekday) prepares for Shabbat and Yom Tov, but Yom Tov and Shabbat cannot prepare for each other.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rabbah's response about rare cases
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rabbah's response about rare cases
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that if Rabbah is correct, then eggs on any Yom Tov or Shabbat should be permitted, yet the Mishnah prohibits only after Shabbat. He suggests a gezera for other days due to this case. Abaye then cites a baraita permitting fully formed eggs found inside a slaughtered hen on Yom Tov, arguing that if the gezera applied, they would be forbidden. Rabbah replies that fully formed eggs in the hen are uncommon, so the Sages did not decree for rare cases.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if Rabbah's reasoning applies, then eggs on any Yom Tov or Shabbat should be permitted, and suggests a gezera (decree) for other days due to the case of Yom Tov after Shabbat or Shabbat after Yom Tov.
Abaye cites a baraita permitting fully formed eggs found inside a slaughtered hen on Yom Tov, arguing that if the gezera applied, they would be forbidden.
Rabbah replies that fully formed eggs in the hen are uncommon, so the Sages did not decree for rare cases.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative: a gezera due to fallen fruit
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative: a gezera due to fallen fruit
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the prohibition is a gezera because of fallen fruit (fruits that fall from trees on Shabbat or Yom Tov). Abaye begins to question the logic behind this gezera.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef proposes that the prohibition of eating an egg laid on Yom Tov is a גזירה (rabbinic decree) due to fallen fruit (פירות הנושרין), which are forbidden on Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef what the rationale is for this גזירה (decree) regarding fallen fruit.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and two answers
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and two answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition of squeezing fruit is a decree due to the concern of uprooting, and notes that this would be a decree upon a decree. Rabbi Yitzchak offers an alternative: the decree is due to liquids that exuded. Abaye objects that this too is a decree upon a decree, but the Gemara concludes that it is all one decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition of squeezing fruit is a decree due to the concern of uprooting, and notes that this would be a decree upon a decree, but concludes that it is all one decree.
Rabbi Yitzchak offers an alternative: the decree is due to liquids that exuded.
Abaye objects that this too is a decree upon a decree, but the Gemara concludes that it is all one decree.

items.text: Explanation of why others do not adopt Rav Nachman's or Rabba's views
items.text_en: Explanation of why others do not adopt Rav Nachman's or Rabba's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all other Amoraim do not accept Rav Nachman's reasoning because of the difficulty, and they do not accept Rabba's because they do not hold of the concept of preparation (הכנה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all other Amoraim do not adopt Rav Nachman's view because of the difficulty with his reasoning.
The Gemara explains that they also do not accept Rabba's view because they do not hold of the concept of preparation (הכנה).

items.text: Debate between Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Debate between Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Yosef does not adopt Rabbi Yitzchak's reasoning, and answers that Rav Yosef distinguishes between an egg and fruit (both are food) and liquids (not food). Then it asks why Rabbi Yitzchak does not adopt Rav Yosef's reasoning, and answers that Rabbi Yitzchak distinguishes between an egg and liquids (both are absorbed) and fruit (which are exposed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Yosef does not adopt Rabbi Yitzchak's reasoning.
Rav Yosef distinguishes between an egg and fruit (both are food) and liquids (not food).
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yitzchak does not adopt Rav Yosef's reasoning.
Rabbi Yitzchak distinguishes between an egg and liquids (both are absorbed) and fruit (which are exposed).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan also holds the decree is due to liquids that exuded, as he resolves a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan also holds the decree is due to liquids that exuded, as he resolves a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution of a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution of a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between squeezing for eating and for drink, and a Baraita where Rabbi Yehuda allows a basket of fruit from the first day of Yom Tov to be eaten on the second, but not an egg laid on the first. Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by saying the traditions are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה), and concludes that the two rulings share one rationale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between squeezing fruit for eating (permitted) and for drink (forbidden).
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that for Rabbi Yehuda, all fruit juices that emerge for eating are considered detached food (אוכל דאפרש), not liquid.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: a Baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda allows a basket of fruit from the first day of Yom Tov to be eaten on the second, and similarly an egg laid on the first may be eaten on the second, but not on the first.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by asserting that the traditions are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה), meaning the attributions in the Mishnah and Baraita are swapped.
The Gemara concludes that since Rabbi Yochanan raised the contradiction, the two rulings share one rationale (חד טעמא הוא).

items.text: Ravina's first explanation: Rabbi Yehuda speaks to the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Ravina's first explanation: Rabbi Yehuda speaks to the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that the Mishnah should not be reversed; Rabbi Yehuda is addressing the Rabbis according to their own logic. He says that for himself, even on the first day (Yom Tov) the egg is permitted because it is food that was prepared, but for the Rabbis, they should at least concede that on the second day it is permitted because there are two distinct sanctities. The Rabbis respond that it is a single sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asserts that the Mishnah should not be reversed; Rabbi Yehuda is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own logic, and for himself even on the first day (Yom Tov) the egg is permitted because it is food that was prepared (אוכלה דאפרת).

Ravina challenges the Rabbis: according to your own reasoning, you should at least concede that on the second day (of Yom Tov) the egg is permitted because there are two distinct sanctities (שתי קדושות).
The Rabbis reject Ravina's argument, asserting that it is a single sanctity (קדושה אחת), so the egg remains forbidden on the second day as well.

items.text: Ravina bar Rav Ulla's explanation: a hen set aside for laying eggs
items.text_en: Ravina bar Rav Ulla's explanation: a hen set aside for laying eggs
items.desc_en: Ravina bar Rav Ulla offers a different explanation: the case involves a hen that is designated for laying eggs, and Rabbi Yehuda follows his own view that מוקצה applies.

sub.desc_en: Ravina bar Rav Ulla explains that the mishnah deals with a hen set aside to lay eggs, so Rabbi Yehuda follows his own view that מוקצה (set-aside items) applies.

items.text: Baraita: egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov is forbidden
items.text_en: Baraita: egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov is forbidden
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: an egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov may not be moved, not even to cover a vessel or support a bed, but one may place a vessel over it to prevent breakage. If there is a doubt (whether it was born on a weekday or holiday), it is forbidden, and if it becomes mixed with a thousand permitted eggs, all are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: an egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov may not be moved, not even to cover a vessel or support a bed.
The baraita continues: one may place a vessel over it to prevent breakage, and if there is doubt or it becomes mixed with a thousand permitted eggs, all are forbidden.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak from the baraita's stringency
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak from the baraita's stringency
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabba, who says the prohibition is due to preparation (הכנה), the doubt is a Torah doubt and is stringent, which fits the baraita. But according to Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak, who say it is a rabbinic decree, the doubt should be lenient, contradicting the baraita's stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak: according to Rabba, who says the prohibition is due to preparation (הכנה), the doubt is a Torah doubt and is stringent, fitting the baraita; but according to Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzchak, who say it is a rabbinic decree, the doubt should be lenient, contradicting the baraita's stringency.

items.text: Answer: the baraita deals with doubt of a treifah
items.text_en: Answer: the baraita deals with doubt of a treifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the latter part of the baraita (about doubt) refers to a case of doubt whether the egg came from a treifah (non-kosher) animal, which is a Torah prohibition, thus explaining the stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the latter part of the baraita deals with doubt whether the egg came from a טריפה (non-kosher) animal, which is a Torah prohibition, thus explaining the stringency.

items.text: Objection: the baraita's ruling on mixture contradicts the treifah explanation
items.text_en: Objection: the baraita's ruling on mixture contradicts the treifah explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the doubt is about a treifah, then when the egg is mixed with a thousand, it should be nullified in a majority, since it is not a דבר שיש לו מתירין. But the baraita says all are forbidden. Even if one argues that an egg is a significant item that is not nullified, this only works for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish who says 'all that is counted' is not nullified, but for Rabbi Yochanan who says 'that which is counted' is not nullified, the egg might not be considered such.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the baraita's ruling on mixture is about a doubt between Yom Tov and weekday, it fits the rule of a דבר שיש לו מתירין (an item that can become permitted later), which is not nullified even in a thousand; but if it is about a doubt of a treifah, it should be nullified.
The Gemara continues: if it is a doubt of a treifah, it is a דבר שאין לו מתירין (an item without a later permitted time), so it should be nullified in a majority.
The Gemara considers a possible answer: the egg is a significant item (חשוב) and not nullified, which works for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish who says 'all that is counted' is not nullified.
The Gemara objects: but for Rabbi Yochanan who says only 'that which is counted' is not nullified, the egg might not be considered such, so what can be said?

items.text: Supporting baraita: dispute about items that are counted
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: dispute about items that are counted
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about bundles of kilayim of the vineyard: Rabbi Meir says they must all be burned if mixed, while the Sages say they are nullified in 1/200. The dispute is based on whether items that are normally counted (דבר שדרכו לימנות) are not nullified. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree on the precise formulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about bundles of kilayim of the vineyard: Rabbi Meir says they must all be burned if mixed, while the Sages say they are nullified in 1/200.

The baraita continues: Rabbi Meir says that items whose manner is exclusively to be counted are significant and cannot be nullified; the Sages list six specific items; Rabbi Akiva adds loaves of a homeowner.

The baraita concludes with the rule for the listed items, and an amoraic dispute is stated: Rabbi Yochanan says the mishna taught 'that whose manner is exclusively to be counted', while Resh Lakish says it taught 'any item whose manner is also to be counted'.

The Gemara notes that this works out well according to Resh Lakish, but according to Rabbi Yochanan, who requires exclusive counting, an egg (which is not exclusively sold by unit) should be nullified — so what can be said?

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution: the baraita follows the Tanna of litra ketsi'ot
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution: the baraita follows the Tanna of litra ketsi'ot
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the baraita's author is the Tanna who rules about litra ketsi'ot (dried figs pressed into a cake), who holds that any item that is counted is not nullified even in rabbinic law, and certainly in Torah law. This resolves the difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan's position.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by identifying the baraita's author as the Tanna of litra ketsi'ot, who holds that any counted item is not nullified even in rabbinic law, and certainly in Torah law.

The Gemara cites the mishna about litra ketsi'ot (dried figs pressed into a cake) where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer dispute the nullification of counted items, supporting Rav Pappa's identification of the Tanna.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about barrels of wine or oil
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about barrels of wine or oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about barrels of wine or oil that become mixed with forbidden ones. Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer argue about whether the mouths (פומין) are considered separated and whether they can be nullified by a majority.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that the upper circles of dried figs are considered separate, and the lower ones nullify them.
Rabbi Yehoshua says that if there are one hundred mouths, the prohibited figs are nullified; otherwise, the mouths are prohibited and the bottoms are permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda reports that Rabbi Eliezer rules like Rabbi Yehoshua in the first version: one hundred mouths nullify the prohibited figs.
Rabbi Yehoshua in this version holds that even three hundred mouths do not nullify the prohibited figs.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of treading in a circle, noting it seems to repeat the dispute. Rav Pappa explains that the case is where one does not know which part of the circle was trodden, and all agree it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one trod the litra into a circular vessel and does not know which vessel, all agree it is nullified.
The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can say 'all agree' when this is precisely the dispute between the sages.
Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where one does not know which side of the circular vessel was trodden, so all agree it is nullified.

items.text: Rav Ashi's principle of something with permittees
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's principle of something with permittees
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that a doubtful case of Yom Tov versus weekday is considered something that has permittees (דבר שיש לו מתירין), and such an item is not nullified even by a rabbinic majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that a doubtful case of Yom Tov versus weekday is considered something that has permittees (דבר שיש לו מתירין), and such an item is not nullified even by a rabbinic majority.

items.text: Baraita: Egg and its mother – analysis and hyperbole
items.text_en: Baraita: Egg and its mother – analysis and hyperbole
items.desc_en: A baraita cites others in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that an egg may be eaten with its mother. The Gemara questions the case, and Rabbi Zeira explains it means the egg is eaten along with its mother. Abaye clarifies the scenario of a hen purchased without specification. Rav Mari suggests it is hyperbole (גוזמא), as another baraita adds 'chick and its shell' which is clearly exaggerated.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Others say in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that an egg laid on a Festival may be eaten together with its mother.
The Gemara asks what case is being discussed: if the hen is designated for food, the ruling is obvious; if designated for laying eggs, both are prohibited.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the egg may be eaten on account of its mother: if the hen is eaten on the Festival, the egg is also permitted.
The Gemara asks for the precise circumstances of this ruling.
Abaye clarifies: it refers to a hen purchased without specification; if slaughtered, it is retroactively clarified that it was for food; if not, it was for laying eggs.
Rav Mari argues that the baraita is an exaggeration (גוזמא), citing another baraita that adds 'a chick and its shell'.

The Gemara questions the meaning of 'its shell', concluding it refers to a chick in its shell, and notes that the Rabbis only dispute Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov regarding a chick that has emerged into the world.
The Gemara resolves that both expressions—'chick and its shell' and 'it and its mother'—are exaggerations, not meant literally.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether an egg born on Shabbat is permitted on Yom Tov. The Gemara suggests Rav holds there is one sanctity, but notes Rav elsewhere rules like Rabbi Eliezer who says there are two sanctities. The Gemara resolves that they argue about the principle of preparation by the mother (הכנה דרבה).

sub.desc_en: States the dispute: Rav says an egg laid on Shabbat is prohibited on Yom Tov, Rabbi Yochanan says it is permitted.
Suggests that Rav holds Shabbat and Yom Tov are one continuous sanctity.
Objects that Rav elsewhere rules like Rabbi Eliezer, who says there are two sanctities.
Resolves that the dispute is about the principle of preparation by the mother (הכנה דרבה).

items.text: Tannaitic support: Baraita on egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov
items.text_en: Tannaitic support: Baraita on egg born on Shabbat or Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an egg born on Shabbat may be eaten on Yom Tov, and vice versa. Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer notes that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel still dispute this.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that an egg born on Shabbat may be eaten on Yom Tov, and one born on Yom Tov may be eaten on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda reports in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that the matter is still disputed.
Beit Shammai rules that the egg may be eaten.
Beit Hillel rules that the egg may not be eaten.

items.text: Practical cases: Rav Adda bar Ahava's guest and Rav Pappa's guest
items.text_en: Practical cases: Rav Adda bar Ahava's guest and Rav Pappa's guest
items.desc_en: Two stories: Rav Adda bar Ahava's guest had eggs from Yom Tov to Shabbat and asked about roasting them. Rav Adda ruled that even Rabbi Yochanan only permits eating them the next day, not on the same day. Rav Pappa's guest had eggs from Shabbat to Yom Tov; Rav Pappa deferred the answer due to intoxication, and later ruled.

sub.desc_en: The host of רב אדא בר אהבה (Rav Adda bar Ahava) had eggs from a festival day (יום טוב) to the Sabbath (שבת) and asked whether he could roast them now and eat them tomorrow.

רב אדא בר אהבה (Rav Adda bar Ahava) answered that even according to רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan), who permits the egg on the next day, one may only swallow it raw the next day, not roast it on the same day.
A ברייתא (baraita) is cited stating that an egg laid on either the Sabbath (שבת) or a festival day (יום טוב) may not be moved at all, even for covering a vessel or supporting a bed.

The host of רב פפא (Rav Pappa) had eggs from the Sabbath (שבת) to a festival day (יום טוב) and asked about eating them the next day; רב פפא (Rav Pappa) deferred the answer due to intoxication from the festival day.
The narrative transitions to the next day when the man returned to receive רב פפא (Rav Pappa)'s ruling.

items.text: Rava's ruling on Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan in three specific cases, both leniently and stringently, establishing a principle for resolving disputes between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rava's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan over Rav in three specific cases, both leniently and stringently.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on wood that fell on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on wood that fell on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that wood that fell from a palm tree on Shabbat is forbidden to be used for heating on Yom Tov, distinguishing it from an egg which is permitted because it was fit for consumption on the day it was laid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that wood that fell from a palm tree on Shabbat is forbidden to burn on Yom Tov, distinguishing it from an egg which is edible on its own day.

items.text: Rav Matna's solution and the objection of nullification
items.text_en: Rav Matna's solution and the objection of nullification
items.desc_en: Rav Matna permits adding prepared wood to the fallen wood in the oven, arguing that since the majority is permitted, handling it is permissible. The Gemara objects that this nullifies a prohibition ab initio, but distinguishes between Torah and rabbinic prohibitions. Rav Ashi adds that if the item has a permitted alternative, it does not become nullified, but here the prohibition is burned away.

sub.desc_en: Rav Matna permits adding prepared wood to fallen wood in the oven on Yom Tov, arguing that since the majority is permitted, handling the mixture is permissible.
The Gemara objects that this nullifies a prohibition לכתחילה (ab initio), citing the rule that one may not intentionally nullify a prohibition.
The Gemara answers that the rule against nullification applies only to Torah prohibitions, but for rabbinic prohibitions one may nullify them.
Rav Ashi objects that according to his principle, an item with a permitted alternative (מתקן) is never nullified even in rabbinic law.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Ashi's principle applies only when the prohibition remains intact, but here the prohibition is burned away (מקלא קלי איסורא).

items.text: Dispute about two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora
items.text_en: Dispute about two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora
items.desc_en: Rav and Rav Asi disagree about an egg laid on the first day of a two-day Yom Tov: Rav permits it on the second day, while Rav Asi forbids it. The Gemara clarifies that Rav Asi is uncertain whether the two days are one sanctity or two, so he acts stringently in both directions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav and Rav Asi dispute the status of an egg laid on the first day of a two-day Yom Tov in the Diaspora: Rav permits it on the second day, Rav Asi forbids it.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Asi holds that the two days are one sanctity (קדושה אחת), noting that he recites Havdalah between the two days, which would contradict that view.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Asi is uncertain whether the two days are one sanctity or two, so he acts stringently in both directions: forbidding the egg on the second day and reciting Havdalah.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira and Abaye debate the reason for two days
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira and Abaye debate the reason for two days
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira supports Rav Asi's stringency because even though we now know the calendar, we still observe two days. Abaye supports Rav's leniency, citing the Mishnah about messengers, and explains that the two-day practice is a safeguard against government decrees that might disrupt the calendar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that Rav Asi's position is correct because even though we now know the calendar, we still observe two days.
Abaye counters that Rav's leniency is correct, citing the Mishnah about messengers and noting that when messengers reached their destination, only one day was observed.
Abaye explains that the current two-day practice is a safeguard against potential government decrees that could disrupt the calendar, as instructed by the sages.

items.text: Two days of Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Two days of Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both rule that an egg laid on the first day of Rosh Hashanah is forbidden on the second day, citing the Mishnah that originally testimony about the new moon was accepted all day, but once witnesses were delayed, the practice changed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute regarding the two days of Rosh Hashanah: Rav and Shmuel both rule that an egg laid on one is forbidden on the other, citing the Mishnah about accepting testimony all day.
Rav and Shmuel both rule that an egg laid on the first day of Rosh Hashanah is forbidden on the second day.
The gemara cites the Mishnah that originally testimony about the new moon was accepted all day, but once witnesses were delayed, the practice changed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah about witness acceptance
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah about witness acceptance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the enactment that witnesses for the new moon are only accepted until mincha; if they come later, the day is treated as sacred and the next day also.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by recounting that the Levites became confused in the song, so the court enacted that witnesses for the new moon are only accepted until mincha.
The Mishnah concludes that if witnesses come after mincha, the day is treated as sacred and the next day also.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment onward, an egg is permitted. Abaye objects, citing Rav and Shmuel who both say the egg is forbidden. Rabbah dismisses the objection, asserting his reliance on Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment onward, an egg laid on Yom Tov is permitted, citing the Mishnah that after the Temple's destruction, witnesses for the new month are accepted all day.
Abaye objects, citing that both Rav and Shmuel hold the egg is forbidden.
Rabbah dismisses Abaye's objection, asserting his reliance on Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's authority over that of Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Resolution for Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Resolution for Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty for Rav and Shmuel by distinguishing between the Mishnah's context (for us, in Babylonia) and their context (for them, in Israel).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the Mishnah's ruling that an egg is permitted contradicts the position of Rav and Shmuel that it is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between the Mishnah's context (for us, in Babylonia) and their context (for them, in Israel).

items.text: Rav Yosef's opposing view
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that even after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment, the egg is forbidden because it is a matter that required a formal count, and such a matter needs another count to permit it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that even after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment, the egg is forbidden because it is a matter that required a formal count (דבר שבמנין), and such a matter needs another count to permit it.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof and supporting sources
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof and supporting sources
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a verse to support his principle, and the Gemara brings a baraita about the fourth-year vineyard and Ulla's explanation that it was to adorn Jerusalem's markets with fruits, along with another baraita about Rabbi Eliezer's vineyard.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef opens by citing a verse to prove his principle that a matter requiring a count needs another count to permit it.
A baraita is cited describing the boundaries of the fourth-year vineyard (כרם רבעי) that was brought up to Jerusalem.

sub.text: Ulla / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ulla / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ulla (or alternatively Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan) explains that the reason for this boundary was to adorn the markets of Jerusalem with fruits.
Another baraita is cited about a fourth-year vineyard belonging to Rabbi Eliezer located east of Lod near Kfar Tavi.

items.text: Opening narrative and inference
items.text_en: Opening narrative and inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when Rabbi Eliezer sought to declare his produce ownerless for the poor, his students told him that his colleagues had already voted and permitted it. The Gemara infers that if they had not voted, it would not be permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Eliezer sought to declare his produce ownerless for the poor, and his students told him that his colleagues, led by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, had already voted and permitted it.
The Gemara infers that the permission depended on the vote; had they not voted, it would not have been permitted.

items.text: Proof from the Torah: a matter in a vote requires another vote
items.text_en: Proof from the Torah: a matter in a vote requires another vote
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'and says' by citing verses: from the juxtaposition of 'be ready for the third day' and 'go say to them return to your tents', it derives that any matter decided by a vote requires another vote to permit it. A second proof is brought from the verse 'when the horn is drawn out they shall ascend the mountain'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'and says' means, and explains that Rav Yosef is asking why the verse 'go say to them return to your tents' is needed if the prohibition already lapsed after three days.
The Gemara concludes that any matter established by a vote requires another vote to permit it.
The Gemara raises an alternative explanation that the verse 'return to your tents' might be for the mitzva of conjugal rights, and then brings a second proof from the verse about the ram's horn.

The Gemara argues that since the prohibition of grazing near the mountain would lapse on its own, the verse 'when the horn is drawn out' is needed to show that a matter established by a vote requires another vote to permit it.

items.text: Proof from rabbinic law: the case of fourth-year vineyard
items.text_en: Proof from rabbinic law: the case of fourth-year vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a potential objection that the principle applies only to Torah law, not rabbinic law. It brings a proof from the case of fourth-year vineyard (kerem revai), which is rabbinic, where the colleagues voted and permitted it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible objection: perhaps the principle that a matter established by a vote requires another vote to permit it applies only to Torah law, but not to rabbinic law.

The Gemara answers by citing the case of kerem revai (fourth-year vineyard), which is a rabbinic prohibition, and yet the colleagues voted and permitted it, proving that the principle applies even to rabbinic law.

items.text: Distinction: egg case vs. testimony
items.text_en: Distinction: egg case vs. testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the egg case was also permitted by a vote of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. It answers that the vote was about testimony (regarding the new moon), not about the egg itself. Abaye explains that the egg's status depends on the testimony: if testimony is prohibited, the egg is prohibited; if testimony is permitted, the egg is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the egg was also permitted by a vote of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and answers that the vote was about testimony (עדות), not about the egg itself.
Abaye explains that the egg's status depends on the testimony: if testimony is prohibited, the egg is prohibited; if testimony is permitted, the egg is permitted.

items.text: Rav Adda and Rav Shalman's opinion: egg prohibited from Rabban Yochanan's enactment onward
items.text_en: Rav Adda and Rav Shalman's opinion: egg prohibited from Rabban Yochanan's enactment onward
items.desc_en: Rav Adda and Rav Shalman argue that from the enactment of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai onward, the egg is prohibited. The reason is that people might mistakenly think that the two days of Yom Tov are one continuous holiness, leading them to eat eggs on the second day. The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply to accepting testimony, but distinguishes: testimony is entrusted to the court, while the egg is entrusted to everyone.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda and Rav Shalman state that from the enactment of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai onward, the egg is prohibited.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning should apply to accepting testimony about the new moon, which would also be mistakenly permitted.
The Gemara distinguishes: testimony is entrusted to the court (בית דין), while the egg is entrusted to everyone, so the concern about public confusion applies only to the egg.

items.text: Rava's opinion and ruling
items.text_en: Rava's opinion and ruling
items.desc_en: Rava agrees that from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment onward, the egg is prohibited, citing that Rabban Yochanan himself would treat the day as sacred if witnesses came after mincha. Rava then rules that the halakha follows Rav in these three matters, both leniently and stringently.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment onward, the egg is prohibited, and he challenges whether Rabban Yochanan himself would not treat the day as sacred if witnesses came after mincha.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Rav in these three matters, both leniently and stringently.

items.text: Rava's ruling on burial on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on burial on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rava states that if someone dies on the first day of Yom Tov, non-Jews should handle the burial; if on the second day, Jews may handle it, even on Rosh Hashanah. This is unlike the case of an egg.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that burial on the first day of Yom Tov is done by non-Jews, on the second day by Jews even on Rosh Hashanah, unlike the case of an egg.

items.text: Nehardeans' dispute on the egg
items.text_en: Nehardeans' dispute on the egg
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans argue that even an egg is permitted on the second day of Yom Tov, because there is no concern about intercalating Elul since the time of Ezra.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans argue that even an egg is permitted on the second day, because Elul is never intercalated.

items.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi on delayed burial
items.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi on delayed burial
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra limits the leniency to cases where burial was delayed; otherwise, we wait. Rav Ashi disagrees, saying even without delay we do not wait, as the Rabbis treated the second day of Yom Tov like a weekday for burial matters, even allowing cutting a cloak or myrtle.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra limits the leniency of not delaying burial to cases where burial was already delayed; otherwise, we wait.
Rav Ashi disagrees, arguing that even without delay we do not wait, because the Rabbis treated the second day of Yom Tov like a weekday for burial matters, even permitting cutting a cloak or myrtle.

items.text: Ravina's concern about חברי
items.text_en: Ravina's concern about חברי
items.desc_en: Ravina adds that nowadays, due to the presence of חברי (associates who might suspect improper conduct), we are concerned and do not allow burial by Jews on the second day.

sub.desc_en: Ravina adds that nowadays, because of the presence of חברי (a sect), we are concerned and do not bury immediately.

items.text: Story of Ravina and Rav Asi about Eruv Tavshilin
items.text_en: Story of Ravina and Rav Asi about Eruv Tavshilin
items.desc_en: Ravina sees Rav Asi sad on Rosh Hashanah because he forgot to prepare an Eruv Tavshilin. Ravina suggests he can set it now based on Rava's ruling, but Rav Asi distinguishes between the two days of Yom Tov of the Diaspora and Rosh Hashanah. Rav Mordechai clarifies that Rav Asi does not accept the Nehardeans' leniency.

sub.desc_en: Ravina sees Rav Asi sitting sadly on Rosh Hashanah and asks why; Rav Asi explains he forgot to prepare an Eruv Tavshilin.
Ravina suggests Rav Asi can still set the Eruv Tavshilin now, citing Rava's ruling that one may set it from one Yom Tov day to the next with a condition.
Rav Asi objects that Rava's leniency applies only to the two days of Yom Tov of the Diaspora, not to Rosh Hashanah.
Rav Mordechai clarifies that Rav Asi explicitly rejected the Nehardeans' leniency, so the objection stands.

items.text: Dispute about a chick born on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute about a chick born on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav forbids a chick born on Yom Tov due to מוקצה, while Shmuel or Rabbi Yochanan permit it because it becomes permitted through slaughter. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav why a chick differs from a calf born on Yom Tov, and Rav answers that a calf is prepared through its mother's slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rav forbids a chick born on Yom Tov, while Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan) permits it.
Rav explains his prohibition: the chick is מוקצה (set aside) because it was not designated before Yom Tov.
Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan) explains his permission: the chick becomes permitted through slaughter, as it is not מוקצה.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: what is the difference between this chick and a calf born on Yom Tov, which is permitted?
Rav answers that a calf is prepared (מוכן) through its mother's slaughter, unlike a chick whose mother is not slaughtered on Yom Tov.

items.text: Further question and Abaye's comment
items.text_en: Further question and Abaye's comment
items.desc_en: They ask Rav about a calf born from a terefah, and Rav remains silent. Rabba or Rav Yosef explains he could have answered that it is prepared for dogs. Abaye begins a comment, but the text cuts off.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: what is the difference between a chick born on Yom Tov and a calf born from a טריפה (terefah) animal, and Rav remains silent.
Rabba (or Rav Yosef) explains that Rav could have answered that the calf is prepared for dogs (מוכן אגב אמו לכלבים), distinguishing it from the chick.
Abaye begins to say something to Rav, but the text cuts off, leaving the comment incomplete.

items.text: Gemara's question on מוכן for animals vs. humans
items.text_en: Gemara's question on מוכן for animals vs. humans
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic that if something is prepared for humans it is not prepared for dogs, citing a Mishnah about cutting gourds for animals. It then presents Rav's answer distinguishing between what is fit for humans and what is fit for dogs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic that if something is not מוכן (prepared) for humans it is not מוכן for dogs, citing a Mishnah about cutting gourds for animals and neveila for dogs, and then asks: if it is מוכן for dogs, is it also מוכן for humans?

Rav answers that indeed, what is מוכן for humans is not מוכן for dogs because a person does not throw to dogs what is fit for himself, but what is מוכן for dogs is מוכן for humans because a person will eat anything fit for him.

items.text: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel/Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel/Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav, stating a calf born on Yom Tov is permitted but a chick is not, because the calf is prepared via its mother's slaughter; the other supports Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan), permitting both, as the chick permits itself through slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The gemara announces that two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav, and one supports Shmuel (or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan).
A baraita supports Rav: a calf born on Yom Tov is permitted, but a chick is forbidden, because the calf is prepared (מוכן) via its mother's slaughter, while the chick is not.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Shmuel / Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Shmuel / Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan): both a calf and a chick born on Yom Tov are permitted, because the calf is prepared via its mother and the chick permits itself through slaughter.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on chicks
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on chicks
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that a chick born on Yom Tov is forbidden, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that even on a weekday it is forbidden because its eyes have not opened. The Gemara identifies a verse that includes such chicks in the category of creeping things.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited stating that a chick born on Yom Tov is forbidden, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that even on a weekday it is forbidden because its eyes have not opened.

The Gemara identifies that the verse 'לְכׇל הַשֶּׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל הָאָרֶץ' (to every creeping thing that creeps on the earth), which includes chicks whose eyes have not opened, aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement on eggs and its initial interpretations
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement on eggs and its initial interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says in Rav's name that an egg is completed upon its exit. The Gemara first considers this means it is permitted with milk, but rejects this because eggs found inside a slaughtered chicken are permitted with milk. It then considers it means permitted on Yom Tov, but rejects this because such eggs are also permitted on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in Rav's name that an egg is completed upon its exit from the hen.
The Gemara asks what the statement means.
The Gemara first suggests that the egg is permitted with milk upon exit, implying that eggs inside the hen are forbidden with milk.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that eggs found fully formed inside a slaughtered hen are permitted with milk.
The Gemara then suggests that the egg is permitted on Yom Tov upon exit, implying that eggs inside the hen are forbidden on Yom Tov.
The Gemara objects again by citing the same baraita that eggs found fully formed inside a hen are permitted on Yom Tov.

items.text: Rejection of interpretations and analysis of Mishnah
items.text_en: Rejection of interpretations and analysis of Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah (Beitzah 1:1) already teaches that eggs found inside a chicken are permitted on Yom Tov, so Rav's statement cannot be about that. It then considers that Beit Hillel might forbid even those, but rejects this because the baraita would then align with neither Beit Shammai nor Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita cannot be teaching something new about eggs found inside a chicken, because the Mishnah (Beitzah 1:1) already explicitly permits them, with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only disputing a laid egg.

The Gemara considers the possibility that Beit Hillel might forbid even eggs found inside the hen, but rejects this because the baraita permitting them would then align with neither Beit Shammai nor Beit Hillel.

items.text: Final interpretation: eggs and chick development
items.text_en: Final interpretation: eggs and chick development
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav's statement means an egg upon exiting is capable of developing a chick, while one inside the mother is not. This distinction is relevant for buying and selling eggs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement means an egg upon exiting is capable of developing a chick, while one inside the mother is not, and this distinction is relevant for buying and selling eggs.

items.text: First case of mistaken purchase: eggs of a slaughtered chicken
items.text_en: First case of mistaken purchase: eggs of a slaughtered chicken
items.desc_en: A person asked for eggs from a slaughtered chicken (דְפָחֲיָא) and was given eggs from a slaughtered one. Rabbi Ami ruled it is a mistaken transaction and must be returned. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, and explains that the buyer might have wanted them for eating and the seller thought they wanted them for hatching, so the ruling teaches that even if the eggs are similar, the transaction is void.

sub.desc_en: A person asked for eggs from a slaughtered chicken (דְפָחֲיָא) and was given eggs from a slaughtered one; Rabbi Ami ruled it is a mistaken transaction and must be returned.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious, since the buyer clearly wanted eggs from a slaughtered chicken.
The Gemara explains that the ruling teaches that even if the eggs are similar, the transaction is void because the buyer wanted them for eating and the seller thought they wanted them for hatching.

items.text: Second case of mistaken purchase: eggs of a rooster
items.text_en: Second case of mistaken purchase: eggs of a rooster
items.desc_en: A person asked for eggs of a rooster (דְּדִכְרָא) and was given eggs from a chicken that laid from the ground (דְּסָפְנָא מֵאַרְעָא). Rabbi Ami again ruled it is a mistaken transaction. The Gemara similarly questions the obviousness and explains that the buyer wanted them for eating, and the seller thought they wanted them for hatching, so the ruling applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a second case: a person asked for eggs of a rooster (בֵּיעֵי דְּדִכְרָא) and was given eggs from a chicken that laid from the ground (דְּסָפְנָא מֵאַרְעָא); Rabbi Ami again ruled it is a mistaken transaction and the sale is reversed.
The Gemara objects that the ruling is obvious, questioning what novel point is being taught.

The Gemara explains the novelty: one might think the buyer wanted them for eating and the seller thought they wanted them for hatching, so the ruling teaches that even in such a case the transaction is mistaken.

items.text: Two interpretations of 'with its exit it is completed'
items.text_en: Two interpretations of 'with its exit it is completed'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of the meaning of the phrase 'עִם יְצִיאָתָהּ נִגְמְרָה' (with its exit it is completed). One version, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan, holds that an egg is considered fully formed when most of it has emerged. The other version holds that it is only completed when the entire egg has emerged, excluding Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: the phrase 'עִם יְצִיאָתָהּ נִגְמְרָה' means 'with the exit of most of it it is completed', in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
The second version holds that the phrase means 'with the exit of all of it it is completed', excluding Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that most of the egg suffices.

items.text: Eggs found inside a slaughtered chicken: kashrut and impurity
items.text_en: Eggs found inside a slaughtered chicken: kashrut and impurity
items.desc_en: A baraita states that eggs found fully formed inside a slaughtered chicken are permitted to be eaten with milk. Rabbi Yaakov prohibits if they are attached by sinews. The Gemara then discusses a tannaitic source about impurity: eating from the 'שלל של ביצים' (egg cluster) is pure. Rav Yosef says this is not in accordance with Rabbi Yaakov, who would prohibit. Abaye objects that Rabbi Yaakov's prohibition might only apply to issur (prohibition) but not to tum'ah (impurity), and we do not increase impurity rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that fully-formed eggs found inside a slaughtered chicken are permitted to be eaten with milk, but Rabbi Yaakov prohibits them if they are attached by sinews.
A second baraita is cited regarding impurity: eating from the 'שלל של ביצים' (egg cluster) is pure, but from the 'אשכול של ביצים' (egg bunch) is impure.
The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of the rule that the 'שלל של ביצים' (egg cluster) is pure.
Rav Yosef answers that the baraita is not in accordance with Rabbi Yaakov, who would prohibit attached eggs.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Yaakov's prohibition might only apply to issur (prohibition) but not to tum'ah (impurity).
The Gemara resolves that even if one would consider extending Rabbi Yaakov's stringency to impurity, we do not increase impurity rabbinically.

items.text: Alternative version: the 'אשכול של ביצים' is impure
items.text_en: Alternative version: the 'אשכול של ביצים' is impure
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that the source about impurity from the 'אשכול של ביצים' (cluster of eggs) being impure is in accordance with Rabbi Yaakov. Abaye questions whether 'אשכול' refers to eggs hanging in a cluster or the cluster itself. The Gemara explains that even the cluster itself needs to be taught because some people do not eat it, similar to the gizzard and intestines.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the source about the cluster of eggs (אשכול של ביצים) being impure is in accordance with Rabbi Yaakov, who holds that eggs attached by sinews are forbidden.
Abaye questions whether 'אשכול' (cluster) refers to the eggs hanging in a cluster or the cluster itself (the ovary).
The Gemara explains that even the cluster itself needs to be taught because some people do not eat it, similar to the gizzard and intestines which are meat but require explicit mention.

items.text: Rule of birth based on mating time and application to eggs
items.text_en: Rule of birth based on mating time and application to eggs
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that animals that mate by day give birth by day, those that mate by night give birth by night, and those that mate both give birth both. The Gemara applies this to a chicken (mates by day, lays by day). Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana rules that if one checked a chicken's nest on Yom Tov eve and found no egg, but found one in the morning, it is permitted. The Gemara explains that perhaps the check was not thorough, or the egg had mostly emerged and retracted, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: A baraita establishes the rule that animals mate and give birth at corresponding times, with the chicken mating by day and laying by day.
The Gemara asks what practical halachic application emerges from the baraita's classification of the chicken.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana rules that if one checked a chicken's nest on Yom Tov eve and found no egg, but found one in the morning, the egg is permitted.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by suggesting either the check was not thorough, or the egg had mostly emerged and retracted, in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

items.text: Dispute about checking the nest and resolution
items.text_en: Dispute about checking the nest and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul citing Rav rules that if one checked and found no egg but found one in the morning, it is prohibited. The Gemara resolves that Rav's case is where the chicken laid from the ground (דְּסָפְנָא מֵאַרְעָא), meaning the egg came from outside. Rav Mari's case is where a rooster is present, and Ravina states a tradition that when a rooster is present, the chicken does not lay from the ground. Rav Gammada cites Rav about the extent of this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Mari's lenient ruling by citing Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul citing Rav, who rules that if one checked the nest and found no egg but found one in the morning, it is prohibited.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav's case involves an egg that the chicken absorbed from the ground (דְּסָפְנָא מֵאַרְעָא), not fertilized by a rooster.
The Gemara objects that even in Rav Mari's case, one could say the chicken absorbed the egg from the ground.
The Gemara answers that Rav Mari's case involves a rooster present with the hen.
The Gemara objects that even with a rooster present, the hen might still absorb from the ground.
Ravina states a tradition that wherever a rooster is present, the hen does not absorb from the ground.
The Gemara asks how close the rooster must be for this principle to apply.
Rav Gammada cites Rav regarding the extent of the rooster's proximity needed.

items.text: Case of a bird crossing a boundary
items.text_en: Case of a bird crossing a boundary
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where a bird heard its mate's call and crossed a boundary. Rav Mari acted on this up to sixty houses. The bird does not cross a river or a field, but does cross a path; in one case it crossed a field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where a bird crossed a boundary after hearing its mate's call, and Rav Mari acted on this up to sixty houses, with details about crossing rivers, fields, and paths.

items.text: Gemara's question on the need for inspection
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the need for inspection
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why inspection is necessary if the bird was merely floating from the ground. It answers that without inspection, one might say the bird was there from yesterday; with inspection, one might say it left and returned, following Rabbi Yochanan's principle, which is uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why checking for the bird is relevant if it was hidden from the ground, and argues that even without checking, the same issue arises.

The Gemara answers that without checking, one might say the bird was from yesterday, but with checking, one might invoke Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the bird mostly left and returned, which is uncommon.
The Gemara resolves: the concern follows Rabbi Yochanan's principle, which is uncommon, so inspection is needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's statement on crushed garlic
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's statement on crushed garlic
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul said in the name of Rav that crushed garlic is dangerous for exposure (to the elements).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul quotes Rav that crushed garlic left uncovered is dangerous.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the shiur of se'or
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the shiur of se'or
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai says se'or is prohibited in the size of a kezayit. The Gemara explains their reasoning: since the Torah wrote both chametz and se'or, each has its own shiur. Beit Hillel argues that both are needed, as each teaches a different aspect. Beit Shammai does not accept Rabbi Zeira's teaching that se'or and chametz are the same.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Beit Shammai's ruling that se'or (leavening agent) is prohibited in the size of a kezayit (olive's bulk).

The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Beit Shammai's position, noting that if the Torah had only written chametz, one could infer se'or by a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument), so why was se'or written separately?
The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai holds the Torah wrote se'or to teach that its shiur (measure) is different from chametz — se'or is a kezayit, while chametz is a k'kotevet (size of an egg).
Beit Hillel argues that both terms are necessary: se'or teaches about its stringent leavening, and chametz teaches about its edibility, so each is needed to derive the other's prohibition.
The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai does not accept Rabbi Zeira's teaching that the Torah's use of both terms indicates se'or and chametz are identical in shiur.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute: removal vs. eating
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute: removal vs. eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is about removal (bi'ur), not eating. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that for eating, all agree both are a kezayit. A baraisa supports this, citing the verse and the disagreement between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is only regarding removal (ביעור), not eating, and explains each side's reasoning.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explicitly states that the dispute is about removal, but for eating, all agree both are a kezayit.
A baraita is cited that supports the distinction, quoting the verse and showing the disagreement between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding removal measures.

items.text: Mishnah on slaughtering on Yom Tov and covering blood
items.text_en: Mishnah on slaughtering on Yom Tov and covering blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who slaughters a non-domesticated animal or bird on Yom Tov. The Gemara questions the wording, and Rabba explains that Beit Shammai permits slaughtering and covering, while Beit Hillel requires prepared earth beforehand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who slaughters a non-domesticated animal or bird on Yom Tov.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording, noting that 'one who slaughters' implies after the fact, but the continuation suggests Beit Shammai permits it לכתחילה (a-priori).
The Gemara initially resolves the difficulty by explaining that Beit Hillel's statement 'one may not slaughter' refers to the entire act of slaughtering and covering.
The Gemara objects based on the later clause where Beit Hillel concedes that if one slaughtered, he may dig and cover, proving the first clause is about לכתחילה (a-priori).

Rabba resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the Mishnah: it refers to one who comes to consult, and Beit Shammai says to slaughter, dig, and cover, while Beit Hillel requires prepared earth from before Yom Tov.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation and Abaye's question
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative explanation and Abaye's question
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef offers a different version of the dispute. Abaye asks if they disagree about Rabbi Zeira's teaching. Rav Yosef explains that both accept Rabbi Zeira, but they differ on whether to worry that the person might change his mind or to encourage joy on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef presents his alternative version of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the order of actions for slaughtering on Yom Tov.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether he and Rabba disagree regarding Rabbi Zeira's teaching that one must place dust both below and above the blood.
Abaye clarifies whether the dispute is that Rav Yosef accepts Rabbi Zeira's teaching while Rabba rejects it.

Rav Yosef explains that both he and Rabba accept Rabbi Zeira's teaching, but they disagree about whether to fear that the person might change his mind (Rabba) or to encourage joy on Yom Tov (Rav Yosef).

items.text: Rav Zrika's statement on covering with a knife
items.text_en: Rav Zrika's statement on covering with a knife
items.desc_en: Rav Zrika said in the name of Rav Yehuda that if one slaughtered, he may dig with a knife only if the knife was inserted beforehand. The Gemara raises an objection about creating a cavity, and Rav Chiya bar Ashi answers in the name of Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quotes Rav Yehuda that the ruling applies only if one had a knife stuck in the ground beforehand.
The Gemara objects that this involves pounding (כתישה), which is prohibited on a Festival.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quotes Rav to address the objection, but the text is cut off.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi provides Rav's answer to the objection, though the answer itself is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about making a pit
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about making a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can cover blood with dirt without making a pit, which is prohibited. It answers by citing Rabbi Abba, who says that one who digs a pit on Shabbat only needing its dirt is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can cover blood with 'עפר תיחוח' (loose dirt) without making a pit (גומא), which is prohibited on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers by citing Rabbi Abba's ruling that one who digs a pit on Shabbat only needing its dirt is exempt (פטור).

items.text: Clarification about ash from a stove
items.text_en: Clarification about ash from a stove
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that ash from a stove is considered prepared (muktzah). It then questions who said this, and Rabba explains that the statement means that ash from a stove is prepared.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that ash from a stove is considered prepared (מוכן) for use on Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks who is the authority behind this statement about ash from a stove.
Rabba explains that the statement means that ash from a stove is prepared (מוכן).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's distinction and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's distinction and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the allowance for using ash applies only if the stove was heated before Yom Tov, but if heated on Yom Tov, it is forbidden unless the ash is still hot enough to roast an egg. A baraita supports this distinction.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that the allowance to use stove ash for covering blood applies only if the stove was heated before Yom Tov, but if heated on Yom Tov it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav adds a leniency: if the ash is still hot enough to roast an egg, it is permitted even if the stove was heated on Yom Tov.
A baraita is cited that supports Rav Yehuda's distinction, stating the same rule about stove ash being prepared only if heated before Yom Tov.
The baraita repeats the leniency that if the ash is hot enough to roast an egg, it is permitted.

items.text: Permissibility of using dirt brought into the garden
items.text_en: Permissibility of using dirt brought into the garden
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one brought dirt into his garden or ruin, it may be used for covering. Rav Yehuda adds that one may bring a full basket of dirt and use it for all needs. Mar Zutra qualifies that this applies only if he designated a corner for it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that dirt brought into one's garden or ruin before Yom Tov may be used for covering blood.
Rav Yehuda adds that one may bring a full basket of dirt and use it for all needs.
Mar Zutra qualifies that the leniency applies only if one designated a corner for the dirt.

items.text: Challenge from the law of the koy
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of the koy
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: a koy may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and if slaughtered, its blood is not covered. If dirt is permitted, why not cover with it? The Gemara answers that the case is where one has no dirt, just as one might lack ash or a fixed peg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita: a koy (a doubtful hybrid animal) may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and if slaughtered, its blood is not covered; if dirt is permitted for covering, why not cover with it according to Rav Yehuda's ruling?

The Gemara answers by turning the objection back: according to your reasoning, why not cover with ash from the stove or a fixed peg? The answer is that the case is where one has none of these; here too, the case is where one has no dirt.

items.text: Refinement of the challenge: why mention uncertainty?
items.text_en: Refinement of the challenge: why mention uncertainty?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies a doubtful animal (koy); even a definite animal would be forbidden. It answers that the Mishnah uses a 'need not say' structure: certainly a definite animal should not be slaughtered, but one might think a doubtful one should be slaughtered for joy and not covered, so it teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why the Mishnah specifically mentions a doubtful animal (koy); even a definite animal would be forbidden to slaughter on Yom Tov.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses a 'need not say' structure: certainly a definite animal should not be slaughtered, but one might think a doubtful one should be slaughtered for joy and not covered, so it teaches otherwise.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection from the mishnah's seifa
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection from the mishnah's seifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah's seifa implies the reisha deals with a case where one has ashes, contradicting the assumption that the reisha is about a case without ashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah's seifa implies the reisha deals with a case where one has ashes, contradicting the assumption that the reisha is about a case without ashes.

items.text: Rabbah's answer: Ash is prepared for certain but not for uncertain
items.text_en: Rabbah's answer: Ash is prepared for certain but not for uncertain
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that stove ash is considered prepared for a definite need but not for an uncertain one. The Gemara questions why uncertain is prohibited due to making a hole, and then reframes the reason as a concern for grinding (כתישה), which is overridden by a positive commandment in the certain case. The Gemara then challenges this by comparing to circumcision and tzitzit, but resolves that here the positive act is simultaneous with the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah answers that stove ash is מוכן (prepared) for a definite need but not for an uncertain one.
The Gemara questions why the uncertain case is prohibited, since both certain and uncertain involve making a hole (גומא).
The Gemara reframes the reason according to Rabbi Abba's principle, shifting from the hole concern to a concern for grinding (כתישה).
The Gemara asks why the uncertain case is prohibited due to grinding (כתישה), and why the certain case should not also be prohibited as a decree against grinding.
The Gemara answers that in the certain case, the positive commandment of covering the blood overrides the negative prohibition against grinding.

The objection raises that the principle of a positive commandment overriding a negative one applies only where the positive act is simultaneous with the prohibition, as in circumcision with leprosy or linen with ציצית (ritual fringes).
The resolution explains that here too, the positive act of covering occurs simultaneously with the grinding, so the objection is resolved.

items.text: Objection: Yom Tov is both a positive and negative commandment
items.text_en: Objection: Yom Tov is both a positive and negative commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Yom Tov itself involves both a positive and negative commandment, so a positive commandment cannot override both a negative and positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Yom Tov is both a positive and negative commandment, so a positive commandment cannot override both a negative and positive commandment.

items.text: Rava's answer: Intention determines preparation
items.text_en: Rava's answer: Intention determines preparation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that stove ash is intended for a definite case but not for an uncertain one. He supports this with his own principle: if one brought dirt to cover feces, it may be used for bird blood, but not vice versa. The Gemara records a dispute among Amoraim about whether a koy is like feces, and concludes that Rava holds the koy is like feces.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that stove ash is intended (דעתו) for a definite case but not for an uncertain one, shifting the criterion from physical preparation to mental intention.
The Gemara notes that Rava follows his own principle: dirt brought for covering feces may be used for bird blood, but not vice versa, illustrating intention-based preparation.
The Nehardeans rule more leniently: even dirt brought for bird blood may be used for feces, rejecting Rava's distinction.
The Gemara records a dispute in the West: one Amora says a koy (כוי) is like feces (i.e., its blood requires covering but is uncertain), and another says it is not like feces.
The Gemara concludes that Rava holds the koy is like feces, based on his own ruling about dirt brought for feces versus bird blood.

items.text: Rami bar Rav Yeiva's explanation: A decree due to permitting its fat
items.text_en: Rami bar Rav Yeiva's explanation: A decree due to permitting its fat
items.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yeiva explains that the reason we do not cover the blood of a koy is a decree due to the permission of its fat. The Gemara questions why this would not apply on a weekday, and answers that on a weekday one can say he needs to clear his courtyard. The Gemara further discusses cases of slaughtering in a garbage dump or consulting, and concludes that on a weekday the Sages tell one to trouble himself, but on Yom Tov they do not.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Rav Yeiva explains that the reason we do not cover the blood of a koy is a decree due to the permission of its fat (חלבו).
The Gemara objects: if so, the same decree should apply on a weekday; the answer is that on a weekday one can say he needs to clear his courtyard.
The Gemara raises further cases: slaughtering in a garbage dump or consulting, where the weekday excuse does not apply.
The Gemara resolves: on a weekday the Sages tell one to trouble himself and cover it, but on Yom Tov they do not.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's baraita: Mixed bloods are prohibited on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's baraita: Mixed bloods are prohibited on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira teaches that not only a koy, but even if one slaughtered a domesticated animal, wild animal, and bird and their bloods mixed, it is prohibited to cover on Yom Tov. Rabbi Yosei bar Yasinia qualifies that this is only if one cannot cover with one stab, but if possible, it is permitted. The Gemara notes that this is obvious, but the teaching is to prevent a decree of one stab due to two stabs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira teaches a baraita that not only a koy, but even if one slaughtered a domesticated animal, wild animal, and bird and their bloods mixed, it is prohibited to cover the blood on Yom Tov.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yasinia qualifies that the prohibition applies only if one cannot cover the blood with a single stab, but if possible with one stab, it is permitted.
The Gemara notes that this qualification is obvious, but the baraita teaches it to prevent a decree that one stab might be prohibited due to concern for two stabs.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling: Bird slaughtered before Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: Bird slaughtered before Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one slaughtered a bird on the eve of Yom Tov, one may not cover its blood on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one slaughtered a bird on the eve of Yom Tov, one may not cover its blood on Yom Tov.

items.text: Dispute about separating challah on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute about separating challah on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one prepared dough before Yom Tov, one may separate its challah on Yom Tov. The father of Shmuel disagrees and prohibits this. The Gemara questions whether Shmuel's own ruling about challah outside the Land contradicts his father, and Rava resolves that Shmuel would agree that once a name is called upon it, it is forbidden to non-priests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one prepared dough before Yom Tov, one may separate its challah on Yom Tov.
The father of Shmuel disagrees and prohibits separating challah on Yom Tov even if the dough was prepared beforehand.
