The Gemara questions whether Shmuel's own ruling about challah outside the Land contradicts his father's position.
Rava resolves that Shmuel would agree that once a name is called upon it, it is forbidden to non-priests, thus reconciling the positions.

items.text: Mishnah: Carrying a ladder on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Carrying a ladder on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding carrying a ladder from one dovecote to another on Yom Tov. Beit Shammai prohibits it but allows tilting it from one window to another, while Beit Hillel permits it entirely.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding carrying a ladder from one dovecote to another on Yom Tov.

items.text: First version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's explanation
items.text_en: First version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami explains that the dispute is specifically in a public domain, where Beit Shammai is concerned that an onlooker might think the ladder is for plastering a roof, while Beit Hillel says the dovecote itself indicates the purpose. In a private domain, all agree it is permitted. The Gemara objects based on Rav Yehuda's statement that wherever the Sages prohibited due to mar'it ha'ayin, it is forbidden even in inner rooms, and resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami explains that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about carrying a ladder on Yom Tov is limited to a public domain, where Beit Shammai fears mar'it ha'ayin (appearance of wrongdoing) and Beit Hillel relies on the dovecote as evidence of permitted use; in a private domain, all agree it is permitted.

The Gemara objects that Rav Yehuda quoting Rav ruled that wherever the Sages prohibited due to mar'it ha'ayin, it is forbidden even in inner rooms, contradicting Rav Chanan bar Ami's allowance in a private domain.

The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im, citing a baraita where the Tanna Kamma permits spreading garments in the sun but not in public, while Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon forbid it even in private, showing that some Tanna'im do not apply the principle of mar'it ha'ayin in private domains.

items.text: Second version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's explanation
items.text_en: Second version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's explanation
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that the dispute is in a private domain, where Beit Shammai holds like Rav Yehuda's principle of mar'it ha'ayin, while Beit Hillel does not. In a public domain, all agree it is forbidden. The Gemara questions whether Rav holds like Beit Shammai, and resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im, citing the same baraitha about spreading garments.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Chanan bar Ami's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the dispute is in a private domain, where Beit Shammai holds like Rav Yehuda's principle of mar'it ha'ayin, while Beit Hillel does not.
It concludes that in a public domain, all agree it is forbidden.
The Gemara questions whether Rav holds like Beit Shammai.
The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im, citing the same baraitha about spreading garments.

items.text: Baraita on ladder and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Baraita on ladder and dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a ladder may be carried from dovecote to dovecote on Yom Tov, but disagree about returning it. Rabbi Yehuda limits the dispute to a dovecote ladder, while Rabbi Dosa allows moving it from window to window, and others permit even dragging it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree a ladder may be taken from dovecote to dovecote on Yom Tov, but disagree about returning it.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the dispute to a dovecote ladder, but for an attic ladder all agree it is forbidden to move.
Rabbi Dosa permits moving the ladder from window to window.
Acherim in the name of Rabbi Dosa permit even dragging the ladder.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and their mistake
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and their mistake
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya's sons permitted a ladder they encountered, but their father rebuked them. They mistakenly thought that since Rabbi Yehuda said there is no dispute about an attic ladder, the first tanna must hold there is a dispute, but in reality Rabbi Yehuda was merely explaining the first tanna's position.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rabbi Chiyya's sons went to a village, and upon returning, their father asked if anything happened; they reported that a ladder came before them and they permitted it.
Rabbi Chiyya rebukes his sons, telling them to go and forbid what they permitted.

The Gemara explains the sons' mistaken reasoning: they thought that since Rabbi Yehuda said there is no dispute about an attic ladder, the first tanna must hold there is a dispute, but in reality Rabbi Yehuda was merely explaining the first tanna's position.

items.text: Proof that the first tanna only permits a dovecote ladder
items.text_en: Proof that the first tanna only permits a dovecote ladder
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves from the baraita's wording that the first tanna only permits a dovecote ladder, not an attic ladder. The alternative view argues that the phrase 'from dovecote to dovecote' implies even multiple dovecotes, not a limitation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we know this? From the fact that the baraita teaches 'they may carry the ladder from dovecote to dovecote' — implying only a dovecote ladder, not an attic ladder.

The Gemara argues: If you thought the first tanna disputed about an attic ladder, the baraita should have said 'they may carry the ladder to a dovecote'; instead it says 'from dovecote to dovecote', proving it permits only a dovecote ladder, not an attic ladder.
The alternative view objects: Does the baraita say 'a dovecote ladder'? It says 'from dovecote to dovecote', implying even multiple dovecotes, not a limitation.

items.text: Alternative version of the story with an attic ladder
items.text_en: Alternative version of the story with an attic ladder
items.desc_en: An alternative version reports that the sons permitted an attic ladder, but their father rebuked them. They mistakenly thought Rabbi Dosa permits what the first tanna forbids, but in reality Rabbi Dosa forbids what the first tanna permits.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that the sons told their father they had permitted an attic ladder, and he rebuked them to reverse their ruling.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the sons' mistake
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the sons' mistake
sub.desc_en: The sons mistakenly thought that Rabbi Dosa permits what the first tanna forbids.
The gemara corrects that in reality Rabbi Dosa forbids what the first tanna permits.

items.text: Inference that Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient regarding simchat Yom Tov
items.text_en: Inference that Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient regarding simchat Yom Tov
items.desc_en: From the baraita, the Gemara infers that regarding simchat Yom Tov, Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that regarding simchat Yom Tov, Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient.

items.text: Contradiction from the slaughtering baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from the slaughtering baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about slaughtering on Yom Tov where Beit Shammai are lenient and Beit Hillel stringent. Rabbi Yochanan says the positions are reversed, but the Gemara suggests possible distinctions: Beit Shammai's leniency only applies when a knife is stuck in the ground, and Beit Hillel's stringency only applies when the dovecote indicates the bird is prepared.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about slaughtering a wild animal or bird on Yom Tov, where Beit Shammai permit covering the blood with a dagger and Beit Hillel require prepared earth.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by stating that the positions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are reversed in the slaughtering baraita.
The Gemara suggests that Beit Shammai's leniency in the slaughtering baraita may be limited to a case where a dagger is stuck in the ground, not a general reversal.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that Beit Hillel's stringency in the dovecote case may be limited to where the dovecote indicates the bird is prepared, unlike the slaughtering case.

items.text: Another contradiction from the taking of birds and its resolution
items.text_en: Another contradiction from the taking of birds and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction from a baraita about taking birds on Yom Tov where Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient, consistent with the earlier inference. Rabbi Yochanan again says the positions are reversed, but the Gemara suggests that Beit Shammai's leniency in the slaughtering case only applies when a knife is stuck in the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about taking birds on Yom Tov, where Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient, which conflicts with the earlier inference about their positions in the slaughtering case.
Rabbi Yochanan again asserts that the positions are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה) to resolve the contradiction.
The Gemara rejects the need for reversal, suggesting that Beit Shammai's leniency in the slaughtering case only applies when a knife is stuck in the ground (דקר נעוץ).

items.text: Rejection of previous resolution
items.text_en: Rejection of previous resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier attempt to reconcile Beit Hillel's leniency here with their stringency elsewhere, arguing that the distinction of a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or the status of מוקצה does not apply to the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier resolution, arguing that without a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or where מוקצה applies, the leniency does not extend to the other case.

items.text: First contradiction and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.text_en: First contradiction and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Beit Shammai are lenient about taking a chopping block (עלי) on Yom Tov, but stringent about slaughtering a non-domesticated animal; Beit Hillel are the opposite. Rabbi Yochanan says the positions are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new contradiction: Beit Shammai are lenient about taking a hide for meat on Yom Tov, but stringent about slaughtering, while Beit Hillel are lenient about slaughtering but stringent about the hide.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the positions of the schools are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה) in the two Mishnayot.

items.text: Challenge to the first answer
items.text_en: Challenge to the first answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's answer, suggesting that the contradiction can be resolved by distinguishing between cases with or without a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or by the utensil status of the item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the contradiction can be resolved without reversing the schools, by distinguishing between cases with or without a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or between cases where the item has the status of a vessel (תורת כלי).

items.text: Second contradiction and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.text_en: Second contradiction and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction regarding placing a hide before a tanner (דורסן) on Yom Tov. Again, Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient, contradicting the slaughter ruling. Rabbi Yochanan again says the positions are reversed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Beit Shammai forbid placing a hide before a tanner (דורסן) on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit it, yet in the slaughter ruling Beit Shammai are lenient and Beit Hillel stringent.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the positions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in the slaughter ruling are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה).

items.text: Challenge to the second answer
items.text_en: Challenge to the second answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges this answer as well, suggesting that the contradiction can be resolved by the presence or absence of a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or by whether the hide is fit for sitting upon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the contradiction can be resolved by distinguishing between cases with or without a fixed peg (דקר נעוץ) or between cases where the hide is fit for reclining (חזי למזגא עלויה).

items.text: Third contradiction and final resolution
items.text_en: Third contradiction and final resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a third contradiction about removing shutters (תריסין) on Yom Tov. Beit Shammai prohibit, Beit Hillel permit. The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai's rulings are consistent (distinguishing by the presence of a fixed peg), but Beit Hillel's are contradictory. Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the positions are reversed, or alternatively, that Beit Hillel's leniency here is because there is no building or demolition in vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a third contradiction: Beit Shammai prohibit removing shutters (תריסין) on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit even returning them, which seems to reverse their usual lenient stance regarding Yom Tov joy.
The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai's rulings are consistent (distinguishing by the presence of a fixed peg), but Beit Hillel's rulings are contradictory.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the positions are reversed, or alternatively, that Beit Hillel's leniency here is because there is no building or demolition in vessels (אין בנין בכלים ואין סתירה בכלים).

items.text: Mishnah: Taking from a stack
items.text_en: Mishnah: Taking from a stack
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Beit Shammai say one may only take utensils from a stack if they were moved (נענע) before Yom Tov; Beit Hillel say one may simply declare 'this and that I will take.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: Beit Shammai say one may only take birds from the dovecote if he shook them before Yom Tov; Beit Hillel say he may stand and say 'this and that I will take.'

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah and the principle of ברירה
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah and the principle of ברירה
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami explains that the dispute applies only to the first pool (בריכה ראשונה) where Beit Shammai fear one might come to deliberate; for the second pool, all agree that declaring 'this and that I will take' suffices. The Gemara then questions why Beit Hillel require a verbal declaration, and discusses the principle of ברירה (retroactive selection) with a baraita about a corpse in a house, citing Rabba, Rabbi Oshaya, and Rava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami explains that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies only to the first pool, where Beit Shammai fear one might come to deliberate, while Beit Hillel do not.
Rav Chanan bar Ami adds that for the second pool, all agree that declaring 'this and that I will take' suffices.
The Gemara questions why Beit Hillel require a verbal declaration, asking why simply saying 'from here I will take tomorrow' is insufficient.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a corpse in a house with many openings, showing that Beit Hillel reject the principle of ברירה (retroactive selection).
The baraita records the dispute: Beit Shammai require intent before death, while Beit Hillel permit intent even after death.
Rabba and Rabbi Oshaya explain that the baraita's ruling applies only prospectively (מכאן ולהבא), not retroactively (למפרע), thus rejecting ברירה.
Rava objects, arguing that the baraita actually applies retroactively, and the reason Beit Hillel require intent is to prevent moving items that are not fit for use.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by noting that the declaration 'this and that I will take' suffices only when made before Yom Tov (מערב יום טוב).

items.text: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's Gemara
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's Gemara
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why on Yom Tov it is forbidden to slaughter a bird found in a nest, unlike on a weekday, due to the concern that one might come to handle something not permitted or refrain from rejoicing on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that on Yom Tov it is forbidden to slaughter a bird found in a nest, because one might come to handle something not permitted or refrain from rejoicing on Yom Tov.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for finding different birds
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for finding different birds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one designated black birds and found white, or vice versa, or designated two and found three, they are forbidden. If one designated three and found two, they are permitted. If one found birds within the nest but before the nest, they are forbidden unless there are no others there.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule: if one designated black birds and found white, or vice versa, or two and found three, they are forbidden; if three and found two, they are permitted.
The Mishnah adds: if one found birds within the nest but before the nest, they are forbidden, unless there are no others there, in which case they are permitted.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the first case: designated black and found white
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the first case: designated black and found white
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Mishnah's case is where one designated both black and white birds, and in the morning found black where white were and white where black were. The Mishnah teaches that these are different birds, not merely the same ones that switched places. This supports Rabbi Chanina's principle that we follow the majority over proximity, but Abaye limits this to a case where the birds are on a board.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling is not obvious, since finding different birds than designated should clearly be forbidden.

Rabbah explains that the Mishnah's case is where one designated both black and white birds, and in the morning found black where white were and white where black were, teaching that these are different birds, not merely the same ones that switched places.
The Gemara suggests that Rabbah's explanation supports Rabbi Chanina's principle that we follow the majority (רוב) over proximity (קרוב).
Abaye limits the application of Rabbi Chanina's principle to a case where the birds are on a board (דף), implying that proximity is considered only in certain contexts.

items.text: Analysis of the cases: two found three, and three found two
items.text_en: Analysis of the cases: two found three, and three found two
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one designated two and found three, they are forbidden because either they are different birds or one is mixed in. If one designated three and found two, they are permitted because the two are the original ones and one flew away.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one designated two birds and found three, they are forbidden, analyzing that either they are different birds or one is mixed in.
The Gemara explains that if one designated three and found two, they are permitted because the two are the original ones and one flew away.

items.text: Attempt to identify the Mishnah with Rabbi's opinion
items.text_en: Attempt to identify the Mishnah with Rabbi's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling (two found three forbidden, three found two permitted) aligns with Rabbi's view in a Tannaitic dispute about money: if one left 100 and found 200, it is mixed; if one left 200 and found 100, it is a separate 100. The Sages disagree, saying all is non-sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi's view, not the Sages, citing a baraita about money.
The baraita presents Rabbi's ruling: if one left 100 and found 200, it is a mixture of non-sacred and second-tithe money.
The baraita records the Sages' dissenting view: all is non-sacred money.
The baraita continues with Rabbi's ruling for the reverse case: if one left 200 and found 100, it is a separate 100 left behind.
The baraita records the Sages' dissenting view in the second case: all is non-sacred money.

items.text: Rejection and resolution: the case of fledglings
items.text_en: Rejection and resolution: the case of fledglings
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the identification, noting that even according to the Sages, the Mishnah can be explained because fledglings are different as they are prone to hop away. Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves tied fledglings and tied purses: fledglings can become untied from each other, but purses do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the identification of the Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, noting that even according to the Sages, the Mishnah can be explained because fledglings are different as they are prone to hop away.
The Gemara questions why a special answer is needed for fledglings, given that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar already disagree about the scope of the dispute regarding money pouches.
The Gemara objects that according to the opinion that the dispute is about one pouch, with two pouches everyone agrees, the special answer for fledglings is unnecessary.
Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves tied fledglings and tied purses: fledglings can become untied from each other, but purses do not.

sub.text: Gemara's question to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.text_en: Gemara's question to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would say in response, noting that even purses can sometimes become untied.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion on bird nests
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion on bird nests
items.desc_en: This segment concludes the previous discussion about birds found in a nest, stating that if their knots are worn away, they are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that if the knots of the birds are worn away, they are permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Chanina's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Chanina's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about birds found before the nest supports Rabbi Chanina's principle that we follow the majority over proximity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about birds found before the nest supports Rabbi Chanina's principle that we follow the majority over proximity.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's explanations of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's explanations of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava offer different interpretations of the Mishnah's case, involving a board or two nests one above the other, explaining when birds are forbidden or permitted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains the Mishnah's case as involving a board (דף) that birds perch on, resolving the difficulty about proximity.
Rava explains the Mishnah as dealing with two nests one above the other, where birds from one nest may have descended into the other.
Rava extends his explanation to the reverse case, where birds from the lower nest may have climbed up to the upper nest.
The Gemara clarifies that if only those birds are present, they are permitted, because otherwise they would be assumed to be different birds.

items.text: Discussion of hopping birds and Mar Ukva's rule
items.text_en: Discussion of hopping birds and Mar Ukva's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the case of hopping birds, invoking Mar Ukva's principle that a bird does not hop more than fifty amot, and discusses a corner case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves hopping birds (מדדין), not flying ones.
The Gemara asks: if there is a nest within fifty amot, the bird could have hopped from there; if not, the birds are clearly permitted.
The Gemara cites Mar Ukva bar Chama's principle that a hopping bird does not hop more than fifty amot.
The Gemara resolves: the case is where a nest exists within fifty amot but around a corner, and the bird only hops if it can see its nest; otherwise it does not hop.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on using tools
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on using tools
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding taking a butcher's block to cut meat and placing hide before a tanner on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding taking a butcher's block to cut meat on it, and regarding placing the hide before a treader.
The Mishnah continues with Beit Shammai forbidding and Beit Hillel permitting placing hide before a tanner (דורסן) on Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara on the butcher's block and Abaye's statements
items.text_en: Gemara on the butcher's block and Abaye's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a Tosefta where both schools agree, and Abaye clarifies the dispute is only about the block, not bones, with two versions of his statement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that both schools agree that if one already cut meat on the pestle, it is prohibited to move it.
Abaye clarifies that the dispute applies only to a pestle, but for a wooden anvil used for breaking bones, everyone agrees it is permitted.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, since the mishna explicitly mentions a pestle.
The Gemara explains that Abaye's statement is necessary lest one think the dispute applies even to a bone-breaking anvil, and the mishna's mention of a pestle is only to show Beit Hillel's leniency.
An alternative version states that Abaye said the statement is necessary only for a new bone-breaking anvil, lest one think the owner might reconsider and not break bones on it.

items.text: Beit Shammai's concern for reconsideration
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's concern for reconsideration
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai is concerned about reconsideration, citing a baraita about not bringing a knife to an animal, and distinguishes the case of the block.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai is concerned about reconsideration, citing a baraita where Beit Shammai prohibits leading a butcher and knife to an animal, and Beit Hillel permits it.
The baraita adds that Beit Shammai also prohibits bringing spices and a pestle to a mortar, while Beit Hillel permits it, showing Beit Shammai's general concern for reconsideration.

The Gemara rejects the comparison, distinguishing that in the case of an animal or pot one might reconsider, but with a block for breaking bones, since the animal is already slaughtered, the bones must be broken, so no reconsideration is possible.

items.text: Discussion of salting meat on hide
items.text_en: Discussion of salting meat on hide
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta that both schools agree one may salt meat on hide for roasting, and Abaye limits this to roasting, not for a pot.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that both schools agree one may salt meat on the hide for roasting, and Abaye limits this to roasting but not for a pot.
The gemara resolves that Abaye's statement teaches that even for roasting, if done in a pot-like manner it is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that the Tosefta explicitly states 'for roasting', so Abaye's limitation seems obvious.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye's statement teaches that even for roasting, if done in a pot-like manner, it is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute about handling hides and Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion
items.text_en: Dispute about handling hides and Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about not salting or turning hides, with Rabbi Yehoshua permitting spreading them on pegs. Rav Matna's ruling is debated, and a question compares this to the earlier case of hide before a tanner.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one may not salt or turn hides on Yom Tov, but Rabbi Yehoshua permits spreading them on pegs in the wind.
Rav Matna rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehoshua's lenient opinion.
An alternative version reports that Rav Matna ruled the הלכה (binding law) does NOT follow Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.text: Gemara's justification for the first version
sub.text_en: Gemara's justification for the first version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first version is necessary: one might have thought the majority opinion prevails, so Rav Matna teaches that the הלכה (binding law) follows the individual (Rabbi Yehoshua).

sub.text: Gemara's justification for the second version
sub.text_en: Gemara's justification for the second version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second version is also necessary: one might have thought Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning is compelling (to prevent people from refraining from slaughter), so Rav Matna teaches that the הלכה (binding law) still follows the majority.
The Gemara asks: what is the difference between this case (hides) and the earlier case of 'עור לפני הדורסן' (a hide before a tanner), where the Sages were more lenient?

items.text: Salting meat on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Salting meat on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says one may salt multiple pieces of meat at once even if only one is needed, and Rav Ada bar Ahava adds that one may even salt each piece individually. The Gemara questions whether this contradicts the earlier ruling about not salting on Yom Tov, and resolves that the earlier case involved a different type of salting.

items.text: Mishnah: Shammai and Hillel on shutters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shammai and Hillel on shutters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai forbids removing shutters on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permits even returning them.

items.text: Gemara: What are shutters?
items.text_en: Gemara: What are shutters?
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that 'terisin' refers to shutters of shops. He then lists three things permitted for their end due to their beginning: hide before a tanner, shop shutters, and returning a bandage in the Temple.

items.text: Rav Yehuda adds opening a barrel
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda adds opening a barrel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may also open a barrel and begin kneading dough on the foot, and this is permitted because the end is allowed for the sake of the beginning.

items.text: Aliba of Rabbi Yehuda: must finish
items.text_en: Aliba of Rabbi Yehuda: must finish
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yehuda's view, one must finish the action once started, implying the end is inherently tied to the beginning.

items.text: Hide before tanner: Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.text_en: Hide before tanner: Beit Hillel's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Beit Hillel's permit for hide before a tanner: because it appears ready for tanning, and even on Yom Tov eve it is permitted, teaching that the end is permitted for the beginning's sake — Yom Tov yes, eve no.

items.text: Shutter shops: Beit Hillel permits return
items.text_en: Shutter shops: Beit Hillel permits return
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Beit Hillel permits returning shutters, implying that the end is permitted for the beginning's sake — shops yes, houses no.

items.text: Returning bandage in Temple: permitted
items.text_en: Returning bandage in Temple: permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that one may return a bandage in the Temple but not in the province, teaching that the end is permitted for the beginning's sake — for service work yes, for non-service no.

items.text: Opening barrel: Mishnah dispute
items.text_en: Opening barrel: Mishnah dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one must finish opening the barrel and kneading, while Sages say one need not finish. The Gemara infers that the Sages permit the end for the beginning's sake — if started, finish; if not started, don't.

items.text: Ulla's question: why not say like this?
items.text_en: Ulla's question: why not say like this?
items.desc_en: Ulla asks why the Gemara didn't present the dispute as between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, noting that Beit Shammai's position is akin to Rabbi Yehuda's (must finish), and Beit Hillel's to the Sages (may stop). The answer: because the Mishnah's dispute is not identical to that between the schools.

items.text: Alternative Tanna: shutters with and without hinges
items.text_en: Alternative Tanna: shutters with and without hinges
items.desc_en: A different Tanna (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar) states that both schools agree on removing shutters on Yom Tov, and dispute only about returning them — with hinges permitted, without hinges forbidden. Abaye clarifies: with side hinges all forbid, without any hinges all permit, and the dispute is about central hinges.

items.text: Abaye's clarification on hinges
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification on hinges
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction: the earlier Tosefta said all forbid when there are side hinges, and all permit when no hinges; the dispute is only about central hinges. This aligns with the alternative Tanna's ruling.

items.text: Opening dispute about the principle of 'mitoch'
items.text_en: Opening dispute about the principle of 'mitoch'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two Sages (Mar) regarding whether we decree against a side attachment (ציר מן הצד) because of a middle attachment (ציר באמצע). One Sage holds we do decree, the other holds we do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two anonymous Sages (Mar) regarding whether we decree against a side attachment (ציר מן הצד) because of a middle attachment (ציר באמצע).

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on carrying on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on carrying on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai prohibit taking out a child, a lulav, or a Torah scroll to the public domain on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai prohibit taking out a child, a lulav, or a Torah scroll to the public domain on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit it.

items.text: Gemara's first explanation: dispute over 'mitoch'
items.text_en: Gemara's first explanation: dispute over 'mitoch'
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi that one who slaughters a free-will burnt-offering on Yom Tov is liable. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains that this follows Beit Shammai, who do not apply the principle of 'mitoch' (since carrying was permitted for need, it is permitted even without need). Beit Hillel, who do apply 'mitoch', would permit slaughtering such an offering.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi a baraita stating that one who slaughters a free-will burnt-offering on Yom Tov is liable to lashes.

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains that the baraita follows Beit Shammai, who reject the principle of 'mitoch' (since carrying was permitted for need, it is permitted even without need), whereas Beit Hillel, who apply 'mitoch', would permit slaughtering such an offering.

items.text: Rabbah's objection: alternative explanation about eiruv
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection: alternative explanation about eiruv
items.desc_en: Rabbah challenges the assumption that the dispute is about 'mitoch'. He suggests that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel might instead be arguing about whether eiruv applies to carrying on Shabbat and Yom Tov. One Sage holds that eiruv applies to both, while the other holds it applies only to Shabbat, based on the verse 'You shall not carry burdens from your houses on the Sabbath day'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects to the assumption that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the 'mitoch' principle, suggesting they might instead argue about whether eiruv applies to carrying on Shabbat and Yom Tov.
One Sage holds that eiruv applies to carrying on both Shabbat and Yom Tov.
The other Sage holds that eiruv applies to carrying on Shabbat but not on Yom Tov, citing the verse 'You shall not carry burdens from your houses on the Sabbath day'.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection: proof from stones
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection: proof from stones
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: if the dispute were about eiruv, they would also argue about stones (which are not subject to eiruv). Since they do not argue about stones, it must be that the dispute is indeed about carrying without need (הוֹצָאָה שֶׁלֹּא לְצוֹרֶךְ).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: if the dispute were about eiruv, they would also argue about stones (which are not subject to eiruv); since they do not, it must be about carrying without need.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is indeed about carrying without need (הוֹצָאָה שֶׁלֹּא לְצוֹרֶךְ).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's support: the case of cooking the sciatic nerve
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's support: the case of cooking the sciatic nerve
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan also holds that the dispute is about the principle of 'mitoch'. A Tanna taught before him that one who cooks the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) in milk on Yom Tov and eats it is liable for five lashes: for cooking the nerve, eating the nerve, cooking meat in milk, eating meat in milk, and for cooking on Yom Tov (since it is not for need). This supports the view that Beit Shammai do not apply 'mitoch'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan also holds that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is about the principle of 'mitoch' (since carrying was permitted for need, it is also permitted without need).
A Tanna recited before Rabbi Yochanan a baraita: one who cooks the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) in milk on Yom Tov and eats it is liable for five lashes.

The Gemara explains the five lashes: for cooking the nerve, eating the nerve, cooking meat in milk, eating meat in milk, and for cooking on Yom Tov (since it is not for need), thereby supporting that Beit Shammai do not apply 'mitoch'.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the Mishnah's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the Mishnah's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about carrying a knife on Yom Tov, suggesting that the principle of 'since it was permitted for need, it is also permitted for no need' might apply to kindling as well. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Beit Shammai, who reject this principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah's ruling is due to the prohibition of kindling a fire on a Festival.

רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) tells the tanna to teach the baraita outside, explaining that the prohibition of kindling and cooking is not a valid mishna; if it were, it follows בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) who reject the principle that permission for need extends to no need.

The Gemara explains that if the baraita followed בית הלל (Beit Hillel), they would apply the principle that since kindling was permitted for need, it is also permitted for no need, contradicting the baraita's ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about carrying challah and gifts to the priest
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about carrying challah and gifts to the priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding whether one may carry challah and other priestly gifts to the priest on Yom Tov. Beit Shammai prohibits it via a gezerah shavah with terumah, while Beit Hillel permits it because one is entitled to separate these gifts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute: Beit Shammai prohibits carrying חלה (challah) and other priestly gifts to the priest on יום טוב (festival day), while Beit Hillel permits it.
Beit Shammai argues via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as one may not carry תרומה (priestly portion) to the priest, so too one may not carry the other gifts.
Beit Hillel rejects the analogy: terumah cannot be separated on Yom Tov, but these gifts may be separated, so carrying them is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption about the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption about the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes the Mishnah refers to gifts separated on Yom Tov itself, and questions which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is neither Rabbi Yosei nor Rabbi Yehuda but Acheirim, based on a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes the Mishnah refers to both cases where the gifts were separated today or yesterday, and questions which Tanna's view it follows.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's view that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only dispute about carrying the gifts alone, not when combined with fresh gifts.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is neither Rabbi Yosei nor Rabbi Yehuda, but rather Acheirim.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only dispute about gifts separated on Yom Tov themselves, not about those from the previous day, which all agree may be brought.

items.text: Baraita according to Rabbi Yehuda's version
items.text_en: Baraita according to Rabbi Yehuda's version
items.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's version of the dispute, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only disagree about carrying gifts that were separated on Yom Tov itself, but agree that gifts separated before Yom Tov may be carried together with those separated on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The baraita repeats Beit Shammai's argument and Beit Hillel's response in the context of Rabbi Yehuda's version.

items.text: Baraita according to Rabbi Yosei's version
items.text_en: Baraita according to Rabbi Yosei's version
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei's version states that the dispute is only about terumah, not about other gifts, with Beit Hillel permitting carrying terumah and Beit Shammai prohibiting it, using a different kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that the dispute is only about תרומה (priestly portion), not about other gifts, and presents Beit Hillel's reasoning.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Acheirim's version matches the Mishnah's assumption, and then Rava reinterprets the Mishnah to refer only to gifts separated on Yom Tov but slaughtered before Yom Tov, reconciling it with Rabbi Yehuda. The difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Acheirim is the status of the 'accompanying' gifts (tefeilah).

sub.desc_en: Acheirim states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only disagree about gifts (מתנות), not about תרומה (priestly portion), which all agree may not be brought.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that gifts separated on Yom Tov may not be brought aligns only with Acheirim and not with Rabbi Yehuda.
Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: it only says 'separated' (הורמו) on Yom Tov, but the slaughter was before Yom Tov, so the Mishnah can even be Acheirim, referring to gifts slaughtered before Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah refers to gifts slaughtered before Yom Tov, then it matches Rabbi Yehuda's position — so what distinguishes Acheirim from Rabbi Yehuda?

The Gemara resolves: the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Acheirim is the status of the 'accompanying' gifts (טפלה) — whether gifts separated on Yom Tov may be brought together with those separated before Yom Tov.

items.text: Practical ruling and a case of mustard stalks
items.text_en: Practical ruling and a case of mustard stalks
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei. A story is told about Rav Tovi who had a skin of terumah wine and asked Rav Yosef whether he could bring it to a priest on Yom Tov, and Rav Yosef ruled accordingly. Then a story about Rava bar Rav Chanan's host who had mustard stalks and asked Rava whether he could crush and eat them on Yom Tov, and Rava permitted it.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Story about Rav Tovi and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Tovi and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: A story is told: Rav Tovi had a skin of terumah wine and asked Rav Yosef whether he could bring it to a priest on Yom Tov, and Rav Yosef ruled accordingly, citing the same principle.

sub.text: Story about Rava bar Rav Chanan's host and Rava
sub.text_en: Story about Rava bar Rav Chanan's host and Rava
sub.desc_en: A second story: the host of Rava bar Rav Chanan had mustard stalks and asked Rava whether he could crush and eat them on Yom Tov, and Rava permitted it, citing the general rule that one may rub ears of grain and crumble legumes on Yom Tov.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding preparing food on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding preparing food on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's ruling by citing a baraita that distinguishes between Erev Shabbat and Erev Yom Tov, implying that on Yom Tov itself one may not crush stalks. The Gemara resolves that the baraita's language is due to the parallel with Shabbat, and then addresses a potential contradiction with the Mishnah's reasoning about terumah, concluding that there is no difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's ruling by citing a baraita that permits crushing stalks on Erev Shabbat and Erev Yom Tov but implies that on Yom Tov itself it is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the baraita's mention of Erev Yom Tov is merely due to the parallel with Erev Shabbat, and it actually permits crushing on Yom Tov itself.

The Gemara questions how the baraita can permit crushing on Yom Tov, since that would imply that one is entitled (זַכַּאי) to separate תרומה (priestly portion) on Yom Tov, contradicting the Mishnah's reasoning that one is not entitled.
The Gemara resolves that there is no difficulty, implying that the crushing is permitted only for immediate consumption and not for separating תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi vs. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda on stalks
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi vs. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda on stalks
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree about whether one who brings in stalks to make dough may eat them casually (arai) and be exempt from tithes, and whether one who intends to rub them out (lemol'lan bimlilot) is liable or exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda disagree about stalks brought in for dough: eating them casually (עראי) exempts from tithes.
The baraita states that when one intends to rub out the stalks (למוללן במלילות), Rabbi holds him liable for tithes while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda exempts him.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: case where even Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda agrees
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: case where even Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda agrees
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda would agree in a case where one brought in stalks for dough and then changed his mind to rub them out on Yom Tov, because the tevel status applies on that day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda agrees in a case where one brought in stalks for dough and then changed his mind to rub them out on Yom Tov, because the tevel status applies on that day.

items.text: Gemara's reinterpretation: 'terumah' means majority of terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's reinterpretation: 'terumah' means majority of terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the term 'terumah' in the Mishnah refers to the majority of terumah, not all of it, to resolve the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by reinterpreting 'terumah' in the Mishnah as referring to the majority of terumah (רוב תרומה), not all of it.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: stalks vs. legumes
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: stalks vs. legumes
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda applies only to stalks, but regarding legumes, everyone agrees that they are forbidden as tevel.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the earlier dispute by distinguishing between stalks, where the Tannaim disagree, and legumes, where all agree they are forbidden as tevel (untithed produce).

items.text: Supporting baraita and analysis: fenugreek bundles
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and analysis: fenugreek bundles
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Abaye's view with a baraita about fenugreek bundles of tevel, where one separates tithes only on the seeds, not the wood. The Gemara analyzes whether this supports Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi, and concludes that fenugreek is a special case because its wood and fruit taste alike.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about fenugreek bundles of tevel, where one separates tithes only on the seeds, not the wood, and suggests it supports Abaye's view that legumes are exempt from tithe liability.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that untithed produce (טבל) is not subject to tithe liability in certain cases.
The Gemara rejects the identification, arguing the baraita follows Rabbi, and objects that if so, the same rule should apply to all produce, not just fenugreek.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita followed Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, it should have mentioned other legumes, not just fenugreek.
The Gemara resolves that fenugreek is a special case because its wood and fruit taste alike, so the baraita teaches that one does not separate tithes on the wood despite the similar taste.

items.text: Alternative version of Abaye's statement and objection
items.text_en: Alternative version of Abaye's statement and objection
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Abaye said the dispute is only about stalks, but regarding legumes, everyone agrees they are not tevel. An objection is raised from the fenugreek baraita, which is resolved by interpreting the tevel as terumat ma'aser, following Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Abaye said the dispute is only about stalks, but regarding legumes, everyone agrees they are not tevel.
The gemara raises an objection from the baraita about fenugreek bundles, which implies that the tevel is terumah tevel, contradicting Abaye's statement.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Avahu and Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Avahu and Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves the objection by interpreting the tevel as terumat ma'aser, following Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish, who said that first tithe which was taken while still in stalks is designated for terumat ma'aser.

items.text: Rava's explanation and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rava's explanation and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the requirement to crush the fenugreek is a penalty (kenasa), and a baraita supports this by describing how a Levite who receives stalks as his tithe must process them and separate terumat ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita requires crushing fenugreek, arguing the Levite could simply give the stalks as-is.
Rava answers that the crushing requirement is a penalty (קנסא) to prevent the Levite from delaying tithe separation.
A baraita supports Rava by describing how a Levite who receives stalks as his tithe must process them into grain before separating תרומת מעשר (the priestly portion from the tithe).

items.text: Terumat Maaser taken by estimation and thought
items.text_en: Terumat Maaser taken by estimation and thought
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether terumat maaser can be taken by estimation and thought, as implied by a previous statement. It resolves that this follows the opinion of Abba Elazar ben Gimel, who derives from a verse that both terumah gedolah and terumat maaser can be taken by estimation and thought.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how terumat maaser can be taken by estimation and thought, since it requires measurement.

The Gemara resolves that this follows Abba Elazar ben Gimel, who derives from a verse that both תרומה גדולה (the great heave-offering) and תרומת מעשר (the heave-offering of the tithe) can be taken by estimation and thought.

items.text: First tithe taken in sheaves exempts from terumah gedolah
items.text_en: First tithe taken in sheaves exempts from terumah gedolah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quoting Reish Lakish states that if first tithe was taken while the grain was still in sheaves, it renders the produce liable for terumat maaser. Rava explains the reason: since it has been called 'tithe'. Reish Lakish further adds that such first tithe is exempt from terumah gedolah, based on a verse that only requires 'tithe from the tithe', not both terumah gedolah and terumat maaser from the tithe.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Reish Lakish states that first tithe taken in sheaves renders the produce liable for תרומת מעשר (the tithe of the tithe).
Rava explains the reason: since the produce has been called 'מעשר (tithe)', it is obligated in תרומת מעשר.
Reish Lakish adds that such first tithe is exempt from תרומה גדולה (the great heave-offering).

The gemara cites the verse 'והרמותם ממנו תרומת ה׳ מעשר מן המעשר' (and you shall lift up from it a heave-offering to the Lord, a tithe from the tithe) to prove that only one tithe (תרומת מעשר) is required, not both תרומה גדולה and תרומת מעשר from the tithe.

items.text: Objection: Why not when taken in a heap?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not when taken in a heap?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if the exemption applies when tithe is taken in sheaves, why not also when taken in a heap? Abaye responds that the verse says 'from all your tithes you shall raise up every terumah of Hashem', implying that only after the produce is fully processed (threshed) is terumah required. The distinction is that sheaves are not yet fully processed, while a heap is.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if the exemption applies when tithe is taken in sheaves, why not also when taken in a heap?

Abaye responds that the verse 'from all your tithes you shall raise up every terumah of Hashem' implies that only after the produce is fully processed (threshed) is terumah required, distinguishing sheaves (not yet processed) from a heap (already processed).

items.text: Peeling barley and rubbing wheat on Shabbat
items.text_en: Peeling barley and rubbing wheat on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who peels barley may peel one by one and eat, but if he peeled and put into his hand, he is liable. Rabbi Elazar says the same applies to Shabbat. The Gemara questions this, noting that Rav and Rabbi Chiyya's wives would peel many at once for them. It concludes that Rabbi Elazar's statement was actually about the case of rubbing wheat: one may rub a few stalks at a time and eat, but if he rubbed and put into his lap, he is liable, and the same applies to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who peels barley may peel one by one and eat, but if he peeled and put into his hand, he is liable; Rabbi Elazar says the same applies to Shabbat.
The Gemara objects: Is that so? But Rav's wife and Rabbi Chiyya's wife would peel barley for them by the cupful on Shabbat, implying that peeling many at once is permitted.

The Gemara resolves: Rather, if Rabbi Elazar's statement was said, it was said about the latter clause of the Mishnah — one who rubs wheat stalks may blow and eat a little at a time, but if he rubbed and put into his lap, he is liable, and the same applies to Shabbat.

items.text: Objection: Is there an act that is not complete for Shabbat but is for tithing?
items.text_en: Objection: Is there an act that is not complete for Shabbat but is for tithing?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects: does the first part imply that for tithing it is considered a complete act but for Shabbat it is not? Rabbi Sheishet bar Rav Idi further objects with a proof from the laws of tithing: for cucumbers and gourds, the 'granary' for tithing is when they are smoothed, and for onions when a pile is made, but for Shabbat, making a pile is exempt. The Gemara resolves that the Torah prohibited only 'intended labor' (melechet machshevet), and here too, the intention matters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects: does the first clause imply that for tithing it is a completed act but for Shabbat it is not?

sub.text: Rabbi Sheishet bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Sheishet bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Sheishet bar Rav Idi objects further, citing a mishna that for tithing, cucumbers and gourds become obligated when smoothed and onions when a pile is made, but for Shabbat, making a pile is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the Torah prohibited only 'intended labor' (מלאכת מחשבת), and here too, the intention matters.

items.text: How to rub and sift grain
items.text_en: How to rub and sift grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the proper method for rubbing (molel) grain: Abaye in the name of Rav Yosef says one by one; Rav Avya in the name of Rav Yosef says one on two; Rava says if he changes the method, even one on all is permitted. For sifting (menape'ach), Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Rav describes the method, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How does one rub (molel) grain on Yom Tov?

sub.text: Abaye in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Abaye in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Abaye in the name of Rav Yosef answers: One rubs one grain at a time.

sub.text: Rav Avya in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Avya in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Avya in the name of Rav Yosef answers: One rubs one grain on two others.
Rava answers: Since he changes the method from the usual threshing, even rubbing one on all is permitted.
The Gemara asks: How does one sift (menape'ach) grain on Yom Tov?

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in the name of Rav begins to describe the sifting method, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about the hand
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about the hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may only use the upper part of the hand for a certain action, arguing that if a change is made, it should be permitted even with the whole hand. Rabbi Elazar resolves by saying one may blow with one hand using full force.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may only use the upper part of the hand (from the knuckles upward) for a certain action.
The Gemara in the West questions: since a change is being made (from the normal way of doing it), why not permit using the entire hand?
Rabbi Elazar resolves: one may blow with one hand using full force, which is the permitted change.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on grinding spices and salt
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on grinding spices and salt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Beit Shammai says spices are ground with a wooden pestle and salt in a cruse with a wooden stirrer; Beit Hillel says spices are ground normally with a stone pestle and salt with a wooden pestle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the dispute: Beit Shammai say spices are crushed with a wooden pestle and salt with a small jug and a wooden stirrer; Beit Hillel say spices are crushed normally with a stone pestle and salt with a wooden pestle.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for salt requiring a change
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for salt requiring a change
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that all agree salt requires a change. Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate the reason: one says all pots need salt but not spices, the other says spices lose flavor but salt does not. The difference between them is whether one knows what to cook or if it is for a broth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all agree salt requires a change (שינוי) in its grinding method on Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks for the reason why salt requires a change.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's debate
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's debate
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda give two reasons: one says all pots need salt but not spices, so salt is more common and requires a change; the other says spices lose flavor when ground but salt does not, so salt is more durable and requires a change.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons.
The Gemara resolves that the difference is whether one knows what pot to cook (so salt is not needed for all pots) or if it is for a broth (מוריקא, where salt is essential).

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: All may be ground normally, even salt
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: All may be ground normally, even salt
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in Shmuel's name that all items may be ground normally, even salt. The Gemara objects that salt requires a change. Shmuel follows Rabbi Meir's Tosefta, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel only dispute when grinding salt alone, but agree it may be ground with spices. The text clarifies that Beit Hillel permits it for any purpose.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: all items that are crushed may be crushed in their normal way, even salt.
The Gemara objects: but you (the earlier discussion) said that salt requires a change!
The Gemara answers: Shmuel holds like the following Tanna (Rabbi Meir), who says that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not dispute about items crushed in their normal way with salt among them.

The baraita continues: they only disputed about crushing salt by itself; Beit Shammai say with a small jug and wooden stirrer for roasting but not for a pot, and Beit Hillel say with any vessel; the Gemara corrects 'with any thing' to 'for any purpose'.
Beit Hillel permits grinding salt for any purpose.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's wording from 'for any thing' to 'for any purpose'.

items.text: Practical advice and sound identification
items.text_en: Practical advice and sound identification
items.desc_en: Rav Acha Bardela advises his son to roast first then grind. Rav Sheshet hears a grinding sound and identifies it as not from his house, deducing it is for roasting because the sound is clear, and not spices because spices make a cracking sound.

sub.text: Rav Acha Bardela to his son
sub.text_en: Rav Acha Bardela to his son
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha Bardela instructs his son: when you crush (salt), first roast it and then crush.
Rav Sheshet heard the sound of a mortar and said: this is not from inside my house (i.e., it is permitted because it is for a festival need).
The Gemara objects: perhaps he roasted it (and that is why the sound was clear)?
The Gemara rejects: perhaps it was spices? Spices make a barking sound (so the sound is different).
The gemara asks: perhaps the sound was from grinding spices (תבלין)?
The gemara answers that spices make a cracking sound, unlike the clear sound Rav Sheshet heard.

items.text: Baraita: No making tisni and no pounding in a mortar
items.text_en: Baraita: No making tisni and no pounding in a mortar
items.desc_en: A Baraita states one may not make tisni (a dish) and not pound in a mortar. The Gemara clarifies the redundancy: the reason for not making tisni is that one may not pound in a mortar. It explains that if only the mortar were mentioned, one might think only a large mortar is prohibited, but a small one is permitted. Another Baraita explicitly permits a small mortar, and Abaye resolves that the Mishnah refers to a large mortar.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita states that one may not make tisni (a dish) and not pound in a mortar, and the Gemara clarifies that the second clause explains the first.
The Gemara questions why the Baraita did not simply say 'one may not pound in a mortar', and explains that without the extra clause one might have permitted a small mortar.
A supporting baraita explicitly permits a small mortar, contradicting the implication of the first baraita.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by stating that the Mishnah refers only to a large mortar.

items.text: Rava's distinction and Rav Pappi's incident
items.text_en: Rava's distinction and Rav Pappi's incident
items.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between Babylonian and Eretz Yisrael customs. Rav Pappi visits Mar Shmuel's house and declines a dish, suspecting it was prepared in a small mortar or from the previous day, but the Gemara offers alternative explanations.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between Babylonian and Eretz Yisrael customs.
Rav Pappi visits Mar Shmuel's house and declines a dish, suspecting it was prepared in a small mortar.
The Gemara offers alternative explanations for Rav Pappi's refusal, including that the dish was from the previous day or that Mar Shmuel's household had lax servants.

items.text: Mishnah: Separating legumes on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Separating legumes on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding how one may separate legumes on Yom Tov. Beit Shammai permits only picking out food to eat, while Beit Hillel allows separating in the usual manner using a lap, basket, or dish, but not with a sieve or strainer. Rabban Gamliel adds that one may wash and skim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute about sorting legumes on Yom Tov: Beit Shammai permits sorting food and eating, Beit Hillel permits sorting in one's lap or a plate but not with a sieve, and Rabban Gamliel permits washing and taking.

items.text: Gemara on Rabban Gamliel's ruling and the washing method
items.text_en: Gemara on Rabban Gamliel's ruling and the washing method
items.desc_en: A baraita clarifies Rabban Gamliel's ruling: when food is more than waste, one may separate normally; when waste is more, all agree one takes the food and leaves the waste. The Gemara questions if anyone permits when waste is more, and resolves it refers to a case where the waste is more in effort but less in quantity. Another baraita describes the practice of Rabban Gamliel's household: they would bring a bucket of lentils and pour water over them, causing food to sink and waste to float. A contradiction between baraitot is resolved by distinguishing between dust and clods.

sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabban Gamliel clarifying that his lenient ruling applies only when food exceeds waste, but when waste exceeds food, all agree one takes the food and leaves the waste.
The Gemara questions whether anyone would permit separating when waste exceeds food, given the baraita's implication that all forbid it.
The Gemara resolves that the case of waste exceeding food refers to a situation where the waste is greater in effort but smaller in quantity, so the leniency still applies.
A baraita describes the practice of Rabban Gamliel's household: they would bring a bucket of lentils and pour water over them, causing the food to sink and the waste to float.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that describes the opposite practice.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between dust (עפר) and clods (גילי), which behave differently in water.

items.text: Mishnah: Sending gifts on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sending gifts on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses what may be sent as gifts on Yom Tov. Beit Shammai limits sending to portions (of food), while Beit Hillel permits sending live or slaughtered animals, wines, oils, flours, and legumes, but not grain. Rabbi Shimon permits grain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute about sending gifts on Yom Tov: Beit Shammai limits to portions, Beit Hillel permits sending animals and produce, and Rabbi Shimon permits grain.

items.text: Gemara on sending gifts and Rabbi Shimon's allowance
items.text_en: Gemara on sending gifts and Rabbi Shimon's allowance
items.desc_en: Rav Yechiel teaches that one may not send gifts in a row (shurah). A baraita defines a row as at least three people. Rav Ashi asks about three people with three types of items, left unresolved. A baraita explains Rabbi Shimon's permission for grain: wheat for making loaves, barley for animal feed, lentils for making porridge.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yechiel teaches that one may not send gifts in a row (שורה).
A baraita defines a row (שורה) as at least three people.
Rav Ashi asks about three people with three types of items, left unresolved.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
A baraita explains Rabbi Shimon's permission for grain: wheat for making loaves, barley for animal feed, lentils for making porridge.

items.text: Mishnah: Sending garments with forbidden mixtures
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sending garments with forbidden mixtures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may send garments, whether sewn or unsewn, even if they contain kilayim (forbidden mixtures), as long as they are needed for the holiday. However, one may not send a nailed sandal or an unsewn shoe. Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may not send a white shoe because it requires a craftsman. The general principle: anything from which one benefits on Yom Tov may be sent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may send garments on Yom Tov, even with forbidden mixtures (כלאים), as long as they are needed for the holiday; Rabbi Yehuda adds restrictions on certain shoes.

items.text: Gemara: The purpose of sending kilayim garments
items.text_en: Gemara: The purpose of sending kilayim garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the use of kilayim garments: sewn ones are for clothing, unsewn for covering, but what is kilayim good for? It considers using them as a mattress, but a baraita prohibits lying on kilayim even with ten mattresses, as per Rabbi Yosi ben Shaul in the name of the holy community of Jerusalem. The Gemara concludes that the garment is a curtain (vilon), but Ulla notes that a vilon is susceptible to impurity because the attendant warms himself against it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of sending kilayim garments, since sewn ones are for clothing and unsewn ones for covering, but what is kilayim good for?
The Gemara objects that one might think kilayim is for lying on, but a baraita prohibits lying on kilayim even under oneself due to the concern that a thread might wrap around one's flesh.

The Gemara rejects the possibility of an intervening layer, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of the holy community of Jerusalem that even ten mattresses over kilayim are forbidden for sleeping.
The Gemara resolves that the kilayim garment is a curtain (וילון), but Ulla notes that a curtain is susceptible to impurity because the attendant warms himself against it.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'hard' items
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'hard' items
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's allowance for sending 'hard' items refers to a type of felt mat, citing Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement that a certain mat is permitted.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation citing Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation citing Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's allowance for sending 'hard' items refers to a felt mat (נמטא גמדא דנרש), citing Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement that it is permitted.

items.text: Discussion of kilayim in various items
items.text_en: Discussion of kilayim in various items
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa, Rava, and Rav Ashi debate whether certain items (ardalin, bundles of straight and seeded plants) are subject to the prohibition of kilayim, with Rav Ashi ruling that none are because they are not a typical method of heating.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that ערדלין (a type of felt shoe) are not subject to the prohibition of כלאים (mixed fabrics).
Rava distinguishes between types of felt shoes: plain ones (צררי דפשיטי) are exempt from כלאים, but patterned ones (דבזרני) are prohibited.
Rav Ashi rules that both types of felt shoes are exempt from כלאים, because their warming function is not the typical way of using mixed fabrics.

items.text: Reason for prohibiting a nailed sandal
items.text_en: Reason for prohibiting a nailed sandal
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a nailed sandal is prohibited from being sent on Yom Tov, and answers that it is due to an incident that occurred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah prohibits sending a studded sandal (סנדל המסומר) on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is due to a historical incident (מעשה שהיה) where such sandals caused a tragedy.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: wearing vs. moving a nailed sandal
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: wearing vs. moving a nailed sandal
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that a nailed sandal is forbidden to wear but permitted to move, deriving the latter from the Mishnah's wording 'one may not send' rather than 'one may not move'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that a studded sandal is forbidden to wear (due to the incident) but permitted to move (טלטול) on Yom Tov.
Abaye proves that moving the sandal is permitted because the Mishnah only says 'one may not send it' — if moving were forbidden, the Mishnah would have stated that more directly.
The Gemara objects: if moving were forbidden, would sending (which involves moving) even be a question?

items.text: Clarification of 'a shoe that is not sewn'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'a shoe that is not sewn'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's prohibition of an unsewn shoe is obvious, but clarifies it is necessary even when held together by pegs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that an untied shoe (מנעל שאינו תפור) cannot be sent — this seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's statement is necessary even when the shoe is held together with pegs (סיכי), teaching that it is still not considered properly sewn.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei about white and black shoes
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei about white and black shoes
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda permits black shoes but prohibits white ones due to needing chalk, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits black shoes due to needing polishing. The Gemara resolves that they do not disagree but refer to different local customs regarding the placement of leather.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda permits black shoes but prohibits white ones due to needing chalk, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits black shoes due to needing polishing.
The Gemara resolves that the two rabbis do not actually disagree, but each refers to the custom of his own locale regarding whether the leather side faces up or down.

items.text: The general rule and Rav Sheshet's permission for tefillin
items.text_en: The general rule and Rav Sheshet's permission for tefillin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's general rule states that anything from which one benefits on Yom Tov may be sent. Rav Sheshet permits sending tefillin on Yom Tov, and Abaye questions this based on the Mishnah. The Gemara clarifies that the rule means anything from which one benefits on a weekday may be sent on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet permitted the rabbis to send תפילין (phylacteries) on Yom Tov.
Abaye objects that the Mishnah's rule 'anything one may benefit from on Yom Tov may be sent' seems to permit sending תפילין, contradicting Rav Sheshet's permissive ruling.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: it means 'anything one may benefit from on a weekday may be sent on Yom Tov' — thus תפילין, which are not used on Yom Tov, are excluded.
The Gemara resolves the objection by clarifying that the Mishnah's rule means anything from which one benefits on a weekday may be sent on Yom Tov.

items.text: Abaye's halakha about tefillin at nightfall and the ensuing discussion
items.text_en: Abaye's halakha about tefillin at nightfall and the ensuing discussion
items.desc_en: Abaye states a halakha that one who is wearing tefillin when Shabbat begins may cover them with his hand until he reaches home. Rav Huna bar Rav Ika challenges this with a baraita that limits the distance to the nearest house. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between secure and insecure places, and further clarifies that even if placed on the ground, tefillin are protected from dogs but not thieves, and that one might think Jewish thieves would not disrespect them, so the baraita teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens a discussion about tefillin (תפילין) and states that if one is on the road with tefillin on his head when nightfall (שבת) begins, he may cover them with his hand until he reaches home.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ika objects by citing a baraita that limits the distance to the nearest house, not the person's own home.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a secure place (מנטרא) and an insecure place (לא מנטרא).

The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies tefillin on the head if the place is insecure, since even if placed on the ground they would be protected, citing the rule that found tefillin are brought in pair by pair.
The Gemara answers by distinguishing between protection from dogs and protection from thieves: the baraita's case is secure from dogs but not from thieves.
The Gemara concludes that one might think Jewish thieves would not disrespect tefillin (תפילין), so the baraita teaches that even so, one must protect them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Eiruv Tavshilin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Eiruv Tavshilin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Yom Tov falls on Friday, one may not initially cook from Yom Tov for Shabbat, but may cook for Yom Tov and let leftovers suffice for Shabbat. One must prepare a cooked dish before Yom Tov to rely on for Shabbat. Beit Shammai require two dishes, Beit Hillel require one, and they agree that a fish and an egg on it count as two. If the dish is eaten or lost, one may not cook anew; if any remains, one may rely on it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: when Yom Tov falls on Friday, one may not cook initially from Yom Tov for Shabbat, but may cook for Yom Tov and rely on leftovers for Shabbat, and must prepare a dish before Yom Tov to rely on.
The Mishnah records the dispute: Beit Shammai require two dishes for the eiruv, Beit Hillel require one, and they agree that a fish and an egg on it count as two.
The Mishnah concludes: if the eiruv dish is eaten or lost, one may not cook anew; if any remains, one may rely on it.
