items.text: Gemara: Source and Rationale for Eiruv Tavshilin
items.text_en: Gemara: Source and Rationale for Eiruv Tavshilin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source. Shmuel cites 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it' — remember it from another day that might cause forgetting. Rava explains the reason is to ensure one selects a fine portion for Shabbat and a fine portion for Yom Tov. Rav Ashi says it is to teach that one may not bake from Yom Tov to Shabbat, a fortiori from Yom Tov to a weekday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the halakha of eiruv tavshilin.
Shmuel cites the verse 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it' — remember it from another day that might cause forgetting.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind the ordinance.
Rava explains the reason is to ensure one selects a choice portion for Shabbat and a choice portion for Yom Tov.
Rav Ashi says the reason is to teach that one may not bake from Yom Tov to Shabbat, a fortiori from Yom Tov to a weekday.

items.text: Gemara: Challenge to Rava and Resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Challenge to Rava and Resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava: according to Rav Ashi, the Mishnah's requirement to prepare the dish before Yom Tov makes sense, but according to Rava, why specifically before Yom Tov? Even on Yom Tov itself one could select a fine portion. The Gemara answers: indeed, but the Sages decreed that one must prepare it before Yom Tov lest one be negligent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava: according to Rav Ashi, the Mishnah's requirement to prepare the dish before Yom Tov is logical, but according to Rava, why specifically before Yom Tov? Even on Yom Tov itself one could select a fine portion.
The Gemara answers: indeed, but the Sages decreed that one must prepare it before Yom Tov lest one be negligent.

items.text: Tannaic Source for Eiruv Tavshilin
items.text_en: Tannaic Source for Eiruv Tavshilin
items.desc_en: A Tanna derives the practice from the verse 'Bake what you will bake and cook what you will cook', from which Rabbi Eliezer deduces that one may only bake from what is already baked and cook from what is already cooked. From here the Sages derived the institution of eiruv tavshilin from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'אֵת אֲשֶׁר תֹּאפוּ אֵפוּ' (Bake what you will bake) as the source from which Rabbi Eliezer derives that one may only bake from what is already baked, and from which the Sages derived the institution of eiruv tavshilin from the Torah.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Eliezer and the Departing Students
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Eliezer and the Departing Students
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Eliezer was teaching Yom Tov laws all day. As groups of students left, he disparaged them as owners of various vessels. When the sixth group began to leave, he called them 'owners of a curse'. Seeing the remaining students' faces change, he clarified he meant those who left, who abandon eternal life for temporal life. At their departure, he blessed them with the verse from Nehemiah about eating and rejoicing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer taught Yom Tov laws all day, and as each of the first five groups of students left, he disparaged them as owners of various vessels.
When the sixth group began to leave, Rabbi Eliezer called them 'owners of a curse'.
Seeing the remaining students' faces change, Rabbi Eliezer clarified that his curse was directed at those who left, who abandon eternal life for temporal life.
At their departure, Rabbi Eliezer blessed them with the verse from Nehemiah about eating and rejoicing.

items.text: Gemara: The Dispute on Joy of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Gemara: The Dispute on Joy of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Eliezer could call Yom Tov rejoicing 'temporal life' when it is a mitzvah. It explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds that Yom Tov joy is optional, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says one may either eat and drink or sit and study; Rabbi Yehoshua says divide the day — half for God, half for yourselves. Rabbi Yochanan says both derive from verses: one says 'an assembly for God', another says 'an assembly for you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Eliezer could call Yom Tov rejoicing 'temporal life' when it is a mitzvah.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer holds that Yom Tov joy is optional.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer says one may either eat and drink or sit and study; Rabbi Yehoshua says divide the day — half for God, half for yourselves.
Rabbi Yochanan says both derive from verses: one says 'an assembly for God', another says 'an assembly for you'.

items.text: Interpretation of 'For Whom Nothing is Prepared'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'For Whom Nothing is Prepared'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'send portions to one for whom nothing is prepared' — Rav Chisda says this refers to one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin. Some say it refers to one who had no opportunity to prepare, but one who had the opportunity and did not is a negligent person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'for whom nothing is prepared' from the verse in Nehemiah.
Rav Chisda answers that the phrase refers to one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin.
Some say the phrase refers to one who had no opportunity to prepare an eiruv tavshilin, but one who had the opportunity and did not is considered negligent.

items.text: God's Encouragement to Borrow for Yom Tov
items.text_en: God's Encouragement to Borrow for Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon explains the verse 'the joy of the Lord is your strength' — God told Israel: My children, borrow on My account, sanctify the day, and trust in Me, and I will repay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does 'כִּי חֶדְוַת ה׳ הִיא מָעֻזְּכֶם' (for the joy of the Lord is your strength) mean?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon explains: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, borrow from Me, sanctify the day, and trust in Me, and I will repay.

items.text: Advice for Preserving Wealth: Planting an Eder
items.text_en: Advice for Preserving Wealth: Planting an Eder
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon says: One who wants his property to endure should plant an eder (a grove of trees) in it, as the verse says 'The Lord is mighty in the heavens'. Alternatively, eder means a lasting grove, as people say: what is an eder? It stands for generations. A baraita supports this: a field with an eder is not robbed or plundered, and its fruits are preserved.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon advises that one who wants his property to endure should plant an eder (a grove) in it, citing the verse 'אַדִּיר בַּמָּרוֹם ה׳' (The Lord is mighty in the heavens).
The gemara offers an alternative explanation: 'eder' is named for its lasting nature, as people say 'what is an eder? It stands for generations (דְּקָיְימָא לְדָרֵי דָּרֵי).'
A baraita supports this: a field with an eder is not robbed or plundered, and its fruits are preserved.

items.text: Introduction of Rav Tachlifa's Teaching
items.text_en: Introduction of Rav Tachlifa's Teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a teaching by Rav Tachlifa, brother of Ravnay the seer, which will be cited next.

sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa, the brother of Ravnai the seer, teaches a baraita (the content is not provided in the given text).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's proof for fixed sustenance
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's proof for fixed sustenance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person's sustenance is fixed from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, except for Shabbat, Yom Tov, and children's Torah study expenses. Rabbi Avahu cites a verse to support this, and the Gemara explains that the word 'חוק' refers to sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person's sustenance is fixed from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, except for Shabbat, Yom Tov, and children's Torah study expenses.
Rabbi Avahu cites a verse from Psalms about the shofar and the word 'חוק' (statute) to connect Rosh Hashanah with fixed sustenance.
The Gemara explains that the word 'חוק' means sustenance, citing verses from Genesis and Proverbs, with Mar Zutra adding a proof from Proverbs.

items.text: Shammai and Hillel's practices regarding Shabbat
items.text_en: Shammai and Hillel's practices regarding Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita describes Shammai the Elder's practice of always eating in honor of Shabbat, and Hillel the Elder's different approach of dedicating all actions to Heaven. The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree on whether to prepare from one Shabbat to the next or daily.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes Shammai the Elder's practice of always eating in honor of Shabbat, buying the best animal first and then eating the previous one when a better one is found.

The baraita contrasts Hillel the Elder's approach of dedicating all actions to Heaven, citing the verse 'ברוך ה׳ יום יום', and notes that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree on whether to prepare from one Shabbat to the next or daily.

items.text: Giving a gift without informing the recipient
items.text_en: Giving a gift without informing the recipient
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says one need not inform a friend when giving a gift, citing Moses. The Gemara objects with the case of Shabbat, where God told Moses to inform Israel. The resolution distinguishes between a gift that will become known and one that will not. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about informing a child's mother is discussed, with Rav Papa addressing concerns about witchcraft.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that one who gives a gift to a friend need not inform him, citing the verse that Moses did not know his face shone.
The Gemara objects with a baraita where God told Moses to inform Israel about the gift of Shabbat, implying that informing is necessary.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a gift that will become known (where informing is unnecessary) and one that will not become known (where informing is required), explaining that Shabbat's reward is not known.

sub.text: Gemara's discussion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's discussion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that one who gives bread to a child must inform the mother, explaining the practice of anointing with oil and applying kohl, and Rav Papa addresses the concern about witchcraft by using the same type of substance.

items.text: Shabbat given in secret and the extra soul
items.text_en: Shabbat given in secret and the extra soul
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says all mitzvot were given publicly except Shabbat, which was given privately. The Gemara questions why gentiles are not punished for violating Shabbat, and answers that while Shabbat itself was publicized, its reward was not. Alternatively, the extra soul (נשמה יתירה) was not publicized, as explained by Reish Lakish.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai taught: all mitzvot were given publicly except Shabbat, which was given privately, as the verse says it is a sign between God and Israel.
The Gemara asks: if Shabbat was given in secret, why are gentiles not punished for violating it?
The Gemara answers: Shabbat itself was publicized to gentiles, but its reward was not publicized.
Alternatively, even the reward was publicized, but the extra soul (נשמה יתירה) was not publicized.
Reish Lakish explains that the extra soul is given on Shabbat eve and removed at its conclusion, as derived from the verse 'שבת וינפש' — once Shabbat ends, woe, the soul is lost.

items.text: Eruv Tavshilin: bread vs. cooked dish
items.text_en: Eruv Tavshilin: bread vs. cooked dish
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that only a cooked dish (תבשיל) can be used for eruv tavshilin, not bread. The Gemara explores the reasoning: whether we need something that wraps (מלפת) or something uncommon. Two versions of Abaye's statement are presented, with different conclusions about the rationale.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the mishna's allowance for a cooked dish (תבשיל) applies only to a cooked dish, not to bread.
The Gemara asks why bread is different, suggesting the reason might be that we require something that accompanies bread (מלפת).

The Gemara rejects the 'accompanies bread' explanation by citing Rabbi Zeira's comment that Babylonians eat bread with porridge, and Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya's statement that one may establish an eiruv with porridge.
The Gemara answers that we require something uncommon, and bread is common, while porridge is uncommon.

An alternative version of Abaye's statement is presented, where the Gemara rejects the 'uncommon' explanation and concludes that we require something that accompanies bread, which neither bread nor porridge does.

items.text: Additional rulings on eruv tavshilin
items.text_en: Additional rulings on eruv tavshilin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches that lentils at the bottom of a pot can be used for eruv tavshilin if they are an olive's bulk. Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda says fat on a knife can be scraped off and used. Rav Asi in the name of Rav says small salted fish are not subject to the prohibition of bishul akum, and Rav Yosef adds that if a gentile roasted them, they can be used for eruv tavshilin, but if made into a fish stew, they are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: רבי חייא (Rabbi Chiya) teaches that lentils at the bottom of a pot can be relied upon for עירובי תבשילין (joining of cooked foods) if they amount to an olive's bulk.
רב יצחק בר יהודה (Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda) adds that fat on a knife can be scraped off and used for עירובי תבשילין (joining of cooked foods) if it is an olive's bulk.

sub.text: Rav Asi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: רב אסי (Rav Asi) in the name of רב (Rav) states that small salted fish are not subject to the prohibition of בישולי גוים (cooking of gentiles).
רב יוסף (Rav Yosef) adds that if a gentile roasted them, they can be used for עירובי תבשילין (joining of cooked foods), but if made into a fish stew (כסא דהרסנא), it is forbidden.

items.text: Incomplete section: beginning of a new discussion
items.text_en: Incomplete section: beginning of a new discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new point with 'פשיטא', suggesting it is obvious, but the text cuts off. This likely introduces a clarification or objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new point with 'פשיטא' (it is obvious), suggesting that the preceding ruling is straightforward, but the text cuts off before completing the anticipated objection or clarification.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about 'flour' being primary is meant to teach that flour is the essential ingredient, not the roasted grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about 'flour' being primary is meant to teach that flour is the essential ingredient, not the roasted grain.

items.text: The size requirement for eruv tavshilin
items.text_en: The size requirement for eruv tavshilin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that eruv tavshilin requires a kezayit. The Gemara questions whether this is one kezayit for all or per person, and attempts to resolve it from a statement by Rav and from the Mishnah and a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that eruv tavshilin requires a kezayit (olive-sized portion).
The Gemara raises a question: is the kezayit for all participants together or for each individual?

sub.text: Rav's statement cited by Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rav's statement cited by Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing Rav's statement that the kezayit applies equally to one or a hundred people.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that if the eruv was eaten or lost one cannot cook, but any leftover suffices.
The Gemara infers that 'any leftover' might mean even less than a kezayit.
The Gemara rejects the inference, clarifying that the leftover must contain a kezayit.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a cooked dish for eruv has no fixed measure.
The Gemara infers that the baraita means there is no minimum measure at all.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita means no upper limit, but there is a lower limit.

items.text: The requirement of intent (da'at) for eruv tavshilin
items.text_en: The requirement of intent (da'at) for eruv tavshilin
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says in the name of Rav that eruv tavshilin requires da'at. The Gemara questions whether this means the intent of the one who sets it or the one for whom it is set, and brings evidence from the practices of Shmuel's father and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in the name of Rav that eruv tavshilin requires da'at (intent).
The Gemara questions whether the required intent is that of the one who sets the eruv or that of the one for whom it is set.

The Gemara brings evidence from the practices of Shmuel's father and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, who set eruvin for entire cities, and from Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's announcement that those who did not set an eruv may rely on his, with a limit up to the Shabbat boundary.

items.text: Story of the blind man and Shmuel
items.text_en: Story of the blind man and Shmuel
items.desc_en: A blind man who was distressed about not having set an eruv tavshilin is told by Shmuel to rely on his. The next year, when the same happens, Shmuel calls him a negligent person and forbids him from relying on his eruv, implying that one may rely on another's eruv only once.

sub.text: Story about Mar Shmuel and a blind man
sub.text_en: Story about Mar Shmuel and a blind man
sub.desc_en: A blind man who was reciting Mishnah before Mar Shmuel was sad because he had not set an eruv tavshilin, and Mar Shmuel told him to rely on his eruv.
The next year the same blind man again had not set an eruv, and Mar Shmuel rebuked him as a negligent person, forbidding him to rely on his eruv.
The next year, Shmuel again sees the blind man distressed about not having set an eruv tavshilin.
Shmuel calls the blind man negligent (פושע) and rules that while everyone else may rely on his eruv, the blind man himself is forbidden to do so, implying one may rely on another's eruv only once.

items.text: Dispute about eruv on Yom Tov that falls on Friday
items.text_en: Dispute about eruv on Yom Tov that falls on Friday
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that when Yom Tov falls on Friday, one may not establish an eruv techumin or an eruv chatzeirot. Rabbi permits eruv chatzeirot but not eruv techumin, because one may not restrict a person in a matter that is permitted to him.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that when Yom Tov falls on Friday, one may not establish an eruv techumin or an eruv chatzeirot.
Rabbi permits eruv chatzeirot but not eruv techumin, because one may not restrict a person in a matter that is permitted to him.

items.text: Determining the halakha in the dispute
items.text_en: Determining the halakha in the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether the halakha follows the Tanna Kamma or Rabbi. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi's ruling is lenient or stringent, and brings evidence from a story about Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi and Rav's reaction, concluding that Rabbi's ruling is lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav rules the halakha follows the Tanna Kamma (the first Tanna), while Shmuel rules it follows Rabbi.
The Gemara asks whether Shmuel's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi is lenient or stringent, noting a contradictory report from Rabbi Elazar that Rabbi is stringent and the Sages lenient.

The Gemara resolves the question by citing a story: Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi acted like Shmuel, and Rav called it a 'corruption' (קִלְקוּלָא), proving that Shmuel's ruling is lenient, since only a lenient ruling would be considered a corruption.

items.text: Rava's ruling on Rabbi's opinion
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on Rabbi's opinion
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Chisda quoting Rav Huna that the halakha follows Rabbi's opinion, but for prohibition (i.e., one must not combine the blessings).

sub.text: Rava quoting Rav Chisda quoting Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava quoting Rav Chisda quoting Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows Rabbi's opinion, but only for prohibition (i.e., one must not combine the blessings).

items.text: Baraita on prayer for Yom Tov on Shabbat and Ravina's correction
items.text_en: Baraita on prayer for Yom Tov on Shabbat and Ravina's correction
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the Amidah when Yom Tov falls on Shabbat, with Rabbi offering a third opinion. A tanna recites a version before Ravina, who corrects the wording, and Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi as corrected by Ravina.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the Amidah when Yom Tov falls on Shabbat.
Rabbi adds a third opinion that one concludes the blessing with both Shabbat and the festivals.
A tanna recites a version before Ravina, who objects that Shabbat is inherently sanctified and does not require Israel's sanctification.
Ravina corrects the wording to 'Who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel, and the seasons.'
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi, as corrected by Ravina.

items.text: Baraita on Shabbat coinciding with Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Baraita on Shabbat coinciding with Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the prayer order when Shabbat falls on Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed, with Rabbi Eliezer differing on where to insert the special mention. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael rule that whenever one recites seven blessings, one begins and ends with Shabbat and inserts the sanctity of the day in the middle. Rav Huna states that the halakha does not follow that pair.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule for Shabbat coinciding with Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed: one prays seven blessings and inserts the special mention in the workda, and if omitted, one repeats.
Rabbi Eliezer differs, placing the special mention in the thanksgiving blessing, and for the additional prayer he rules to begin and end with Shabbat and insert the sanctity of the day in the middle.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael rule that whenever one recites seven blessings, one begins and ends with Shabbat and inserts the sanctity of the day in the middle.
Rav Huna states that the halakha does not follow that pair (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael).

items.text: Eiruv techumin and eiruv tavshilin from Yom Tov to Shabbat
items.text_en: Eiruv techumin and eiruv tavshilin from Yom Tov to Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav permits one to place an eiruv techumin from Yom Tov to Shabbat with a condition. Rava permits eiruv tavshilin similarly. The Gemara explains the logical relationship between the two rulings: one who permits eiruv techumin certainly permits eiruv tavshilin, but the reverse is not true because eiruv techumin involves acquiring a resting place on Shabbat, which is more stringent.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav rules that one may place an eiruv techumin from Yom Tov to the next day with a condition.
Rava similarly permits placing an eiruv tavshilin from Yom Tov to the next day with a condition.

The Gemara explains the logical relationship: one who permits eiruv techumin certainly permits eiruv tavshilin, but the reverse is not true because eiruv techumin involves acquiring a resting place on Shabbat, which is more stringent.

items.text: Baraita on baking from Yom Tov to Shabbat and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's leniency
items.text_en: Baraita on baking from Yom Tov to Shabbat and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's leniency
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not bake from Yom Tov to Shabbat, but permits filling a pot with meat or a barrel with water even if not all is needed. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits filling the entire oven with bread because it bakes better when full. Rava rules the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: one may not bake from Yom Tov to Shabbat, but permits filling a pot with meat or a barrel with water beyond immediate need, though for baking one may only bake what is needed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds a leniency: a woman may fill the entire oven with bread because bread bakes better when the oven is full.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's lenient position.

items.text: Inquiry: Is one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin prohibited along with his flour?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Is one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin prohibited along with his flour?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who failed to prepare an eiruv tavshilin is prohibited from using his flour as well, or only he is prohibited. The practical difference is whether he must transfer ownership of his flour to others. A baraita is brought as proof: one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin may not cook for himself or others, and must transfer his flour to others, implying both he and his flour are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin is prohibited along with his flour, or only he is prohibited, and explains the practical difference regarding transferring ownership of the flour to others.
A baraita is brought as proof: one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin may not cook for himself or others, and must transfer his flour to others, implying both he and his flour are prohibited.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that both he and his flour are prohibited, resolving the inquiry.

items.text: Inquiry: If one violated and baked, what is the law?
items.text_en: Inquiry: If one violated and baked, what is the law?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is if one who did not prepare an eiruv tavshilin violated the prohibition and baked. The answer is derived from the baraita: he must transfer his flour to others, and they bake for him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question: if one violated the prohibition and baked, what is the law?
The gemara brings a baraita: one who did not place an עירוב תבשילין should transfer ownership of his flour to others, and they bake and cook for him.

items.text: Question about baking without an eruv
items.text_en: Question about baking without an eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not teach that if one transgressed and baked without an eruv, it is permitted. Rav Adda bar Mattana explains that the Tanna only teaches leniencies, not prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach that if one transgressed and baked without an eruv, it is permitted.
Rav Adda bar Mattana explains that the Tanna only teaches leniencies (תקנתא דהיתרא), not prohibitions (תקנתא דאיסורא).

items.text: Bringing a Mishnah about one who ate his eruv
items.text_en: Bringing a Mishnah about one who ate his eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that one who set an eruv may bake, cook, and keep food warm, but if he ate the eruv before doing so, he may not do these things for himself or others. However, he may cook for Yom Tov, and if leftovers remain for Shabbat, it is permitted provided he does not scheme.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that details the rules for one who set an eruv tavshilin, including that if he ate the eruv before baking or cooking, he may not do so for himself or others, but he may cook for Yom Tov and leftovers for Shabbat, provided he does not scheme.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction regarding scheming
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction regarding scheming
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case of scheming is different because the Sages were more stringent about scheming than about intentional transgression.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the case of scheming (הערמה) is different because the Sages were more stringent about scheming than about intentional transgression.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's attribution to Chananyah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's attribution to Chananyah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests that the Mishnah follows Chananyah in the name of Beit Shammai, who require separate eruvin for baking and cooking, while Beit Hillel permit a single dish for all needs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies the Mishnah's anonymous ruling as following Chananyah's version of Beit Shammai's position.
The baraita cites Chananyah reporting Beit Shammai's requirement for separate eruvin for baking, cooking, and insulating.
The baraita then presents Beit Hillel's contrasting view that a single dish suffices for all needs.

items.text: Attempts to prove from other cases of Shabbat transgression
items.text_en: Attempts to prove from other cases of Shabbat transgression
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to bring proofs from cases of tithing, immersing vessels, and cooking on Shabbat, but each is rejected: tithing and immersion are distinguished by having other produce or vessels, and cooking on Shabbat is a different prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about one who tithes his produce on Shabbat: if done unintentionally he may eat, but if intentionally he may not, attempting to prove a parallel to cooking on Yom Tov.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that the case of tithing is different because the person has other produce available, so the prohibition is not comparable to cooking on Yom Tov.
The Gemara cites another baraita about one who immerses his vessels on Shabbat: if done unintentionally he may use them, but if intentionally he may not, attempting another proof.
The Gemara rejects this proof as well, distinguishing that the person has other vessels available or can borrow them, so the case is not analogous to cooking on Yom Tov.
The Gemara cites a baraita about one who cooks on Shabbat: if done unintentionally he may eat, but if intentionally he may not, attempting a third proof.
The Gemara rejects this proof, stating that the prohibition of Shabbat is fundamentally different from that of Yom Tov, so the case is not comparable.

items.text: Dispute about two dishes and the ruling
items.text_en: Dispute about two dishes and the ruling
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai require two dishes for the eruv, but a baraita records that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says they agree on the need for two dishes, disagreeing only about fish and egg. Rava rules like our Tanna in accordance with Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai states that two cooked dishes are required for the eruv tavshilin.

A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on the need for two dishes, disagreeing only about fish and egg, and that if one mixes egg into fish or leeks into fish it counts as two dishes.
Rava rules in accordance with our Tanna (the Mishnah) and in accordance with Beit Hillel.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on beginning dough
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on beginning dough
items.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition: if one began his dough and his eruv was eaten, he may finish it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's eruv was eaten or lost, he may not cook based on it.
Abaye states a tradition: if one began his dough (עיסה) and his eruv was eaten, he may finish (גומר) the baking.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on immersion when Yom Tov follows Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on immersion when Yom Tov follows Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Yom Tov falls after Shabbat, Beit Shammai require immersion before Shabbat, while Beit Hillel allow vessels before Shabbat and people on Shabbat. The Gemara begins to explain why vessels may not be immersed on Shabbat, citing Rabbah's reason of a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules on immersion when Yom Tov follows Shabbat: Beit Shammai require everything before Shabbat; Beit Hillel distinguish vessels (before Shabbat) from people (on Shabbat).

The Mishnah adds a further ruling: both schools agree that one may touch water to a stone vessel for purification, but not immerse; and one may immerse from one cavity to another or from one group to another.
The Gemara notes that everyone (both schools) agrees that vessels may not be immersed on Shabbat, and asks for the reason.
Rabbah answers that the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) — a rabbinic safeguard — without finishing the full explanation (continued on next daf).

items.text: Initial decree and its extension to Yom Tov
items.text_en: Initial decree and its extension to Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye asks what reason there is to forbid immersion if one has a pit in his courtyard (no carrying concern). The Gemara answers that the decree extends from a pit in the public domain to a pit in the courtyard, and from Shabbat to Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks: if one has a pit in his own courtyard, what reason is there to forbid immersion (since there is no concern of carrying in the public domain)?
The Gemara answers: the decree extends from a pit in the public domain to a pit in the courtyard, and from Shabbat to Yom Tov.

items.text: Challenge from the law of hatching water
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of hatching water
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of decreeing one case because of another: the Mishnah permits hatching water in a stone vessel for purification, yet we do not decree hatching because of immersion. The Gemara answers that one who lacks good water is careful with it, so no decree is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of decreeing one case because of another, citing the Mishnah that permits hatching water in a stone vessel for purification but does not decree hatching because of immersion.
The Gemara answers that one who lacks good water is careful with it, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Challenge from drawing water with a tamei bucket
items.text_en: Challenge from drawing water with a tamei bucket
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: one may draw water with a tamei bucket, and it becomes tahor, yet we do not decree that he might immerse the bucket itself. The Gemara answers that since he is only permitted to use the bucket, he remembers not to immerse it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: one may draw water with a tamei bucket and it becomes tahor, yet we do not decree that he might immerse the bucket itself.
The Gemara answers that since he is only permitted to use the bucket, he remembers not to immerse it.

items.text: Challenge from a vessel that became tamei on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Challenge from a vessel that became tamei on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Another objection: a vessel that became tamei on Yom Tov may be immersed on Yom Tov, yet we do not decree Yom Tov because of the eve of Yom Tov. The Gemara answers that impurity on Yom Tov is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree for uncommon cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a vessel that became impure on the eve of Yom Tov may be immersed on Yom Tov, yet we do not decree Yom Tov because of the eve of Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that impurity on Yom Tov is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree for uncommon cases.

items.text: Challenge from primary vs. secondary impurity
items.text_en: Challenge from primary vs. secondary impurity
items.desc_en: An objection: a vessel that became tamei with a primary source of impurity may not be immersed on Yom Tov, but one with a secondary source may—yet we do not decree one for the other. The Gemara answers that secondary impurity is only found among priests, who are vigilant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if we decree immersion on Yom Tov due to Shabbat, why not decree that a vessel with primary impurity (אב הטומאה) is forbidden for immersion, while one with secondary impurity (ולד הטומאה) is permitted, without decreeing one for the other?
The Gemara answers: secondary impurity is only found among priests, who are vigilant (זריזין) and will not confuse the two cases, so no decree is needed.

items.text: Challenge from a niddah without clothes
items.text_en: Challenge from a niddah without clothes
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav: a niddah who has no clothes immerses in her garments, yet we do not decree that she might immerse them separately. The Gemara answers that since she is only permitted to immerse with the garment, she remembers not to immerse it alone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the decree by citing Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's ruling that a niddah without clothes immerses in her garments, arguing that if the decree were valid, we should also fear she might immerse the garments separately.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the niddah is only permitted to immerse with the garment, so she remembers not to immerse it alone.

items.text: Rav Yosef's rationale: decree because of squeezing
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's rationale: decree because of squeezing
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains the decree is due to squeezing (of water from the vessel). Abaye objects that this applies only to vessels that are squeezed, not to those that are not. Rav Yosef answers that we decree one type because of the other. The Gemara notes that all previous objections are answered similarly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that the decree against immersing vessels on Yom Tov is due to the concern of squeezing (water from the vessel).
Abaye objects that the concern of squeezing applies only to vessels that are squeezable, but what about vessels that are not squeezable?
Rav Yosef answers that we decree regarding non-squeezable vessels because of squeezable vessels.
The Gemara notes that all the earlier objections (from segments 2-9) were raised against Rav Yosef, and he answered each as we have already explained.

items.text: Rav Bivi's rationale: decree lest one delay immersion
items.text_en: Rav Bivi's rationale: decree lest one delay immersion
items.desc_en: Rav Bivi explains the decree is lest one delay immersion (until Yom Tov). A baraita supports him: a vessel that became tamei on the eve of Yom Tov may not be immersed on Yom Tov, a decree lest one delay.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bivi states that the decree against immersing a vessel on Yom Tov is a גזירה (decree) lest one delay immersion until Yom Tov.
A baraita supports Rav Bivi: a vessel that became טמא (impure) on the eve of Yom Tov may not be immersed on Yom Tov, a decree lest one delay.

items.text: Rava's rationale: appearing to repair a vessel
items.text_en: Rava's rationale: appearing to repair a vessel
items.desc_en: Rava explains the decree is because immersion appears like repairing a vessel. The Gemara objects that a person immersing appears to be cooling off. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that sometimes a person comes (to cool off, so it is not a problem).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the decree against immersing a vessel on Yom Tov is because it appears like repairing a vessel.
The Gemara objects that if the concern is appearing to repair, then a person immersing should also be forbidden.
The Gemara answers that a person immersing appears to be cooling off, not repairing.
The Gemara objects that while cooling off is plausible with good water, with bad water one would not cool off, so the decree should still apply.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that sometimes a person comes to cool off even with bad water, so the appearance of cooling off still applies.

items.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling on bathing
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's ruling on bathing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may bathe even in a water reservoir, asking what applies in the rainy season. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that one may come from the field dirty with mud and bathe even in the rainy season.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that while the Mishnah's ruling about bathing in a water reservoir works for the dry season, what applies during the rainy season.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that a person may come from the field dirty with mud and bathe even in the rainy season.

items.text: Question about Yom Kippur and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Question about Yom Kippur and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what applies on Yom Kippur, since bathing is prohibited. Rava answers that since it is permitted on Shabbat, it is also permitted on Yom Kippur, invoking the 'ho'il' principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that while the Mishnah's ruling works for Shabbat, what applies on Yom Kippur.
Rava answers that since bathing is permitted on Shabbat, it is also permitted on Yom Kippur by the principle of הוֹאִיל (since it is permitted in one case, it is permitted in the other).

items.text: Challenge to Rava's consistency on 'ho'il'
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava's consistency on 'ho'il'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's use of 'ho'il' by citing a baraita about vinegar for tooth pain, where Rava did not apply 'ho'il'. The Gemara concludes that Rava retracted from that earlier position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's use of the 'ho'il' principle by citing a baraita about vinegar for tooth pain, where Rava did not apply 'ho'il'.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the baraita and another source about swallowing versus spitting vinegar.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to spitting out the vinegar.
Rava offers an alternative resolution: the distinction is between before and after the ritual dipping (טבול).
The Gemara objects that if Rava consistently applied 'ho'il', he should have permitted swallowing vinegar after dipping based on the permission before dipping.
The Gemara concludes that Rava retracted from his earlier position regarding the 'ho'il' principle.

items.text: Proof that Rava retracted from the vinegar case
items.text_en: Proof that Rava retracted from the vinegar case
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Rava retracted from the vinegar case, not from the bathing case, by citing a baraita that all obligated in immersions may immerse on Yom Kippur, supporting the 'ho'il' logic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rava retracted from the vinegar case or from the bathing case.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rava retracted from the bathing case, citing a baraita that all who are obligated to immerse may do so even on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah on immersion on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah on immersion on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's ruling about not immersing a vessel on Yom Tov, citing Shmuel's interpretation. It then identifies the anonymous author as either Rabbi or the Rabbis, resolving the contradiction by suggesting the baraita's first clause refers to Yom Tov and its latter clause to Shabbat, while the Mishnah entirely deals with Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'but they do not immerse' regarding Yom Tov.
Shmuel explains that the Mishnah prohibits immersing a vessel on top of its water to purify it on Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows, noting it matches neither Rabbi nor the Rabbis.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita's first clause refers to Yom Tov and its latter clause to Shabbat, while the entire Mishnah deals with Yom Tov, so it can align with either Rabbi or the Rabbis.

items.text: Alternative resolution of the earlier dispute
items.text_en: Alternative resolution of the earlier dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the entire Mishnah is discussing Shabbat, not Yom Tov, thus resolving the earlier contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the entire Mishnah is discussing Shabbat, not Yom Tov, thus resolving the earlier contradiction.

items.text: Baraita on immersing a vessel between twilight
items.text_en: Baraita on immersing a vessel between twilight
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a vessel which became impure on Yom Tov eve may not be immersed between twilight. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds that even on a weekday it may not be immersed because it requires sunset. Rava explains that the dispute is about whether one's intention is recognizable through his actions, illustrated by a case where one runs to immerse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling: a vessel that became impure on Yom Tov eve may not be immersed between twilight.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds that even on a weekday the vessel may not be immersed because it requires sunset (הערב שמש).
The Gemara asks: does the Tanna Kamma not require sunset (הערב שמש) for immersion?
Rava explains that the dispute is about whether one's intention is recognizable through his actions (במחשבתו ניכרת מתוך מעשיו).
Rava illustrates: a case where one holds a vessel in his hand and runs between twilight to immerse it.

sub.text: First opinion (Sages of the house of Rav)
sub.text_en: First opinion (Sages of the house of Rav)
sub.desc_en: One opinion holds that the runner knows he needs sunset (הערב שמש), so his action reveals his intention.

sub.text: Second opinion (Sages of the house of Rav)
sub.text_en: Second opinion (Sages of the house of Rav)
sub.desc_en: The other opinion holds that he runs merely because of his work, not because he knows about sunset.

items.text: Rava's own explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's own explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that all agree on the principle of intention being recognizable through actions; the dispute is about a case where one was impure with less than a lentil's bulk and came to ask the Sages, where one Sage thinks he is ignorant of the need for sunset, and the other thinks he knows about sunset but not about the impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that all agree on the principle that intention is recognizable through actions.

Rava resolves the dispute by explaining that the disagreement is about a case where one was impure with less than a lentil's bulk and came to ask the Sages: one Sage thinks he is ignorant of the need for sunset, and the other thinks he knows about sunset but not about the impurity.

items.text: Immersing from one basket to another
items.text_en: Immersing from one basket to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the concept of 'from one basket to another' regarding immersion, and then discusses 'from one group to another' in the context of eating.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule of immersing from one basket to another.
The baraita explains the method of 'from one basket to another' by giving an example of placing a vat on top of a winepress.
The baraita then explains 'from one group to another' regarding eating, stating that one may switch eating groups at will.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on bringing offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on bringing offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai say one may bring peace-offerings but not lay hands on them, and may not bring burnt-offerings; Beit Hillel say one may bring both and lay hands. Ulla explains the dispute is about the festival peace-offering and the burnt-offering of appearance, based on the verse 'and you shall celebrate it as a festival to the Lord'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Beit Shammai permit bringing peace-offerings but not laying hands, and forbid burnt-offerings; Beit Hillel permit both and allow laying hands.

Ulla explains that the dispute is specifically about the festival peace-offering (שלמי חגיגה) regarding laying hands, and the burnt-offering of appearance (עולת ראייה) regarding being offered, based on the verse 'וְחַגֹּתֶם אוֹתוֹ חַג לַה׳'.

items.text: Vows and freewill offerings do not apply on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Vows and freewill offerings do not apply on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree vows and freewill offerings are not sacrificed on Yom Tov, and Rav Ada bar Ahava confirms this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree vows and freewill offerings are not sacrificed on Yom Tov.
Rav Ada bar Ahava confirms that vows and freewill offerings are not sacrificed on Yom Tov.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is cited, which seems to contradict Ulla's explanation. The Gemara resolves by rephrasing the baraita to align with Ulla's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar) that seems to contradict Ulla's explanation, stating that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on certain offerings.
The baraita specifies the point of disagreement: a burnt-offering that is part of the Festival and peace-offerings that are not, with Beit Shammai prohibiting and Beit Hillel permitting.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by rephrasing the baraita to align with Ulla's view, stating that the dispute is only about a burnt-offering of the Festival, while vow-offerings and gift-offerings are universally excluded.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative: a Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative: a Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the dispute is actually between Tanna'im, citing a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue about when to lay hands on peace-offerings brought on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to the previous resolution, arguing that the dispute is actually between Tanna'im and not settled by the earlier baraita.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about when to lay hands on peace-offerings brought on Yom Tov, showing the dispute is Tannaic.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that vow and free-will offerings are not brought on a Festival.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vow and free-will offerings are not brought on a Festival.

items.text: Tosefta dispute about bringing a thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Tosefta dispute about bringing a thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tosefta where the first Tanna prohibits bringing a thanksgiving offering on Passover due to leaven, and on Shavuot because it is a Festival, but permits it on Sukkot. Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon offer different opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tosefta dispute about bringing a thanksgiving offering on the three pilgrimage festivals.
Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon offer their own opinions on the matter.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the first Tanna's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the first Tanna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first Tanna prohibits bringing a thanksgiving offering on Passover, and Rav Adda bar Yitzchak explains it refers to the fourteenth of Nisan, when leaven is prohibited. The Gemara then clarifies that the prohibition on Shavuot is because vow offerings are not brought on a Festival, and the permission on Sukkot applies to Chol HaMoed.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the first Tanna's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the first Tanna's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the first Tanna's ruling that one does not bring a thanksgiving offering on Passover because of the leaven (חמץ) it contains.
The Gemara objects that the prohibition is obvious, since a thanksgiving offering contains leaven and leaven is forbidden on Passover.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Yitzchak (or Rav Shmuel bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Yitzchak (or Rav Shmuel bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Yitzchak explains that the ruling refers to the fourteenth of Nisan, when leaven is still permitted but one may not bring sacred offerings to the Temple when it is in a state of disrepair (בית הפסול).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first Tanna prohibits bringing a thanksgiving offering on Shavuot because he holds that vow offerings (נדרים ונדבות) are not brought on a Festival.
The Gemara asks when one may bring a thanksgiving offering on Sukkot, given the first Tanna's ruling.
The Gemara objects that if the permission were for the Festival day itself, it would contradict the first Tanna's prohibition on Shavuot, which is also a Festival.
The Gemara resolves that the permission applies to חול המועד (the intermediate days of the Festival), not the Festival day itself.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Shimon's opinion that offerings not brought on Passover cannot be brought on later festivals, arguing that even the Omer offering is brought on Shavuot. Abaye resolves that the dispute is about the prohibition of delaying (bal te'acher), not about the permissibility of sacrifice itself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Shimon's position: if we bring the Omer offering (סַלּוֹתֵי) on Shavuot even though it was not brought on Passover, then surely voluntary offerings (נְדָרִים וּנְדָבוֹת) should also be permitted.
Abaye resolves that all agree the sacrifice itself is permitted (שְׁרֵי); the dispute is only about the prohibition of delaying (בַּל תְּאַחֵר).
The Tanna Kamma holds that the Torah requires three pilgrimage festivals even if they occur out of order (שֶׁלֹּא כְּסִדְרָן), so delaying is permitted.

Rabbi Shimon holds that the festivals must be observed in order (כְּסִדְרָן); if a sacrifice was not brought on Passover, it cannot be brought on later festivals, thus the prohibition of delaying applies.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion and its rationale
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion and its rationale
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits bringing a thanksgiving offering on Sukkot even on the Festival itself, as he holds vow offerings are brought on a Festival. The Gemara explains why Sukkot is singled out, citing Rabbi Shimon's teaching that Sukkot is the last festival, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view that it causes the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits bringing the thanksgiving offering on חול המועד (the intermediate days) or on the Festival itself, concluding he permits it on the Festival because he holds that vow offerings are brought on a Festival.
The Gemara asks why Sukkot is singled out, and cites Rabbi Shimon's teaching that the verse mentions Sukkot last to indicate it is the final festival.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon explains that Sukkot is singled out because it is the last festival and thus causes the obligation of the vow offering to apply.

items.text: Discussion on exiting obligation with a thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Discussion on exiting obligation with a thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why it is obvious that one cannot fulfill the obligation of the Festival peace-offering (chagigah) with a thanksgiving offering, since it is a vow. It explains that even if one designates it for that purpose, it is not valid, and cites a query from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish to Rabbi Yochanan about a person who vows a thanksgiving offering to fulfill the chagigah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why it is obvious that one cannot fulfill the obligation of the Festival peace-offering (חגיגה) with a thanksgiving offering, since the rule is that an obligatory offering must come from non-sacred funds.
The Gemara answers that the statement is necessary even if one explicitly designates the thanksgiving offering for the purpose of the chagigah.
The Gemara cites a query from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish to Rabbi Yochanan about a person who vows a thanksgiving offering to fulfill the chagigah, illustrating the need for the ruling.

items.text: Gemara's discussion of a conditional vow
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of a conditional vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a case where someone says to give 400 zuz to a person and for him to marry his daughter. Rav Pappa explains that if the condition is phrased as 'give him and he will marry,' the recipient can take the money and choose whether to marry; but if phrased as 'he will marry and give him,' the money is contingent on marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may shave with second-tithe money, and receives an answer that the vow is valid but the nazirite does not shave.

Rav Pappa explains that if the condition is phrased as 'give him and he will marry,' the recipient may take the money and choose whether to marry; but if phrased as 'he will marry and give him,' the money is contingent on marriage.

items.text: Marimar's teaching and Ravina's correction
items.text_en: Marimar's teaching and Ravina's correction
items.desc_en: Marimar was teaching a halakhah in his own name, but Ravina corrected him, noting that they (the Babylonian academies) teach it as a question that Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Marimar was sitting and teaching a halakhah (הלכה) in his own name.
Ravina corrected Marimar, stating that they (the Babylonian academies) teach this tradition as a question that Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Tanna's teaching on obligatory burnt-offering requiring semikhah
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching on obligatory burnt-offering requiring semikhah
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba that the verse 'And he brought the burnt-offering and made it according to the ordinance' teaches that an obligatory burnt-offering requires semikhah, just like a voluntary burnt-offering.

sub.text: Tanna's teaching before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba that the verse 'וַיַּקְרֵב אֶת הָעוֹלָה וַיַּעֲשֶׂהָ כַּמִּשְׁפָּט' teaches that an obligatory burnt-offering requires semikhah (laying of hands), just like a voluntary burnt-offering.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on deriving obligatory from voluntary offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on deriving obligatory from voluntary offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Tanna's teaching follows Beit Shammai, who do not derive obligatory peace-offerings from voluntary ones. Beit Hillel would derive obligatory burnt-offerings from voluntary ones without a verse. The Gemara questions this, proposing alternative derivations, and concludes that the derivation comes from a combination of both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that the Tanna's teaching follows Beit Shammai, who do not derive obligatory peace-offerings from voluntary ones, implying that Beit Hillel would derive obligatory burnt-offerings from voluntary ones without a verse.
The Gemara objects: how do we know that Beit Hillel derive obligatory peace-offerings from voluntary ones? Perhaps they derive from obligatory burnt-offerings, which themselves require a verse.
The Gemara questions why Beit Hillel would not derive from voluntary peace-offerings (since they are common) and not from obligatory burnt-offerings (since they are entirely consumed).
The Gemara resolves that the derivation comes from a combination of both types of offerings.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on semikhah and its timing
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on semikhah and its timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosi states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that semikhah is required, but disagree on whether slaughter must immediately follow semikhah. Another version by Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda reverses the dispute: they agree on the timing but disagree on the requirement of semikhah itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai really hold that obligatory peace-offerings do not require semikhah (placing of hands).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosi (Rabbi Yosei) states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree semikhah is required, but disagree on whether slaughter must immediately follow semikhah.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing a second baraita from Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda, which reverses the dispute: they agree on the timing but disagree on the requirement of semikhah itself.

items.text: Story of Hillel the Elder bringing his offering on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Story of Hillel the Elder bringing his offering on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Hillel the Elder brought a female animal for a peace-offering on Yom Tov to perform semikhah. Beit Shammai's students challenged him, and he deceived them by saying it was a female (which cannot be a burnt-offering). That day Beit Shammai nearly established the halakhah according to their view, but Bava ben Buta, a student of Shammai who knew the halakhah follows Beit Hillel, intervened.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Hillel the Elder brought his burnt-offering to the Temple courtyard on a festival to perform סמיכה (placing hands), and when Beit Shammai's students challenged him, he deceived them by claiming it was a female peace-offering and swung its tail, causing them to leave.

The Gemara reports that on that day Beit Shammai gained the upper hand and sought to establish the הלכה (binding law) according to their view, but Bava ben Buta, a student of Shammai who knew the law follows Beit Hillel, intervened and sent a message.

items.text: Stories of Beit Hillel's victory and a sharp retort
items.text_en: Stories of Beit Hillel's victory and a sharp retort
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate how Beit Hillel prevailed in establishing that semikhah is permitted on Yom Tov. In the second story, a Beit Hillel student retorts to a Beit Shammai student's challenge with a clever comeback, which Abaye later uses to teach a lesson about measured responses.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes how Beit Hillel brought all the sheep of Kedar to the Temple courtyard, invited anyone who wished to perform semikhah (leaning on the sacrifice) to do so, and thereby established the halacha (binding law) in their favor without any opposition.
A second story relates that a Beit Hillel student, when challenged by a Beit Shammai student about performing semikhah, retorted with a sharp comeback and silenced him.

Abaye derives a lesson from the story: a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) should not respond to a colleague's remark with more than the colleague said, as the Beit Hillel student only matched the Beit Shammai student's question with an equally terse retort.

items.text: Abaye's lesson from the exchange
items.text_en: Abaye's lesson from the exchange
items.desc_en: Abaye derives a practical lesson: when a colleague says something to a scholar, the scholar should not respond with more than what was said to him, as illustrated by the student's retort.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives a practical lesson: a scholar should not respond to a colleague with more than what was said to him, as illustrated by the student's retort.

items.text: The formal debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai
items.text_en: The formal debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel argues that if an action is permitted for an individual on Yom Tov, it should certainly be permitted for the altar. Beit Shammai counters with nedarim u'nedavot, which are permitted for individuals but not for the altar. Beit Hillel distinguishes by noting that the olat re'iyah has a fixed time, while Beit Shammai argues it does not. Beit Hillel then cites a mishnah that after the festival, one is no longer liable. Finally, Beit Shammai cites the verse 'lachem' to exclude the altar, and Beit Hillel responds with 'laHashem' to include it, explaining 'lachem' excludes non-Jews and dogs.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel opens the debate with a kal vachomer argument: if an action forbidden for an individual is permitted for the altar, then an action permitted for an individual should certainly be permitted for the altar.
Beit Shammai objects with nedarim u'nedavot (vows and freewill offerings), which are permitted for individuals but forbidden for the altar on Yom Tov.
Beit Hillel distinguishes: nedarim u'nedavot have no fixed time, but the olat re'iyah (appearance-offering) has a fixed time.
Beit Shammai counters that even the olat re'iyah has no fixed time, citing a mishnah that one who did not celebrate on the first festival day may do so throughout the entire festival.
Beit Hillel rebuts that the olat re'iyah does have a fixed time, citing a mishnah that after the festival passes, one is no longer liable to bring it.
Beit Shammai cites the verse 'לָכֶם' (for yourselves) to exclude the altar from the permission of Yom Tov.
Beit Hillel responds with the verse 'לַה׳' (to the Lord) to include the altar, and explains that 'לָכֶם' excludes non-Jews and dogs, not the altar.

items.text: Abba Shaul's alternative formulation
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's alternative formulation
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul presents the same argument in different language, comparing the individual's closed table to the master's open table, and concluding that one's table should not be full while the master's is empty.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul presents the argument in a different formulation: if when your table is empty your master's table is full, then when your table is full, it is certainly fitting that your master's table be full.

items.text: The underlying dispute about nedarim u'nedavot
items.text_en: The underlying dispute about nedarim u'nedavot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the debate between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai hinges on whether nedarim u'nedavot may be offered on Yom Tov. One opinion holds they are offered, the other that they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the underlying dispute is between the two positions in the baraita, and explains that one holds nedarim and nedavot are offered on Yom Tov, while the other holds they are not.
One opinion holds that nedarim u'nedavot (vow and freewill offerings) are offered on Yom Tov, permitting semikhah.
The other opinion holds that nedarim u'nedavot are not offered on Yom Tov, prohibiting semikhah.

items.text: Rav Huna's clarification: nedarim u'nedavot are not even biblically valid on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rav Huna's clarification: nedarim u'nedavot are not even biblically valid on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Huna argues that according to the opinion that nedarim u'nedavot are not offered on Yom Tov, it is not merely a rabbinic decree but a biblical prohibition. He proves this from the two loaves, which are a chovat hayom and yet do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that according to the opinion that nedarim and nedavot are not offered on Yom Tov, this is not merely a rabbinic decree lest one delay, but rather a Torah-level prohibition, as demonstrated by the two loaves (שתי הלחם) which are a חובת היום (obligation of the day) and yet do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Rav Huna concludes that even biblically they are not valid, proving this from the two loaves (שתי הלחם), which are a חובת היום (obligation of the day) and yet do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

items.text: Dispute about the status of an animal slaughtered on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute about the status of an animal slaughtered on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one transgressed and slaughtered a neder or nedavah on Yom Tov, what is the law? Rava says the blood is sprinkled to permit the meat for eating; Rabbah bar Rav Huna says the blood is sprinkled to permit the burning of the fats in the evening. The difference between them is a case where the meat became impure or was lost.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question: according to the opinion that nedarim and nedavot are not offered on Yom Tov, if one transgressed and slaughtered such an animal, what is the law regarding the blood?
Rava answers: the blood is sprinkled to permit the meat for eating.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna answers: the blood is sprinkled to permit the burning of the fats in the evening.
The gemara asks: what is the practical difference between these two positions?
The gemara answers: the difference is a case where the meat became impure or was lost — according to Rava the blood is not sprinkled, but according to Rabbah bar Rav Huna it is sprinkled.

items.text: Objection from the law of the two loaves
items.text_en: Objection from the law of the two loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about the two loaves of Shavuot: if slaughtered improperly or at the wrong time, the blood is sprinkled and the meat eaten, but on Shabbat the blood is not sprinkled. This challenges the earlier positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about the lambs of Shavuot (כבשי עצרת) that were slaughtered improperly: the blood may be sprinkled and the meat eaten, but if it is Shabbat, one may not sprinkle, and if one did sprinkle — the baraita is cut off.

items.text: Transition from previous daf: distinction between Shabbat and Yom Tov shevut
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf: distinction between Shabbat and Yom Tov shevut
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between Rava and Rabbah bar Rav Huna by distinguishing between shevut of Shabbat and shevut of Yom Tov, allowing the offering to be accepted conditionally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Rava and Rabbah bar Rav Huna by distinguishing between shevut of Shabbat and shevut of Yom Tov, allowing the offering to be accepted conditionally.

items.text: Rav Avya's question about a half-owned animal
items.text_en: Rav Avya's question about a half-owned animal
items.desc_en: Rav Avya the Elder asks Rav Huna whether an animal half-owned by a Jew and half by a non-Jew may be slaughtered on Yom Tov. Rav Huna permits it, but when pressed about the difference from nedarim u'nedavot, he dismisses the question cryptically.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya Saba asks Rav Huna whether an animal half-owned by a gentile and half by a Jew may be slaughtered on Yom Tov.
Rav Huna answers that it is permitted.
Rav Avya Saba objects: what is the difference between this case and vowed or freewill offerings, which are forbidden to slaughter on Yom Tov?
Rav Huna dismisses the question with the idiom 'a raven flew away,' indicating he had no answer at the moment.

items.text: Rabbah's astonishment and Rav Huna's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbah's astonishment and Rav Huna's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbah, Rav Huna's son, questions why his father dismissed Rav Avya so abruptly. Rav Huna explains that he was in a state of weakness and needed support, and Rav Avya asked a question requiring a reasoned answer.

sub.desc_en: After they left, Rabbah, Rav Huna's son, remarks that Rav Avya Saba is a great man, questioning why his father did not give a proper answer.
Rav Huna explains that he was distracted by the verse 'support me with raisin cakes' and that Rav Avya asked a matter requiring reasoning.

items.text: Reason for permitting the half-owned animal
items.text_en: Reason for permitting the half-owned animal
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the half-owned animal is permitted because it is impossible to get an olive's worth of meat without slaughtering the whole animal, unlike nedarim u'nedavot which are entirely for the Most High.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning: a half-owned animal is permitted because it is impossible to get a kezayit of meat without slaughter, whereas vowed offerings are forbidden because the priests receive their portion from the table of the Most High.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on half-owned dough
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on half-owned dough
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda permits slaughtering a half-owned animal for the same reason, but forbids baking half-owned dough because it is possible to divide it before kneading.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a half-owned animal is permitted to slaughter on Yom Tov because it is impossible to get a kezayit of meat without slaughter, but a half-owned dough is forbidden to bake because it can be divided before kneading.

items.text: Objection from the baraita of dog dough and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita of dog dough and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Chanilai objects with a baraita that permits baking dog dough on Yom Tov even though it could be divided. The Gemara answers that dog dough is different because one can appease the dogs with neveilah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Chanilai objects by citing a baraita that permits baking dog dough on Yom Tov, even though it could be divided.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing dog dough, since one can appease the dogs with neveilah (carrion), making the dough unnecessary for them.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda's use of 'ho'il' and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda's use of 'ho'il' and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda accepts the principle of 'ho'il', citing a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah about baking from Yom Tov to a weekday. It concludes that the case of dog dough is not based on 'ho'il' but on the certainty of having neveilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda's use of the principle of 'ho'il' by citing a dispute where Rav Chisda rejects it regarding baking from Yom Tov to a weekday.
The Gemara resolves that the case of dog dough is not based on 'ho'il' but on the certainty of having neveilah to feed the dogs.

items.text: Question about soldiers' dough and Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Question about soldiers' dough and Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about dough given to soldiers by the government: may it be baked on Yom Tov? Rav Huna rules that if each portion is fit for a child, it is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.

sub.text: Question from the students to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Question from the students to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Huna whether the bread of the soldiers' children, who are given flour, may be baked on Yom Tov.
Rav Huna answers that if the soldiers give bread to a child without being particular, each loaf is fit for a child and it is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.

items.text: Story of Shimon HaTimni and the principle 'lachem'
items.text_en: Story of Shimon HaTimni and the principle 'lachem'
items.desc_en: A story is told about Shimon HaTimni who slaughtered a calf for soldiers on Yom Tov. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava criticizes him, citing the verse 'lachem' — not for non-Jews. The Gemara explains that the calf was tereifah, and a dispute among Tannaim about whether food fit for dogs is included in the permission is cited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Shimon HaTimni missed the study hall because soldiers came and he slaughtered a calf for them on Yom Tov.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava objects, citing the verse 'לָכֶם' (for yourselves) to argue that Yom Tov slaughter is permitted only for Jews, not for non-Jews.
The Gemara questions why the slaughter was problematic, since the calf was fit for human consumption.
Rav Yosef answers that the calf was a טריפה (ritually unfit animal), so it was not fit for human consumption.
The Gemara objects that even a טריפה is fit for dogs, so it should still be permitted under the Yom Tov allowance.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a dispute among Tannaim: one opinion holds that 'לָכֶם' excludes food fit only for dogs, while another opinion includes it.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on 'for you'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on 'for you'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili interprets 'for you' (Exodus 12:16) to exclude dogs, while Rabbi Akiva includes animals. The Gemara explains the rationale: dogs' sustenance is your responsibility, but gentiles' is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yose HaGelili interprets 'for you' (Exodus 12:16) to exclude dogs, while Rabbi Akiva includes animals, and the Gemara explains that 'for you' excludes gentiles.
The Gemara explains the rationale: dogs are included because their sustenance is your responsibility, while gentiles are excluded because their sustenance is not.

items.text: Abaye's question to Rav Yosef about feeding animals on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Abaye's question to Rav Yosef about feeding animals on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef how one may throw animal feed on Yom Tov according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili. Rav Yosef answers that the feed is fit for fuel (heating), and on Shabbat it can be moved with bread, following Shmuel's principle.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef how one may throw animal feed on Yom Tov according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who excludes animals from the permission of 'לָכֶם'.
Rav Yosef answers that dry feed is fit for fuel (heating), and even wet feed is fit for a large fire, so it may be moved on Yom Tov.
Rav Yosef adds that on Shabbat the feed can be moved together with bread, following Shmuel's principle that one may accomplish all needs with bread.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling on inviting a gentile
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling on inviting a gentile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi permits inviting a gentile on Shabbat but forbids it on Yom Tov due to a decree lest one cook extra for him.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that one may invite a gentile on Shabbat but not on Yom Tov, due to a decree lest one cook extra for him.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and discussion on leftover wine
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and discussion on leftover wine
