items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov forbids inviting a gentile even on Shabbat due to leftover wine (which may be used for idolatry). The Gemara discusses moving the cup with the wine, citing Rava's precedent, but distinguishes between prohibited benefit and non-prohibited items.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that even on Shabbat one may not invite a gentile due to the leftover wine in the cups, which is forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara asks: If so, our own leftover wine should also be prohibited.
The Gemara answers: Our leftover wine is fit for chickens, so it is not muktzeh.
The Gemara objects: Their leftover wine is also fit for chickens.
The Gemara rejects this: Their leftover wine is forbidden for benefit (due to idolatry), so it cannot be handled.
The Gemara asks: Could one move the leftover wine along with the cup itself, as a secondary object?
The Gemara cites Rava's ruling that one may move a coal pan along with its ashes, even if there are broken wood pieces on it, to support moving the cup with the wine.
The Gemara distinguishes: There, the broken wood is not forbidden for benefit, but here the leftover wine is forbidden for benefit, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Rav Acha of Difti's question about a waste shovel
items.text_en: Rav Acha of Difti's question about a waste shovel
items.desc_en: Rav Acha of Difti asks Ravina whether the cup could be treated like a waste shovel (which is moved for its own sake). Ravina responds that one does not initially make a waste shovel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha of Difti asks Ravina whether the cup with wine remnants could be treated like a גרף של רעי (waste shovel), which is moved for its own sake.
Ravina responds that one does not make a גרף של רעי (waste shovel) לכתחילה (the ideal standard), implying that one may not initially create a situation requiring such handling.

items.text: Rava's public ruling and Marimar and Mar Zutra's practice
items.text_en: Rava's public ruling and Marimar and Mar Zutra's practice
items.desc_en: Rava publicly rules like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Marimar and Mar Zutra, when a gentile visits on Yom Tov, tell him they will only serve what they already prepared, avoiding extra cooking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rava publicly ruled like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and that Marimar and Mar Zutra, when a gentile visited on Yom Tov, would tell him they would only serve what they had already prepared, avoiding extra trouble.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on heating water and making a fire
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on heating water and making a fire
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records Beit Shammai's prohibition and Beit Hillel's permission to heat water for feet on Yom Tov, and permits making a fire to warm oneself. The Gemara questions who authored the fire clause, and a baraita clarifies that Beit Shammai prohibits it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai prohibit heating water for feet unless fit for drinking, Beit Hillel permit it, and one may make a fire and warm oneself.
The Gemara asks whether the fire clause is agreed upon by all (with Beit Shammai distinguishing whole-body vs. limb benefit) or only Beit Hillel's view.
A baraita clarifies that Beit Shammai prohibit making a fire to warm oneself, so the fire clause is only Beit Hillel's view.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's stringencies and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's stringencies and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three stringencies of Rabban Gamliel following Beit Shammai: not insulating hot water, not setting up a candelabrum, and baking only thin loaves. The Gemara questions the case, and Rav Huna explains it refers to one who did not prepare an eruv tavshilin, and the Sages permitted only enough for his needs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three stringencies of Rabban Gamliel following Beit Shammai: not insulating hot water, not setting up a candelabrum, and baking only thin loaves, with a supporting story about his father's household.

The Gemara asks what the circumstances are regarding the insulation of hot water, questioning the reasoning of both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel depending on whether an עירוב תבשילין (joining of cooked foods) was prepared.
Rav Huna answers that the case is where one did not prepare an עירוב תבשילין (joining of cooked foods), and the Sages permitted only what is needed for his basic sustenance.

The Gemara notes that Rav Huna's ruling is consistent with his own principle that one who did not prepare an עירוב תבשילין (joining of cooked foods) may have only one loaf baked and one pot cooked for him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and baraita on eruv tavshilin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and baraita on eruv tavshilin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may light a lamp for someone who did not prepare an eruv tavshilin. A baraita adds that one may also fry a small fish for him, and lists other permitted actions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may light a lamp for someone who did not prepare an eruv tavshilin.
In the name of Rabbi Yitzchak, it is added that one may also fry a small fish for him.
A baraita is cited that supports the Mishnah, listing permitted actions for one who did not prepare an eruv tavshilin, including baking, insulating, lighting, heating, and frying a small fish.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding insulation
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding insulation
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the leniency for insulation applies only when one did not prepare an eruv, because insulation is a conspicuous act that appears to be done for Shabbat, so it is forbidden if one did prepare an eruv.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the leniency for insulation applies only when one did not prepare an eruv, because insulation is a conspicuous act that appears to be done for Shabbat, so it is forbidden if one did prepare an eruv.

items.text: Abaye's objection from Chananya's statement
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from Chananya's statement
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's distinction, citing Chananya who says that according to Beit Shammai, one may only bake if he prepared an eruv with bread, and may only insulate if he had hot water insulated from before Yom Tov. This implies that even though insulation is conspicuous, it is permitted if he had hot water.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's distinction, citing Chananya's statement that according to Beit Shammai, one may only bake if he prepared an eruv with bread, and may only insulate if he had hot water insulated from before Yom Tov, implying that even conspicuous insulation is permitted if he had hot water.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: case of two people
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: case of two people
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves two people, one who prepared an eruv and one who did not, and the ruling follows Chananya's opinion in accordance with Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves two people, one who prepared an eruv and one who did not, and the ruling follows Chananya's opinion in accordance with Beit Shammai.

items.text: Discussion on erecting a candelabrum
items.text_en: Discussion on erecting a candelabrum
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what action is prohibited when one may not erect a candelabrum on Yom Tov. Rav Chinana bar Bisna explains that it refers to a sectional candelabrum, which appears like building. Beit Shammai hold that there is building in vessels, while Beit Hillel hold there is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what prohibited action is involved in erecting a candelabrum on Yom Tov.
Rav Chinana bar Bisna explains that the case involves a sectional candelabrum, which appears like building.

sub.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's positions
sub.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's positions
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai hold that there is building in vessels, while Beit Hillel hold that there is no building or dismantling in vessels.

items.text: Ulla's incident and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.text_en: Ulla's incident and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.desc_en: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda's house, and Rav Yehuda's attendant erected a lamp. Rav Yehuda objected, citing that putting oil in a lamp is liable for kindling, and taking oil from it is liable for extinguishing. Ulla admitted he was unaware of this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Ulla visited Rav Yehuda's house, and Rav Yehuda's attendant erected a lamp.
Rav Yehuda objected to Ulla, citing that putting oil in a lamp is liable for kindling (מבעיר), and taking oil from it is liable for extinguishing (מכבה).
Ulla admitted that he was unaware of this ruling.

items.text: Rav permits kinba
items.text_en: Rav permits kinba
items.desc_en: Rav rules that kinba (a type of wick or lamp) is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that kinba (a type of wick or lamp) is permitted for use on Yom Tov.

items.text: Inquiry about extinguishing a lamp for another reason
items.text_en: Inquiry about extinguishing a lamp for another reason
items.desc_en: Abba bar Marta asks Abaye whether one may extinguish a lamp for another reason (not to save the lamp). Abaye responds that if possible, one should use another room, make a partition, or cover the lamp; if none are possible, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Abba bar Marta asks Abaye whether one may extinguish a lamp on Yom Tov for a reason other than saving the lamp itself.
Abaye responds that if possible, one should use another room, make a partition, or cover the lamp with a vessel.
When no alternative is available, Abaye rules that extinguishing the lamp is forbidden.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on extinguishing a coal
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on extinguishing a coal
items.desc_en: Abaye objects with a baraita that permits extinguishing a coal to prevent smoke damage. Abaye responds that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, while he rules according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects with a baraita that permits extinguishing a coal to prevent smoke damage, contradicting his earlier ruling.
Abaye responds that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, while he rules according to the Rabbis.

items.text: Inquiry about extinguishing a fire on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Inquiry about extinguishing a fire on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one may extinguish a fire on Yom Tov to prevent financial loss. Rabbah rules it is forbidden, as only life-threatening situations override Shabbat and Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one may extinguish a fire on Yom Tov to prevent financial loss, distinguishing it from life-threatening situations.
Rabbah rules that extinguishing a fire on Yom Tov for financial loss is forbidden.

items.text: Objection from the same baraita
items.text_en: Objection from the same baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye again objects with the baraita permitting extinguishing to prevent smoke damage. Rabbah responds that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, while he rules according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing the baraita that permits extinguishing a flame to prevent smoke damage, implying a contradiction to Rabbah's ruling.
Rabbah answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view, while he himself rules according to the Rabbis who forbid it.

items.text: Inquiry about applying eye makeup on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Inquiry about applying eye makeup on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Ameimar whether one may apply eye makeup on Yom Tov. For dangerous conditions it is permitted even on Shabbat; for non-dangerous conditions like the end of an eye ailment or to brighten the eye, Ameimar rules it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Ameimar whether applying eye makeup is permitted on Yom Tov, distinguishing between dangerous conditions (already permitted on Shabbat) and non-dangerous ones like the end of an eye ailment or cosmetic brightening.
Ameimar rules that applying eye makeup for non-dangerous purposes is forbidden on Yom Tov.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on extinguishing a coal
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on extinguishing a coal
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects with the same baraita about extinguishing a coal. Ameimar distinguishes as before.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar's ruling using the same baraita about extinguishing a coal, and Ameimar distinguishes as before.

items.text: Ameimar permits eye makeup via a non-Jew on Shabbat
items.text_en: Ameimar permits eye makeup via a non-Jew on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Ameimar permits applying eye makeup via a non-Jew on Shabbat, citing Ulla and Rav Hamnuna that non-Jews may perform non-dangerous medical needs. Rav Ashi objects that Ameimar assists the non-Jew by opening and closing his eye, but Ameimar cites Rav Zevid that such assistance is insignificant.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar permits or himself applies eye makeup via a non-Jew on Shabbat.
Rav Ashi objects that Ameimar assists the non-Jew by opening and closing his eye, which is forbidden.
Ameimar responds that Rav Zevid holds such assistance is insignificant (אֵין בּוֹ מַמָּשׁ).

items.text: Ameimar permits eye makeup on the second day of Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Ameimar permits eye makeup on the second day of Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Ameimar permits applying eye makeup on the second day of Rosh Hashanah. Rav Ashi objects based on Rava's ruling that a corpse on the first day of Yom Tov is handled by non-Jews, but on the second day by Jews, even on Rosh Hashanah.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar permits applying eye makeup on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.
Rav Ashi objects, citing Rava's ruling that a corpse on the second day of Yom Tov is handled by Jews even on Rosh Hashanah, implying the day is fully sanctified.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the egg
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the egg
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous ruling does not apply to an egg, but the speaker explains he follows Nehardeans who include eggs. He dismisses the concern about a leap month in Elul by citing Rav Chinana bar Kahana that since Ezra's time there has been no leap Elul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous ruling does not apply to an egg.

The speaker explains he follows the Nehardeans who include eggs, and dismisses the concern about a leap month in Elul by citing Rav Chinana bar Kahana that since Ezra's time there has been no leap Elul.

items.text: Mishnah and Baraita on baking thick bread on Pesach
items.text_en: Mishnah and Baraita on baking thick bread on Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may only bake thin loaves, not thick ones. A Baraita records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, with Rav Huna defining thick bread as a handbreadth, based on the showbread.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that on Passover one may only bake thin loaves, not thick ones, and Beit Hillel permits thick bread; Rav Huna defines thick bread as a handbreadth, citing the showbread.
A Baraita records the dispute: Beit Shammai forbid baking thick bread on Pesach, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Rav Huna defines 'thick bread' as a handbreadth (טפח), deriving this measure from the showbread (לחם הפנים).

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection to the comparison with showbread
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection to the comparison with showbread
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges the analogy to the showbread, arguing that the showbread was made by priests who are diligent, with kneaded dough, dry wood, a hot oven, and a metal oven, whereas ordinary people are not so diligent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that if the leniency applies to the diligent and to kneaded bread, it should not apply to the non-diligent and to non-kneaded bread.
Rav Yosef continues his objection, arguing that if the leniency applies to dry wood and a hot metal oven, it should not apply to wet wood and a cold clay oven.

items.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's inquiry about 'thick bread'
items.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba's inquiry about 'thick bread'
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba asked Rabbi (or Rav) in private what 'thick bread' means, and was told it means 'abundant bread'. The Gemara explains that it is called 'thick' because it requires much kneading, or because in that Tanna's locale, abundant bread is called thick bread.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that he asked Rabbi (or Rav) in private: what is 'thick bread'?
The answer given is that 'thick bread' means 'abundant bread'.
An alternative version of the tradition is cited, where Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said in the name of Rav that he asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in private, and the answer was 'abundant bread'.
The Gemara explains why it is called 'thick bread': either because it requires much kneading, or because in that Tanna's locale, abundant bread is called thick bread.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on the restriction applying to all Yom Tov
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on the restriction applying to all Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the restriction on thick bread is specifically for Pesach, since it is unnecessary labor. It answers that indeed it applies to all Yom Tov, but the Tanna is discussing Yom Tov of Pesach. A Baraita confirms that Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit abundant bread on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the prohibition of baking thick bread is specific to Passover, since it involves unnecessary labor and should apply to all festivals.

The Gemara answers that indeed it applies to all festivals, and the Tanna is discussing the festival of Passover; a baraita confirms that Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit abundant bread on any festival.
A Baraita confirms that Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit abundant bread on Yom Tov, supporting the Gemara's answer.

items.text: Mishnah: Three leniencies of Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three leniencies of Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabban Gamliel ruled leniently in three matters: sweeping the house, placing incense on Yom Tov, and roasting a whole kid on Passover night. The Sages forbid these.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah said three leniencies: sweeping between beds, placing incense on a festival, and roasting a kid on Passover night; the Sages forbid them.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the dispute about incense
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the dispute about incense
items.desc_en: Rav Asi initially says the dispute is only about burning incense completely, but for smelling it is permitted. The Gemara brings a Baraita that seems to contradict this, showing that Rabban Gamliel's household used a pre-smoked iron vessel. The Gemara concludes that Rav Asi's statement was actually reversed: the dispute is about smelling, but for burning completely it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages is only about burning incense completely (לגמר), but for smelling it, all agree it is permitted.

The Gemara raises a contradiction from a Baraita: Rabban Gamliel's household did not place incense on Yom Tov but used a pre-smoked iron vessel, implying that even smelling was forbidden, contradicting Rav Asi's leniency.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Asi's statement was actually reversed: the dispute is about smelling, but for burning completely (לגמר) it is forbidden.

items.text: Debate on smoking coals on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Debate on smoking coals on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised about smoking coals. Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav forbids it, Shmuel permits it. Rav Huna forbids because it extinguishes, and Rav Nachman questions if it is because it ignites. Rav Huna explains that initially it extinguishes and later ignites. Rav Yehuda adds that on a coal it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is it permitted to smoke (coals) on Yom Tov?

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba in the name of Rav rules that smoking coals is forbidden.
Shmuel permits smoking coals on Yom Tov.
Rav Huna forbids smoking coals because it extinguishes the coal.
Rav Nachman objects: why not say the prohibition is because it ignites (the coal)?
Rav Huna explains that initially the coal is extinguished and later it ignites, so both concerns apply.
Rav Yehuda concludes that smoking directly on a coal is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute about placing incense on a shard vs. a coal
items.text_en: Dispute about placing incense on a shard vs. a coal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing incense on a shard on Yom Tov. Rabbah forbids it because it creates a new fragrance (מוליד ריחא), while Rava permits it on a coal, comparing it to roasting meat on coals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that placing incense on a shard on Yom Tov is permitted.
Rabbah forbids placing incense on a shard because it creates a new fragrance (מוליד ריחא).
Rabbah and Rav Yosef both rule that covering a vessel with a cloth on Yom Tov is forbidden because it creates a new fragrance.
The Gemara asks why this is different from rubbing a fruit and smelling it, or cutting it and smelling it, which is permitted.
The Gemara answers that there the fragrance already exists and one merely adds to it, whereas here one creates a new fragrance entirely.
Rava permits placing incense on a coal, comparing it to roasting meat on coals where the smoke is a byproduct, not a new creation.

items.text: Gemara's question and distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why creating fragrance is forbidden while smelling a fruit and enhancing its scent is permitted. It answers that in the latter case the fragrance already exists, whereas here a new fragrance is generated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why creating fragrance is forbidden while smelling a fruit and enhancing its scent is permitted.
The Gemara answers that in the case of smelling a fruit the fragrance already exists, whereas here a new fragrance is generated.

items.text: The dispute about קטורא (incense burning)
items.text_en: The dispute about קטורא (incense burning)
items.desc_en: Rav Geviha permitted קטורא (burning incense) on Yom Tov. Amemar questioned whether it is a craftsman's act (if done by hand) or forbidden because it extinguishes or creates fragrance. Rav Ashi explained it is permitted like roasting meat on coals. A second version records Amemar's concern about creating fragrance, and Rav Ashi reaffirms the leniency.

sub.desc_en: Rav Geviha taught at the entrance of the Exilarch's house that burning incense (קטורא) is permitted on Yom Tov.
Amemar questioned what 'קטורא' means: if done by hand it is a craftsman's act, and if for smoke it is forbidden because it extinguishes the coals.
Rav Ashi answered that it is always for smoke, and it is permitted like roasting meat on coals.
An alternative version of the discussion is introduced.
In the alternative version, Amemar questioned whether 'קטורא' is a craftsman's act if done by hand, or forbidden because it creates fragrance.
Rav Ashi reaffirmed that it is always for smoke, and it is permitted like roasting meat on coals, citing the authority of a great man.

items.text: The case of גדי מקולס (roasted kid)
items.text_en: The case of גדי מקולס (roasted kid)
items.desc_en: A baraita relates that Todos of Rome instituted eating a roasted kid on Passover eve. The Sages threatened him with excommunication for causing Israelites to eat what resembles sacrifices outside the Temple. The Gemara clarifies that it is only similar to sacrifices, not actual consecrated meat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Yosei taught that Todos of Rome instituted eating a roasted kid on Passover eve, and the Sages threatened him with excommunication for causing Israelites to eat consecrated meat outside the Temple.
The Gemara objects that it cannot be actual consecrated meat, and resolves that the Sages meant it resembled consecrated meat.

items.text: Mishnah: Three leniencies of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three leniencies of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three matters where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits and the Sages forbid: a cow going out with a strap between its horns, combing an animal on Yom Tov, and grinding pepper in its mill. Rabbi Yehuda adds a distinction between combing (קירוד) and scraping (קרצוף).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits three things which the Sages forbid, and lists the first: a cow going out with a strap between its horns.
The Mishnah lists the second and third leniencies: combing an animal on Yom Tov and grinding pepper in its mill.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between combing (קירוד), which causes a wound and is forbidden, and scraping (קרצוף), which is permitted.
The Sages rule that neither combing nor scraping is permitted on Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification about the cow
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification about the cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had only one cow, given that he tithed 13,000 calves annually. It answers that the cow belonged to his neighbor, but because he did not protest, it was called by his name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had only one cow, given that he tithed 13,000 calves annually.
A baraita answers that the cow belonged to his neighbor, but because he did not protest, it was called by his name.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute about combing
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute about combing
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines קירוד (small comb, causes a wound) and קרצוף (large comb, no wound). It explains the three opinions: Rabbi Yehuda holds דבר שאינו מתכוין is forbidden but does not decree קרצוף because of קירוד; the Sages also hold it forbidden and decree; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya follows Rabbi Shimon that דבר שאינו מתכוין is permitted, allowing both.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines קירוד (small comb, causes a wound) and קרצוף (large comb, no wound).
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's view: דבר שאינו מתכוין (an unintended act) is forbidden, but he does not decree קרצוף because of קירוד.
The Gemara explains the Sages' view: they agree with Rabbi Yehuda that דבר שאינו מתכוין is forbidden, but they decree קרצוף because of קירוד.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view: he follows Rabbi Shimon that דבר שאינו מתכוין is permitted, allowing both combing methods.

items.text: Ruling in accordance with Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Ruling in accordance with Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, since Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya agrees with him. Rava challenges that one could also rule like Rabbi Yehuda since the Sages agree with him, but Rav Nachman maintains his position.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Nachman citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rava provides the reason that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya agrees with Rabbi Shimon.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman, arguing that one could equally rule like Rabbi Yehuda since the Sages agree with him.
Rav Nachman maintains his position, stating that he personally holds like Rabbi Shimon, and adds the further support that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya agrees with him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Pepper mill impurity
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Pepper mill impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a pepper mill is susceptible to impurity because it serves three functions: as a receptacle, a metal vessel, and a sieve.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a pepper mill is susceptible to impurity because it serves three functions: as a receptacle, a metal vessel, and a sieve.

items.text: Gemara: Clarification of the three parts
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarification of the three parts
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the bottom part is a receptacle, the middle part is a sieve, and the top part is a metal vessel.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna clarifies the Mishnah's three parts of the pepper mill: the bottom is a receptacle, the middle is a sieve, and the top is a metal vessel.

items.text: Mishnah: Small wagon and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah: Small wagon and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a small wagon is susceptible to midras impurity, may be carried on Shabbat, and may only be dragged over vessels. Rabbi Yehuda adds that no vessels may be dragged except the wagon, because it presses down.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the initial ruling: a small wagon is susceptible to midras impurity, may be carried on Shabbat, and may only be dragged over vessels.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that no vessels may be dragged on Shabbat except the wagon, because it presses down (כובשת) rather than plowing a furrow.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the wagon's laws and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the wagon's laws and attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the wagon is susceptible to midras impurity and why it may be carried. It then notes that the prohibition against dragging on the ground is because it creates a furrow, and attributes this view to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended act, unlike Rabbi Shimon who permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the child's wagon is susceptible to midras impurity (because the child leans on it) and why it may be carried on Shabbat (because it retains the status of a vessel).
The Gemara asks why the wagon may not be dragged on the ground, and answers that it creates a furrow (a prohibited act).
The Gemara attributes the prohibition to Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended act (דבר שאין מתכוין).

The Gemara contrasts Rabbi Shimon's position, who permits an unintended act, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon allows dragging a bed, chair, or bench as long as one does not intend to create a furrow.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statement and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's statement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda permits dragging the wagon if it creates a furrow, and resolves that there are two Tannaitic opinions regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier attribution of the Mishnah's first clause to Rabbi Yehuda by citing the second clause, where Rabbi Yehuda permits dragging the wagon specifically because it 'כובשת (presses down the ground)' — implying it does not create a furrow (חריץ), contradicting the earlier assumption.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that there are two Tannaitic traditions (תרי תנאי) regarding Rabbi Yehuda's opinion — one holding he forbids any unintended furrow, the other holding he permits dragging the wagon because it only presses down (כובשת) without creating a furrow.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah: Trapping on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: Trapping on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new chapter, stating that one may not trap fish from fishponds on Yom Tov, but may trap animals and birds from enclosures. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that not all enclosures are equal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens a new chapter, stating that one may not trap fish from fishponds on Yom Tov.
The Mishnah adds that one may not place food before the fish, but may trap animals and birds from enclosures and provide them food.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a qualification that not all enclosures are equal, introducing a general rule.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal lacking hunting (i.e., not yet caught) is forbidden on Yom Tov, while one not lacking hunting is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: an animal lacking hunting (not yet caught) is forbidden on Yom Tov, while one not lacking hunting is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction from baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction from baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita forbids trapping from enclosures of animals and birds on Yom Tov, seemingly conflicting with the Mishnah's leniency for animals not lacking hunting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita forbids trapping from enclosures on Yom Tov, conflicting with the Mishnah's permission for animals not lacking hunting.

items.text: First resolution for animals, difficulty with birds
items.text_en: First resolution for animals, difficulty with birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for animals by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita to the Rabbis, citing a dispute about trapping. However, the contradiction for birds remains, and a proposed distinction between covered and uncovered enclosures fails because a house is like a covered enclosure yet both agree that a bird in a house is not trapped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for animals by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita to the Rabbis.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute the definition of trapping, supporting the attribution.
The Gemara raises the remaining contradiction for birds and proposes a distinction between a covered and uncovered enclosure.
The Gemara rejects the distinction because a house is like a covered enclosure, yet both Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages agree that a bird in a house is not considered trapped.

items.text: Resolution for birds: the case of the צפור דרור
items.text_en: Resolution for birds: the case of the צפור דרור
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah deals with the צפור דרור (swift), which does not accept dominion and is considered wild even in a house, thus requiring hunting.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah deals with the ציפור דרור (swallow), which does not accept domestication, as taught by the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael supports this by explaining that the swift is called 'דרור' because it dwells in a house as if in a field, i.e., it remains wild.

items.text: Resolution for animals: small vs. large enclosure
items.text_en: Resolution for animals: small vs. large enclosure
items.desc_en: The Gemara now resolves the animal contradiction by distinguishing between a small enclosure (where the animal can be caught easily) and a large one (where it cannot). Rav Ashi defines the size based on whether one can run and catch it in one lunge, or by other criteria.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding animals by distinguishing between a small enclosure (ביבר קטן) where the animal can be caught easily, and a large enclosure (ביבר גדול) where it cannot.
The Gemara asks for the definition of a small enclosure versus a large enclosure.

Rav Ashi defines a small enclosure as one where one can run after the animal and catch it in one lunge, and offers alternative criteria based on the presence of corners or the shadow of the walls meeting.

items.text: Dispute about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a ruling that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says not all enclosures are equal. Abaye questions whether this implies a dispute, and Rav Yosef rebukes him for asking a pointless question.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that not all enclosures are equal regarding the permissibility of hunting on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef transmits a tradition in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Abaye questions Rav Yosef: the statement that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel implies that there was a dispute — who disagreed?
Rav Yosef rebukes Abaye, saying 'What does it matter to you? Learn the Gemara thoroughly — do you want to be a pruner?' (i.e., don't waste time on irrelevant questions).

items.text: Definition of 'lacking hunting' and further clarifications
items.text_en: Definition of 'lacking hunting' and further clarifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'lacking hunting' as an animal that requires saying 'bring a net and trap it.' Abaye objects that geese and chickens fit this yet are exempt from liability for trapping. Rabbah bar Rav Huna distinguishes based on whether they come to their coop at evening. A further objection about doves leads to a refined criterion: whether their food is your responsibility. Rav Mari offers an alternative: whether they are accustomed to being raised.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a definition of 'lacking hunting' and Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers: any animal that requires saying 'bring a net and trap it.'
Abaye objects that geese and chickens fit this definition yet a baraita exempts one who traps them from liability.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Shmuel distinguishes: geese and chickens do not come to their coop at evening, so they are considered lacking hunting.
The Gemara objects that doves of a dovecote come to their coop at evening yet trapping them is prohibited, contradicting the criterion.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's refined answer
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's refined answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Shmuel refines the criterion: the animal must both come to its coop at evening and have its food be your responsibility.
Rav Mari offers an alternative criterion: whether the animals are accustomed to being raised, and the Gemara clarifies that the reference is to being accustomed to a coop.

items.text: Mishnah on traps and the rule of uncertain preparedness
items.text_en: Mishnah on traps and the rule of uncertain preparedness
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses traps set before Yom Tov and the case of a gentile bringing fish to Rabban Gamliel. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah actually teaches that uncertain preparedness is forbidden, and Rabban Gamliel permits it. Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the halakha does not follow Rabban Gamliel but rather Rabbi Yehoshua, who forbids.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that traps set before Yom Tov may not be taken from on Yom Tov unless one knows the animals were caught before Yom Tov.
The Mishnah recounts a story where a gentile brought fish to Rabban Gamliel, who said they are permitted but he does not wish to accept them.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah brings a story that seems to contradict its own ruling.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it actually teaches that uncertain preparedness (ספק מוכן) is forbidden, and Rabban Gamliel permits it, and then the story illustrates Rabban Gamliel's position.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the halakha does not follow Rabban Gamliel.
An alternative version states that the dispute is between Rabban Gamliel (who permits) and Rabbi Yehoshua (who forbids), and Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may slaughter from traps (negarin) on Yom Tov, but not from nets or snares. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that if one finds animals already damaged from before Yom Tov, they are permitted; if damaged on Yom Tov, they are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may slaughter from traps on Yom Tov but not from nets or snares, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between animals found damaged before Yom Tov (permitted) and those damaged on Yom Tov (forbidden).

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies that only if found damaged from before Yom Tov are they permitted, but a doubt would forbid them; the second clause implies that only if found damaged on Yom Tov are they forbidden, but a doubt would permit them. The Gemara resolves this by reinterpreting the Mishnah: the first clause states that if found damaged from before Yom Tov, they are permitted; but a doubt is treated as if caught on Yom Tov and forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies that only if found damaged from before Yom Tov are they permitted, but a doubt would forbid them.
The Gemara continues: the second clause implies that only if found damaged on Yom Tov are they forbidden, but a doubt would permit them.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the Mishnah: the first clause states that if found damaged from before Yom Tov, they are permitted; but a doubt is treated as if caught on Yom Tov and forbidden.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: Halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: Halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi: permitted for receipt or consumption
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi: permitted for receipt or consumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'permitted' means: Rav says permitted for receipt (to accept from the trapper), while Levi says permitted for consumption. Rav then recounts that he and Levi were before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi when he taught this ruling; at night he said 'permitted for consumption,' but in the morning he said 'permitted for receipt.' Rav, who was in the study hall, retracted, but Levi, who was not, did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'permitted' means in the context of the earlier ruling.
Rav says 'permitted' means permitted for receipt (to accept from the trapper), while Levi says it means permitted for consumption.

Rav recounts that he and Levi were before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi when he taught the ruling; at night he said 'permitted for consumption,' but in the morning he said 'permitted for receipt.' Rav, who was in the study hall, retracted, but Levi, who was not, did not.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a gentile's gift
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a gentile's gift
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a gentile who brings a gift to a Jew on Yom Tov, even fish and fruits that are 'day-old,' are permitted. This challenges Levi's view that they are permitted for consumption, as day-old fruits would not be permitted for eating. The Gemara retorts that according to Rav's view, day-old fruits would also be problematic for handling, and resolves that the baraita deals with fish that are already preserved and fruits that are pickled in vegetables, and 'day-old' means they appear fresh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that a gentile's gift of even day-old fish and fruits is permitted, challenging Levi's view that they are permitted for eating, since day-old fruits would not be permitted for consumption.

The Gemara retorts that according to Rav's view, day-old fruits would also be problematic for handling, and resolves that the baraita deals with fish that are already preserved and fruits that are pickled in vegetables, and 'day-old' means they appear fresh.

items.text: Rav Pappa's halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules: if a gentile brings a gift to a Jew on Yom Tov, if there is that species still attached to the ground, it is forbidden, and even after Yom Tov it is forbidden until enough time has passed for it to have been harvested. If there is no such species attached, and it came from within the techum, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens his halakhic ruling: if a gentile brings a gift to a Jew on Yom Tov and that species is still attached to the ground, it is forbidden.
Rav Pappa adds that even after Yom Tov, the gift remains forbidden until enough time has passed for it to have been harvested.
Rav Pappa concludes: if there is no such species attached and the gift came from within the techum, it is permitted.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: animals beyond the techum
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: animals beyond the techum
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal found beyond the techum is forbidden, but if it came for one Jew it is permitted for another.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that an animal found beyond the techum is forbidden, but if it came for one Jew it is permitted for another.

items.text: Rav's ruling on damming a water channel
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on damming a water channel
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if one dams a water channel on Erev Yom Tov and finds fish in it the next day, the fish are permitted.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if one dams a water channel on Erev Yom Tov and finds fish in it the next day, the fish are permitted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's inference about a wild animal nesting in an orchard
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's inference about a wild animal nesting in an orchard
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda infers from Rav's ruling that a wild animal nesting in an orchard does not require prior designation (zimmun). Rav Nachman objects, noting that in Rav's case no action was taken, whereas here an action is performed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda infers from Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling about fish that a wild animal nesting in an orchard does not require prior designation (זימון).
Rav Nachman objects that in Rav's case no action was taken, whereas here an action (the animal nesting) is performed, so the inference is invalid.

items.text: First objection: a baraita requiring zimmun
items.text_en: First objection: a baraita requiring zimmun
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita stating that a wild animal nesting in an orchard does require zimmun, and a bird called tzipor dror must have its wings tied to avoid confusion with its mother. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does the wild animal not require zimmun? But a baraita states otherwise.

The baraita states that a wild animal nesting in an orchard does require zimmun, and a bird called tzipor dror must have its wings tied to avoid confusion with its mother; this testimony was given in the name of Shmaya and Avtalyon, constituting a refutation.

items.text: Second objection: a baraita exempting certain animals from zimmun
items.text_en: Second objection: a baraita exempting certain animals from zimmun
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita that explicitly exempts a wild animal nesting in an orchard from zimmun, contradicting the first baraita. The baraita also discusses tied and swinging birds, which are forbidden due to theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that explicitly exempts a wild animal nesting in an orchard from zimmun, contradicting the earlier baraita.
The baraita adds that for a ציפור דרור (swallow), one must tie its wing to prevent confusion with its mother, and lists other cases.

The baraita rules that tied and swinging birds in pits, houses, cisterns, and caves are permitted, but in trees they are forbidden due to fear of climbing and detaching; everywhere they are forbidden due to theft.

items.text: Rav Nachman's first resolution: mother vs. offspring
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's first resolution: mother vs. offspring
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the mother animal (which requires zimmun) and the offspring (which does not). The Gemara questions this, noting that the mother would still need proper trapping.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the offspring (which requires zimmun) and the mother (which does not).
The Gemara objects that the mother still requires proper trapping (צידה מעליותא), not just zimmun.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: garden proximity
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: garden proximity
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a garden adjacent to the city (requires zimmun) and one not adjacent (does not require zimmun).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a garden adjacent to the city (requires zimmun) and one not adjacent (does not require zimmun).

items.text: Mishnah: slaughtering a dangerously ill animal on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: slaughtering a dangerously ill animal on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not slaughter a dangerously ill animal on Yom Tov unless there is enough time to eat an olive-sized portion of roasted meat. Rabbi Akiva permits even an olive-sized portion of raw meat from the place of slaughter. If slaughtered in the field, one may not bring it on a pole but may bring it in pieces by hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a dangerously ill animal may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov unless there is time to eat an olive-sized portion of roasted meat from it.
Rabbi Akiva permits even an olive-sized portion of raw meat from the place of slaughter.
The Mishnah concludes that if slaughtered in the field, one may not bring it on a pole but may bring it in pieces by hand.

items.text: Gemara: Rami bar Abba's teaching on flaying and butchering
items.text_en: Gemara: Rami bar Abba's teaching on flaying and butchering
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba teaches that flaying and butchering apply to an olah and likewise to butchers, teaching derech eretz not to eat meat before flaying and butchering. The Gemara questions whether this excludes Rav Huna's principle that an animal is in a state of prohibition until known how it was slaughtered, and then in a state of permission until known it was treif. The Mishnah supports Rav Huna, but Rabbi Chiya's baraita contradicts the interpretation of Rabbi Akiva's statement.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba teaches that the requirement of flaying and cutting applies to an עולה (burnt-offering) and likewise to butchers, teaching דרך ארץ (proper conduct) that one should not eat meat before flaying and cutting.
The Gemara asks what new halakha Rami bar Abba is teaching us.

The Gemara suggests that Rami bar Abba might be excluding Rav Huna's principle that an animal is in a presumptive state of prohibition until known how it was slaughtered, and then in a presumptive state of permission until known it was a טריפה (ritually unfit).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah supports Rav Huna, as Rabbi Akiva says it is sufficient to eat an olive-bulk of raw meat from the place of slaughter, implying no need for examination.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva's statement refers to the place where the animal digests its food, i.e., the intestines, not the actual slaughter site.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chiya taught a baraita stating that it means the actual place of slaughter, contradicting the previous answer.
The Gemara shifts to a new line of reasoning, returning to Rami bar Abba's statement.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about not carrying a slaughtered animal on a pole is merely teaching proper conduct (דרך ארץ), not a strict prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's ruling about not carrying a slaughtered animal on a pole is merely teaching proper conduct (דרך ארץ), not a strict prohibition.

items.text: Baraita on proper eating and drinking
items.text_en: Baraita on proper eating and drinking
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited teaching that one should not eat garlic or onion from the top, nor drink a cup in one gulp, as these are gluttonous behaviors. It further distinguishes between one gulp (glutton), two gulps (proper), and three (arrogant).

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one should not eat garlic or onion from the top, nor drink a cup in one gulp, and distinguishes between one gulp (glutton), two (proper), and three (arrogant).

items.text: Aggadic teachings on vegetables and Israel's stubbornness
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on vegetables and Israel's stubbornness
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba and others teach that certain vegetables (חצובא, נטיעה, תורמוסא) metaphorically 'cut off the legs' of the wicked. A verse about Israel worshipping idols is interpreted by Rabbi Elazar: God says that even with the humble lupine, Israel did not serve Him.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba teaches that the vegetable חצובא (a bitter herb) metaphorically 'cuts off the legs' of the wicked.

sub.text: Anonymous continuation of Rami bar Abba's teaching
sub.text_en: Anonymous continuation of Rami bar Abba's teaching
sub.desc_en: The teaching continues that the vegetable נטיעה (a plant) cuts off the legs of butchers and those who engage in intercourse with a menstruant.

sub.text: Anonymous continuation of Rami bar Abba's teaching
sub.text_en: Anonymous continuation of Rami bar Abba's teaching
sub.desc_en: The teaching concludes that the vegetable תורמוסא (lupine) cuts off the legs of Israel's enemies, citing the verse about Israel's idolatry.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the apparent redundancy in the verse, explaining that God laments that Israel did not serve Him even with the humble lupine, which requires extensive preparation.

items.text: Why the Torah was given to Israel and the three brazen ones
items.text_en: Why the Torah was given to Israel and the three brazen ones
items.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir says the Torah was given to Israel because they are brazen. The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets a verse to mean that God deemed Israel worthy of a fiery law. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish lists three brazen entities: Israel among nations, dog among animals, and rooster among birds.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: A Tanna citing Rabbi Meir asks why the Torah was given to Israel and answers: because they are brazen.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'מִימִינוֹ אֵשׁ דָּת לָמוֹ' (from His right hand a fiery law for them) to support that Israel's nature is fiery, and without the Torah no nation could withstand them.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish lists three brazen entities: Israel among nations, dog among animals, and rooster among birds.
Some add a goat among small cattle and a caper bush among trees to the list of brazen entities.

items.text: Baraita on what a blind person and shepherd may not carry out
items.text_en: Baraita on what a blind person and shepherd may not carry out
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a blind person may not go out with his staff, nor a shepherd with his bag, and one may not go out with a chair (כסא) – whether man or woman.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a blind person may not go out with his staff, nor a shepherd with his bag, nor may one go out with a chair (כסא), whether man or woman.

items.text: Exception for a chair when many need it
items.text_en: Exception for a chair when many need it
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita, citing a case where an elder went out with his chair (גלודקי) and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi permitted it if many need him. The Gemara supports this with the practice of Rabbis who carried chairs for Rav Huna and Shmuel, but only when many needed them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita that forbids going out with a chair, citing a case where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi permitted an elder to go out with his גלודקי (chair) if many need him.
The Gemara supports the exception by citing the practice of Achai Shakkya and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, who carried chairs for Rav Huna and Shmuel, but only when many needed them.

items.text: Inquiry about the chair and the ruling of not carrying it on the shoulder
items.text_en: Inquiry about the chair and the ruling of not carrying it on the shoulder
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs Chama bar Ada to ask Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi about the chair, but Rabbi Yaakov dies. He then asks Rabbi Zerika, who reports in the name of Rabbi Ami that it is permitted provided one does not carry it on the shoulder (אלונקי). The Gemara notes exceptions for Yalta (due to fear) and for Amemar and Mar Zutra (due to crowd pressure).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs Chama bar Ada to ask Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi about the ruling on a chair (כיסא) on Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Before Chama bar Ada arrives, Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi dies, so he instead finds Rabbi Zerika.

sub.text: Rabbi Zerika's report in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zerika's report in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika reports in the name of Rabbi Ami that a chair is permitted provided one does not carry it on the shoulder (אלונקי).
The Gemara asks what 'provided one does not carry it on the shoulder' means.
Rav Yosef brei d'Rava explains that the prohibition refers to carrying it on a shoulder-pole (אלונקי).
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman permitted Yalta to go out on an אלונקי (shoulder-pole), contradicting the prohibition.
The Gemara resolves that Yalta's case is different because she was fearful (בעתיתא) and needed the support.
The Gemara adds that Amemar and Mar Zutra were carried on shoulders on the festival Shabbat due to fear (בעתותא) or crowd pressure (דוחקא דציבורא), showing exceptions to the general rule.

items.text: Mishnah: Firstborn that fell into a pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Firstborn that fell into a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new topic: if a firstborn animal fell into a pit on Yom Tov, Rabbi Yehuda says an expert may descend and examine it for a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the topic: if a firstborn animal fell into a pit on Yom Tov, Rabbi Yehuda permits an expert to descend and examine it for a blemish.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says if a firstborn animal has a blemish, one may bring it up and slaughter it on Yom Tov; if not, one may not. Rabbi Shimon says any blemish not recognizable from before Yom Tov is not considered prepared.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda permits bringing up and slaughtering a firstborn animal with a blemish on Yom Tov, while Rabbi Shimon says any blemish not recognizable from before Yom Tov is not considered prepared.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the precise point of dispute? If they argue about examining blemishes on Yom Tov, why not argue about that in general?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the precise point of dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, suggesting that if they argue about examining blemishes on Yom Tov, they should argue about that in general.

items.text: First answer: The case of a firstborn in a pit
items.text_en: First answer: The case of a firstborn in a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is necessary for the case of a firstborn that fell into a pit. One might think that due to the suffering of animals, one could bring it up (like Rabbi Yehoshua permits), so the Mishnah teaches that this is not allowed without a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is necessary for the case of a firstborn that fell into a pit, where one might think to bring it up due to צער בעלי חיים (suffering of animals), so the Mishnah teaches that this is not allowed without a blemish.

items.text: Objection and refinement
items.text_en: Objection and refinement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If so, the Mishnah should say 'he may not bring up and slaughter' rather than 'he may not slaughter'. The Gemara refines: The case is where one already brought it up, and one might think he may slaughter it, so the Mishnah teaches he may not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If so, the Mishnah should have said 'he may not bring up and slaughter' rather than 'he may not slaughter'.
The Gemara refines: The case is where one already brought it up, and one might think he may slaughter it, so the Mishnah teaches he may not.

items.text: Further objections and resolution
items.text_en: Further objections and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: Why would one think to slaughter it? It is a תם (unblemished firstborn)! The Gemara answers: The case is where a temporary blemish occurred before Yom Tov and now became permanent. One might think his mind is on it and he may slaughter, so the Mishnah teaches he may not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why would one think to slaughter it? It is a תם (unblemished firstborn)!
The Gemara answers: The case is where a temporary blemish occurred before Yom Tov and now became permanent; one might think his mind is on it and he may slaughter, so the Mishnah teaches he may not.

items.text: Baraita with additional dispute
items.text_en: Baraita with additional dispute
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says a firstborn that fell into a pit may be examined by an expert; if it has a blemish, bring it up and slaughter. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya objects, citing the rule that blemishes are not examined on Yom Tov. The Baraita then discusses the case of a blemish that arose before Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says a מומחה (expert) may descend and examine the blemish; if there is one, he may slaughter; Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya objects that blemishes are not examined on Yom Tov, and explains the proper procedure.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya objects, citing the established rule that blemishes are not examined on Yom Tov.
The baraita resolves the dispute by specifying the case: a blemish that arose before Yom Tov is not examined on Yom Tov.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages regarding a firstborn animal that developed a blemish on Yom Tov. Rabbi Shimon rules it is not prepared (mukhan), but both agree that if the blemish was present at birth, it is prepared.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Yom Tov, Rabbi Shimon rules a firstborn animal with a blemish that developed on Yom Tov is not prepared (mukhan), but both he and the Sages agree that if the blemish was present at birth, it is prepared.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling and Rav Nachman's objection
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling and Rav Nachman's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna teaches that if a blemish was present at birth, one may inspect the animal on Yom Tov even initially. Rav Nachman objects, citing a baraita that only permits inspection after the fact.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna teaches that if a blemish was present at birth, one may inspect the animal on Yom Tov even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
Rav Nachman objects, citing a baraita that only permits inspection בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Abaye's support for Rabbah bar Rav Huna from the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Abaye's support for Rabbah bar Rav Huna from the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the Mishnah's three clauses support Rabbah bar Rav Huna: the first clause implies that inspection after the fact is valid, the second (Rabbi Shimon) forbids even after the fact, and the third (agreed case) permits even initially.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating that the Mishnah's first clause supports Rabbah bar Rav Huna: inspection after the fact is valid.

sub.text: Abaye's citation of the second clause
sub.text_en: Abaye's citation of the second clause
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the second clause where Rabbi Shimon forbids even after the fact, contrasting with the first clause.

sub.text: Abaye's citation of the third clause
sub.text_en: Abaye's citation of the third clause
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the third clause where all agree that if the blemish was congenital, inspection is permitted even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Rav Oshaya's contradictory baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's contradictory baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya brings a baraita where the Sages rule that a blemish from before Yom Tov or on Yom Tov is not prepared, contradicting the Mishnah. The Gemara resolves that the baraita is from the school of Adda bar Ukamei, who is known to confuse traditions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya brings a baraita stating that the Sages rule a blemish from before Yom Tov or on Yom Tov is not prepared, contradicting the Mishnah.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: the baraita contradicts the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is from the school of Adda bar Ukamei, who is known to confuse traditions, so it is not authoritative.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that the Mishnah says 'whose blemish is not recognizable', which must mean that it was not examined by an expert before Yom Tov to determine if it is permanent. This implies that if it was examined, it is prepared.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak opens by asserting that the Mishnah's wording is precise, noting that the phrase 'whose blemish is not recognizable' cannot mean it is unrecognizable at all, as that would be obvious.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the Mishnah means the blemish was not examined by a sage before Yom Tov to determine if it is permanent, implying that if it had been examined, the animal would be considered prepared.

items.text: Hillel's question about muktzeh for half of Shabbat
items.text_en: Hillel's question about muktzeh for half of Shabbat
items.desc_en: Hillel asks Rava whether the principle of muktzeh applies to half of Shabbat, i.e., if an item was set aside (muktzeh) and then became permitted again. Rava answers that muktzeh does apply.

sub.desc_en: Hillel asks Rava whether the principle of muktzeh applies for half of Shabbat, clarifying the scenario where the item was fit at twilight, then rejected, then became fit again.
Rava answers that muktzeh does apply in such a case.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's agreed case
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's agreed case
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the Mishnah's agreed case (blemish at birth) permits the animal, but why? It was initially fit through its mother, then became unfit at birth, then became fit again after inspection. This seems to contradict the principle of muktzeh for half of Shabbat. Abaye (or Rav Safra) answers that the case is where judges were present, so there was no interruption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the Mishnah's agreed case (blemish at birth) permits the animal, but why? It was initially fit through its mother, then became unfit at birth, then became fit again after inspection, contradicting the principle of muktzeh for half of Shabbat.
Abaye (or Rav Safra) answers that the case is where judges were present, so there was no interruption in the animal's status.

items.text: Alternative version: Hillel's answer that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbat
items.text_en: Alternative version: Hillel's answer that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbat
items.desc_en: Some say that Hillel answered that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbat. The Gemara then attempts to support this from the Mishnah's agreed case, but Abaye (or Rav Safra) again explains that judges were present.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Hillel answered Rava that there is no muktzeh (set-aside) for half of Shabbat.
The Gemara attempts to support this view from the Mishnah's agreed case of a firstborn born with its blemish, which is permitted despite being set aside earlier.
Abaye (or Rav Safra) explains that the Mishnah's case is exceptional because judges were present, so the animal was never fully set aside.

items.text: Proof from the case of dried fruits
items.text_en: Proof from the case of dried fruits
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about fruits left to dry: one may not eat them without prior designation. The Gemara analyzes whether this proves muktzeh for half of Shabbat, and resolves that the case is where some people eat them and some do not, so designation clarifies intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about fruits left to dry, which may not be eaten without prior designation, as a proof regarding muktzeh.
The Gemara questions the baraita: if the fruits were fit, why need designation; if unfit, what good would designation do?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the case involves uncertainty about fitness, citing Rav Kahana's ruling that dried muktzeh is permitted even without designation.
The Gemara posits that the case must involve fruits that were fit, then rejected, then fit again, and questions why designation would be needed if there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves fruits that some people eat and some do not, so designation clarifies the owner's intent, not muktzeh status.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's proof from beans and lentils
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's proof from beans and lentils
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira attempts to bring a proof from beans and lentils that were initially fit for a meal, then cooked in a pot (becoming unfit), and then... (the segment is cut off).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira proposes a proof from beans and lentils that were initially fit for a meal, then cooked in a pot (becoming unfit), and then... (the segment is cut off).

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the earlier assumption that cooking on Yom Tov is permitted only if the food was fully cooked before the holiday. He argues that ordinary pots are boiling at twilight and eaten at night, yet this is allowed. The Gemara resolves that the question is not about cooking completed by human hands, but about cooking completed by natural means (heaven).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the cooking of the food was completed (by human hands) before Yom Tov, it is fit to eat.
Abaye objects that according to this logic, ordinary pots which are boiling at twilight and eaten at night should be forbidden, yet they are permitted.
The Gemara resolves that the question is not about cooking completed by human hands, but about cooking completed by natural means (heaven).

items.text: The case of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's firstborn
items.text_en: The case of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's firstborn
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent a firstborn animal to Rabbi Ami, who thought not to inspect it. Rabbi Zerika (or Rabbi Yirmeya) ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda (who requires inspection before Yom Tov). He then sent it to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, who also thought not to inspect it, and again was told the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Abba questioned why they didn't allow the sages to act according to Rabbi Shimon, and was told that Rabbi Zeira said the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia had a firstborn animal and sent it to Rabbi Ami, who considered not inspecting it.
Rabbi Zerika (or Rabbi Yirmeya) told Rabbi Ami that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, requiring inspection before Yom Tov.
The animal was then sent to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, who also considered not inspecting it, and Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Zerika) again ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Abba questioned why the sages were not allowed to act according to Rabbi Shimon's lenient opinion.
The responder dismissively asked Rabbi Abba what authority he had to intervene.
Rabbi Abba responded that Rabbi Zeira had said the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: The anonymous sage's quest and Rabbi Zeira's clarification
items.text_en: The anonymous sage's quest and Rabbi Zeira's clarification
items.desc_en: An anonymous sage expressed a desire to ascend to the land of Israel and learn the ruling from Rabbi Zeira himself. When he arrived, he found Rabbi Zeira and asked if he indeed said the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Zeira clarified that he only said it was reasonable (מסתברא), not a definitive ruling.

sub.desc_en: An anonymous sage expresses a desire to ascend to the land of Israel and learn the ruling from Rabbi Zeira himself.

sub.text: Anonymous sage's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Anonymous sage's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Upon arriving, the sage finds Rabbi Zeira and asks him if he indeed ruled that the law follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Zeira clarifies that he only said it was reasonable (מסתברא), not a definitive ruling.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in the Mishnah, Rabbi Shimon says that any blemish not visible before the holiday is not considered prepared, and the Baraita states this in the language of the Sages. This implies that the reasonable view (מסתברא) aligns with Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah and Baraita that the reasonable view (מסתברא) aligns with Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef brings a tradition from Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul that Rabbi Shimon and his colleagues said the law follows Rabbi Meir. The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon could say this, since he was much older than Rabbi Meir. It resolves that they said it in the manner (בשיטת) of Rabbi Meir, not as a direct ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is on the matter.

Rav Yosef brings a tradition from Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul that Rabbi Shimon and his colleagues said the law follows Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon and his colleagues were much older than Rabbi Meir, so how could they rule like him? It resolves that they said it in the manner (בשיטת) of Rabbi Meir, not as a direct ruling.

items.text: The Mishnah about slaughtering a firstborn and showing its blemish
items.text_en: The Mishnah about slaughtering a firstborn and showing its blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: If one slaughters a firstborn and then shows its blemish, Rabbi Yehuda permits it, but Rabbi Meir prohibits it because it was slaughtered without expert authorization. This shows that Rabbi Meir holds that inspection of a firstborn is not like inspection of a treifa; firstborn inspection must be done while alive, while treifa inspection can be after slaughter. From this, it is inferred that treifa inspection is even on Yom Tov, but firstborn inspection must be before Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about slaughtering a firstborn and then showing its blemish, where Rabbi Yehuda permits and Rabbi Meir prohibits, and infers that Rabbi Meir distinguishes between inspection of a firstborn (before Yom Tov) and inspection of a treifa (even on Yom Tov).

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is not about inspecting blemishes per se, but about a penalty (קנסא). He cites Rabbi Yochanan that all agree that defects in the eye are forbidden because they change, and the dispute is only about body blemishes: Rabbi Meir decrees a penalty to prevent confusion with eye defects, while Rabbi Yehuda does not. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this from the Mishnah's language, which implies a penalty.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is not about inspecting blemishes per se, but about a penalty (קנסא).
Abaye cites Rabbi Yochanan that all agree defects in the eye are forbidden because they change, narrowing the dispute to body blemishes.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Meir decrees a penalty on body blemishes to prevent confusion with eye defects, while Rabbi Yehuda does not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's support from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports Abaye's interpretation by noting that the Mishnah's language implies a penalty.

items.text: The case of Ami Vardina'a and Rabbi Ami's practice
items.text_en: The case of Ami Vardina'a and Rabbi Ami's practice
items.desc_en: Ami Vardina'a used to inspect the firstborn of the house of the Nasi, but on Yom Tov he would not inspect. They reported this to Rabbi Ami, who approved. The Gemara questions this, since Rabbi Ami himself inspected on Yom Tov. It answers that Rabbi Ami inspected from the previous day.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Ami Vardina'a used to inspect firstborn animals for the house of the Nasi, but on Yom Tov he would not inspect.
They reported this to Rabbi Ami, who approved of Ami Vardina'a's practice.
The gemara objects: But Rabbi Ami himself inspected on Yom Tov!
The gemara answers that Rabbi Ami inspected from the previous day, not on Yom Tov itself.

items.text: Story of Rava and the firstborn with a blemish
items.text_en: Story of Rava and the firstborn with a blemish
items.desc_en: A man brings a firstborn animal to Rava on the eve of Yom Tov. Rava sees a blemish and tells him to come back tomorrow. The next day, the man describes how the blemish occurred, and Rava asks if he caused it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about Rava examining a firstborn animal on the eve of Yom Tov and sending the man away until the next day.
The next day, Rava asks the man how the blemish occurred, and after hearing the description, asks if he caused it; the man denies causing it.

items.text: Proof that causing a blemish is prohibited
items.text_en: Proof that causing a blemish is prohibited
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'כׇּל מוּם' that one may not cause a blemish in a firstborn animal, e.g., by placing dough on its ear for a dog to take.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'כל מום' (any blemish) that one may not cause a blemish in a firstborn animal, even indirectly.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'מוּם לֹא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ' (a blemish shall not be in it) and the extra word 'כׇּל מוּם' (every blemish) that one may not cause a blemish indirectly, e.g., by placing dough on the animal's ear for a dog to take.
