items.text: Mishnah: Dead animal on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dead animal on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an animal dies on Yom Tov, one may not move it. A story is told about Rabbi Tarfon who asked about this and about a defiled challah, and the Sages ruled they may not be moved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that an animal that died on Yom Tov may not be moved, and recounts a story where Rabbi Tarfon asked about this and the Sages confirmed the prohibition.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does this contradict Rabbi Shimon?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does this contradict Rabbi Shimon?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Shimon, who permits cutting up a carcass for dogs. It answers that even Rabbi Shimon agrees that a dead animal (בעלי חיים שמתו) is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's anonymous ruling contradicts Rabbi Shimon, who permits cutting up a carcass for dogs, and cites the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Shimon, he agrees that a live animal that died is prohibited from being moved.

items.text: Dispute between Mar bar Amemar and Mar brei d'Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Dispute between Mar bar Amemar and Mar brei d'Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Mar bar Amemar in the name of Rava, Rabbi Shimon agrees that dead animals are prohibited, which fits. But according to Mar brei d'Rav Yosef in the name of Rava, Rabbi Shimon disputes even this, so what can be said?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this answer works for Mar bar Amemar citing Rava, who says Rabbi Shimon agreed, but challenges: what about Mar brei deRav Yosef citing Rava, who says Rabbi Shimon disputed even in this case?

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah deals with consecrated animals
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah deals with consecrated animals
items.desc_en: Ze'eri explains that the Mishnah refers to a consecrated animal (בהמת קדשים). This resolves the issue for Mar brei d'Rav Yosef, but then the Gemara asks about Mar bar Amemar. It answers that the case is a dangerously ill animal (מסוכנת), and all agree it is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Ze'eri resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah deals with a consecrated animal (בהמת קדשים), as indicated by the parallel to the consecrated dough (חלה).

sub.text: Gemara's question for Mar bar Amemar
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for Mar bar Amemar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah's prohibition is only for consecrated animals, then for Mar bar Amemar who holds that Rabbi Shimon agrees that dead animals are forbidden, what can be said to explain the Mishnah's leniency for non-consecrated animals?
The Gemara answers that the case here involves a dangerously ill animal (מסוכנת), and all agree it is forbidden to move it.

items.text: Mishnah: No fixing prices on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: No fixing prices on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not initially count people for an animal on Yom Tov (to fix a price), but one may do so from before Yom Tov, then slaughter and divide it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not initially count partners for an animal on Yom Tov, but may do so from before Yom Tov, then slaughter and divide it.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation and alternative method
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation and alternative method
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that 'אין נמנין' means one may not fix a price initially. Rav suggests bringing two animals and saying 'this is like this'. A baraita supports this, saying one may not say 'I am with you for a selah' but may say 'for half, third, or quarter'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'אין נמנין' (one may not count shares).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that 'אין נמנין' means one may not fix a price for the animal on Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks how one should proceed instead.
Rav suggests bringing two animals and saying 'this is like this' to avoid fixing a price.
A baraita supports this, stating one may not say 'I am with you for a selah' but may say 'for half, third, or quarter'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Weighing meat on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Weighing meat on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda, who permits weighing meat against a vessel or a cleaver, and the Sages, who prohibit any use of scales.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda, who permits weighing meat against a vessel or a cleaver, and the Sages, who prohibit any use of scales.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Sages' prohibition and related rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Sages' prohibition and related rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages' prohibition includes even using scales to protect meat from mice, and adds restrictions on a butcher weighing by hand or in water, and on making a handle in meat. It also permits making a sign in meat, as illustrated by Rabba bar Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'כל עיקר' (at all) in the Mishnah's prohibition means.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the prohibition applies even to using scales merely to protect meat from mice.
Rav Idi bar Avin adds that this applies specifically when the scale is suspended from a peg (i.e., it is a recognizable scale).
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a professional butcher is forbidden to weigh meat by hand on Yom Tov.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel further rules that a professional butcher is forbidden to weigh meat in water on Yom Tov.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi rules that it is forbidden to make a handle in meat on Yom Tov.
Ravina adds that doing so by hand is permitted.
Rav Huna rules that it is permitted to make a sign in meat on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Supporting story about Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Supporting story about Rabba bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the practice of Rabba bar Rav Huna, who would cut meat into three-cornered pieces as a sign.

items.text: Gemara: Questioning the practice of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Questioning the practice of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi would weigh a portion against a portion on Yom Tov, and questions whose opinion they follow, since it aligns with neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi would weigh a portion against a portion on Yom Tov, and questions whose opinion they follow, since it aligns with neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Sages.

items.text: Answer: They follow Rabbi Yehoshua, supported by a baraita
items.text_en: Answer: They follow Rabbi Yehoshua, supported by a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that they follow Rabbi Yehoshua, who permits weighing a portion against a portion on Yom Tov. Rav Yosef rules like Rabbi Yehoshua, citing a parallel in Bekhorot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon follow Rabbi Yehoshua, who permits weighing a portion against a portion on Yom Tov.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita from Bekhorot where Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling is paralleled, supporting the halachic conclusion.

items.text: Abaye's objection: Distinction between cases
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: Distinction between cases
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are different: in Bekhorot there is no desecration of sanctified items, but here there is; alternatively, the Sages there permit because it doesn't appear as weekday activity, but here it does.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the case in Bekhorot is different because there is no desecration of sanctified items (ביזיון קדשים), unlike here.
Abaye offers an alternative distinction: the Sages there permit because it does not appear as weekday activity, but here it does.

items.text: Gemara: Questioning whether they were particular with each other
items.text_en: Gemara: Questioning whether they were particular with each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon were particular about each other's presence, citing an incident where five came to Rabbi's house and were found with Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Shimon was not particular. Rav Pappa resolves the ambiguity about who was present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were particular about each other's presence, citing an incident where five people came to Rabbi's house and were found with Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi was not particular.
Rav Pappa resolves the ambiguity by explaining that a different person was between them: either Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei, or Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi and Bar Kappara.

items.text: Mishnah: Sharpening a knife on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sharpening a knife on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not sharpen a knife on Yom Tov, but may rub it against another knife.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not sharpen a knife on Yom Tov, but may rub it against another knife.

items.text: Gemara: Distinctions between sharpening and removing grease, and between stone and wood whetstones
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinctions between sharpening and removing grease, and between stone and wood whetstones
items.desc_en: Rav Huna distinguishes between stone and wood whetstones; Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds distinctions between sharpening and removing grease. Four versions of the tradition are presented, each with different implications.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who prohibits a whetstone
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who prohibits a whetstone
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna who prohibits a whetstone as not Rabbi Yehuda, who permits even food preparations. Rava reports that Rav Chisda rules like Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Chisda blesses him for teaching good things in his name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that using a whetstone is prohibited.
Rav Chisda answers that this Tanna does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who permits even food preparations on a Festival.

sub.text: Rava's report and Rav Chisda's blessing
sub.text_en: Rava's report and Rav Chisda's blessing
sub.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Chisda that he teaches in his name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Chisda blesses him for teaching such good things in his name.

items.text: Rav Nechemya's testimony about Rava's practice
items.text_en: Rav Nechemya's testimony about Rava's practice
items.desc_en: Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef testifies that he stood before Rava, who was sharpening a knife on Yom Tov, indicating a practical ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef testifies that he stood before Rava, who was sharpening a knife on Yom Tov, providing practical evidence for the permissibility of sharpening.

items.text: Two incidents of sharpening a knife on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Two incidents of sharpening a knife on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Two stories are recounted where a knife was sharpened on Yom Tov. In both cases, the action was performed ostensibly to remove oiliness, but the intent was actually to sharpen it, and the ruling was that the halakha permits it but one should not instruct others to do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where someone ran a knife over a basket rim on Yom Tov; when asked, he claimed it was to remove oiliness, but the narrator perceived his true intent was sharpening, and the ruling is that the הלכה (binding law) permits it but one should not instruct others to do so.

אביי (Abaye) reports a parallel incident where his master ran a knife over a millstone edge on Yom Tov; the master claimed it was to remove oiliness, but אביי perceived the true intent was sharpening, and the same ruling applies: the הלכה permits it but one should not instruct others to do so.

items.text: Showing a knife to a Sage on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Showing a knife to a Sage on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether one may show a knife to a Sage on Yom Tov for inspection. Rav Mari bar Rav Bizna permits it, the Rabbis forbid it, and Rav Yosef says a Torah scholar may inspect it for himself and lend it to others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: what is the law regarding showing a knife to a Sage on a Festival for inspection?
Rav Mari bar Rav Bizna permits showing a knife to a Sage on a Festival.
The Rabbis forbid showing a knife to a Sage on a Festival.
Rav Yosef says that a Torah scholar may inspect the knife for himself and then lend it to others.

items.text: Sharpening a knife that became blunt
items.text_en: Sharpening a knife that became blunt
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that a knife that became blunt is permitted to be sharpened on Yom Tov, but only if it became blunt due to pressure (i.e., from use).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that a knife that has become blunt is permitted to be sharpened on Yom Tov, but only if it broke due to pressure.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on preparatory acts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on preparatory acts
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda or Rav Yosef teaches that the permissibility of repairing a knife, spit, or oven on Yom Tov depends on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. The Rabbis forbid preparatory acts for food, citing the verse 'it alone shall be done for you,' while Rabbi Yehuda permits them, citing 'for you' meaning all your needs. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between acts that could have been done before Yom Tov and those that could not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda or Rav Yosef teaches that repairing a knife, spit, or oven on Yom Tov depends on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages, where Rabbi Yehuda permits even preparatory acts for food.

The baraita explains the scriptural basis: the Tanna Kamma derives from 'הוּא' (it alone) that only food, not its preparations, is permitted, while Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'לָכֶם' (for you) that all your needs are included.
The Gemara objects: how does the Tanna Kamma interpret 'לָכֶם'? The answer: it excludes gentiles, not preparatory acts.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the verses: preparatory acts that could have been done before Yom Tov are forbidden, while those that could not are permitted.

items.text: Laws of a spit on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Laws of a spit on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a spit that was bent is forbidden to be fixed on Yom Tov, even if it can be easily straightened. He also rules that a spit used for roasting meat is forbidden to be moved on Yom Tov, but Rav Adda bar Ahava says one may remove it and place it in a corner. Rav Huna and Ravina debate whether this leniency applies only if there is an olive's bulk of meat on it or even without meat.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a bent spit is forbidden to be fixed on Yom Tov, even if it can be easily straightened.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, with Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav Malkiyo
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, with Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav Malkiyo
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel forbids moving a spit used for roasting meat on Yom Tov, but Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav Malkiyo permits removing it and placing it in a corner.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav Huna, and Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav Huna, and Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna limits the leniency to when there is an olive's bulk of meat on the spit, while Ravina permits moving it even without meat, arguing it would otherwise be a utensil set aside for forbidden use (מוקצה).

items.text: Distinguishing between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.text_en: Distinguishing between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Ika notes that certain halakhot are attributed to Rav Malkiyo and others to Rav Malkiya. Rav Pappa clarifies that Rav Malkiya is associated with Mishnayot and baraitot, while Rav Malkiyo is associated with Gemara teachings. The practical difference between them is the case of 'sh'fachot' (spits).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Ika states that certain halakhic items (shapud, sh'fachot, gumot) are attributed to Rav Malkiyo, while others (blorit, efer mikleh, gevinah) are attributed to Rav Malkiya.

Rav Pappa clarifies that Rav Malkiya is associated with Mishnayot and baraitot, while Rav Malkiyo is associated with Gemara teachings, and the practical difference between them is the case of sh'fachot (spits).

items.text: Mishnah: Not specifying a price to a butcher
items.text_en: Mishnah: Not specifying a price to a butcher
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not say to a butcher 'weigh for me a dinar's worth of meat' on Yom Tov, but one may slaughter and divide the meat among them. The Gemara begins to discuss how this is done.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not specify a price to a butcher on Yom Tov, but may slaughter and divide the meat among the group.
The Gemara asks how the division is actually performed, introducing a supporting story.

items.text: Opening anecdote about regional measuring terms
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about regional measuring terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a list of regional terms for half-measures, setting the stage for the discussion of measuring on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists regional terms for half-measures used in Sura, Naresh, Pumbedita, and Nehar Pekod.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of measuring on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of measuring on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may ask another to fill a vessel but not with a measuring vessel. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits even a vessel designated for measuring. A story about Abba Shaul ben Batnit illustrates the practice of filling measures before Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may ask another to fill a vessel but not with a measuring vessel.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the vessel is a measuring vessel, one may not fill it.

sub.text: Story about Abba Shaul ben Batnit
sub.text_en: Story about Abba Shaul ben Batnit
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Abba Shaul ben Batnit who would fill his measures before Yom Tov and give them to customers on Yom Tov.
Abba Shaul says he would do the same even on Chol Hamoed because of clarifying the measures.
The Sages say he would do the same even on a weekday because of the residual liquid in the measures.

items.text: Gemara's first interpretation of 'but not with a measure'
items.text_en: Gemara's first interpretation of 'but not with a measure'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the Mishnah prohibits only a vessel specifically designated for measuring, but a vessel that merely stands for measuring is permitted. Rabbi Yehuda then prohibits even the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'but not with a measure'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the prohibition applies only to a vessel specifically designated for measuring, but a vessel that merely stands for measuring is permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even a vessel that merely stands for measuring may not be filled on Yom Tov.

items.text: Contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda and Sages in two Mishnayot
items.text_en: Contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda and Sages in two Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: in our Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda is stringent and the Sages lenient, but in another Mishnah about weighing meat, Rabbi Yehuda is lenient and the Sages stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: in our Mishnah, Rabbi Yehuda is stringent and the Sages lenient, but in another Mishnah about weighing meat, Rabbi Yehuda is lenient and the Sages stringent, creating a contradiction for both positions.

items.text: First resolution of the contradictions
items.text_en: First resolution of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions: Rabbi Yehuda's leniency in the weighing case applies to a vessel not designated for measuring, while his stringency here applies to a vessel designated for measuring. The Sages' stringency in weighing is because it resembles weekday practice, while their leniency here is because it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's positions: the lenient ruling (weighing meat) applies to a vessel not designated for measuring, while the stringent ruling (filling a measuring vessel) applies to a vessel designated for measuring.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction in the Sages' positions: their stringency in the weighing case is because it resembles weekday practice, while their leniency in the filling case is because it does not resemble weekday practice.

items.text: Rava's alternative interpretation and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative interpretation and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different interpretation: the Mishnah prohibits mentioning the name of a measure, but a vessel designated for measuring is permitted. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits even that. The same contradictions are raised and resolved similarly, with an added detail that people sometimes drink wine from a measuring vessel.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah's phrase 'but not with a measure' to mean one may not mention the name of a measure, but a vessel designated for measuring may be filled.
Rava adds that Rabbi Yehuda prohibits even filling a vessel designated for measuring.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: here Rabbi Yehuda is stringent and the Sages lenient, but elsewhere the opposite is found.

The Gemara resolves both contradictions: Rabbi Yehuda's cases differ by whether the vessel is designated for measuring, and the Sages' cases differ by whether the action resembles weekday practice, adding that people sometimes drink wine from a measuring vessel.

items.text: Story of Abba Shaul and the surplus from measures
items.text_en: Story of Abba Shaul and the surplus from measures
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the story of Abba Shaul ben Batnit: he and his colleagues collected surplus wine and oil from measuring, brought them to Jerusalem, and were told to use them for public needs, citing a baraita about using stolen goods for public benefit.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's story
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's story
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's story of Abba Shaul ben Batnit, who filled his measures on the eve of Yom Tov and gave them to customers on Yom Tov, and a baraita adds that he did so even during the intermediate festival days to prevent neglect of the study hall.

A baraita relates that Abba Shaul collected 300 jars of wine from the surplus of his measures, and his colleagues collected 300 jars of oil from the dregs of their measures, and they brought them to the Temple treasurers in Jerusalem.
The treasurers told them they did not need the surplus, and Abba Shaul and his colleagues replied that they also did not want it back.

sub.text: Treasurers' directive and Rav Chisda's explanation
sub.text_en: Treasurers' directive and Rav Chisda's explanation
sub.desc_en: The treasurers directed them to use the surplus for public needs, citing a baraita that one who stole from an unknown victim should use the proceeds for public needs, and Rav Chisda specifies these are cisterns, ditches, and caves.

items.text: Additional rulings on measuring on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Additional rulings on measuring on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that one may not measure grain for his animal but may take a fixed amount. A baker may measure spices. Rav permits measuring flour for challah, but Shmuel prohibits it, though a baraita from Shmuel's school permits it. Abaye notes the contradiction.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's teaching via Rabban Uqba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's teaching via Rabban Uqba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs Rabban Uqba to teach that one may not measure grain for his animal on Yom Tov but may take a fixed amount, and a baker may measure spices to avoid burning his dish.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav permits a woman to measure flour on Yom Tov for her dough in order to separate חלה (the priestly portion) generously.
Shmuel prohibits measuring flour on Yom Tov, contradicting Rav.
A baraita from Shmuel's own school permits measuring flour, creating an internal contradiction with Shmuel's own ruling.
Abaye notes the contradiction between Shmuel's prohibition and the permission in the baraita from his school, leaving it unresolved.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on sifting flour
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on sifting flour
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the halakha le-ma'aseh (practical law) is that one may sift flour on Yom Tov, implying a lenient ruling.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the practical law (הלכה למעשה) permits sifting flour on Yom Tov, implying a lenient ruling.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on sifting flour
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on sifting flour
items.desc_en: The Sages prohibit sifting flour on Yom Tov, but Rabbi Pappias and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira permit it. They agree that if a pebble or splinter falls into the flour, one may sift it out.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the Sages forbid sifting flour on Yom Tov, but Rabbi Pappeyas and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira permit it, and all agree that if a pebble or splinter falls in, one may sift it out.

items.text: Ravina's objection to a baraita
items.text_en: Ravina's objection to a baraita
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Ravina that one may not sift flour but may pick out a pebble by hand. Ravina objects, arguing that this is even more forbidden because it resembles the prohibited act of selecting.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites before Ravina: one may not sift flour on Yom Tov, but if a pebble or splinter falls in, one may pick it out by hand.
Ravina objects: picking out by hand is even more forbidden, as it constitutes the prohibited act of selecting (בורר).

items.text: Rava bar Rav Huna's lenient ruling and Rav Nachman's rebuke
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna's lenient ruling and Rav Nachman's rebuke
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna Zuti teaches publicly that one may sift flour on Yom Tov. Rav Nachman tells his students to rebuke him, citing the many sifters in Nehardea who would be misled.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Huna Zuti's ruling
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna Zuti's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna Zuti teaches at the entrance of Neharde'a that one may sift flour on Yom Tov, and Rav Nachman sarcastically tells his students to inform him that his leniency is worthless, as many sifters surround Neharde'a.
Rav Nachman instructs his students to rebuke Rava bar Rav Huna Zuti, saying his leniency is worthless and will mislead the many sifters in Nehardea.

items.text: Stories of sifting flour by rabbis' wives
items.text_en: Stories of sifting flour by rabbis' wives
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef's wife sifted flour on a sieve, and he asked for fine bread. Rav Ashi's wife sifted on a table, and he justified it because she was the daughter of Rami bar Hama, a master of deeds, implying she acted properly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef's wife sifted flour on a sieve, and Rav Yosef told her he wanted good bread, implying tacit approval of the method.
Rav Ashi's wife sifted flour on a table, and Rav Ashi notes that she is the daughter of Rami bar Chama, a master of practice, who would not have done so without seeing it from a great authority.

items.text: Mishnah: Buying from a familiar vendor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Buying from a familiar vendor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may go to a familiar storekeeper and ask for eggs or nuts by count, as it is normal for a householder to count items in his home.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a person may go to a familiar storekeeper and ask for eggs and nuts by count, since it is normal for a householder to count items in his home.

items.text: Gemara: Expanding the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Gemara: Expanding the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that extends the principle to a shepherd, butcher, poulterer, and baker, allowing one to ask for a single item. It then details the case of a storekeeper, where one may ask for a specific number of items, provided one does not mention a sum of money or a fixed price, according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita extends the Mishnah's permission to a shepherd, butcher, poulterer, and baker, allowing one to request a single item from each.
The baraita details the case of a storekeeper, where one may ask for a specific number of items.
The baraita states the condition that one may not mention a sum of money or a fixed price.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds the condition that one may not mention a sum of money or a fixed price.

items.text: Transition to the next chapter: Bringing wine and straw
items.text_en: Transition to the next chapter: Bringing wine and straw
items.desc_en: The daf concludes with the beginning of the next chapter, which discusses the prohibition of bringing wine in a basket or straw in a sack on Yom Tov, but allowing carrying by hand or on the shoulder.

sub.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and begins the next chapter, which discusses the prohibition of bringing wine in a basket or straw in a sack on Yom Tov, but allowing carrying by hand or on the shoulder.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may begin using a pile of straw, but not wood that is set aside (muktzeh).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may begin using a pile of straw on Yom Tov, but not wood that is set aside (muktzeh).

items.text: Gemara's initial ruling and Rava's enactment
items.text_en: Gemara's initial ruling and Rava's enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tanna that if it is impossible to change, it is permitted. Rava then instituted a series of changes for carrying loads on Yom Tov, culminating in the principle that if change is impossible, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if it is impossible to make a change (from the weekday practice), the action is permitted on Yom Tov.

items.text: Challenge from women drawing water and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from women drawing water and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: the Sages said to change as much as possible, yet women draw water without changing, and we say nothing. Rav Ashi responds that it is impossible to change because any alternative leads to a greater prohibition, such as increasing carrying distance or risk of squeezing.

sub.desc_en: Rava established a graded system of changes for carrying wood on Yom Tov, culminating in permission if change is impossible.
Rav Chanan bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: the Sages require maximal change on Yom Tov, yet women draw water without any change and we say nothing.
Rav Ashi explains that change is impossible because every alternative leads to a greater prohibition, such as increased carrying distance or risk of squeezing.

items.text: Challenge from clapping and dancing, and the principle of leaving Israel alone
items.text_en: Challenge from clapping and dancing, and the principle of leaving Israel alone
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanin asks Abaye: we learned that one may not clap, slap, or dance on Yom Tov, yet women do so and we say nothing. Abaye responds with a general principle: leave Israel alone; it is better they be inadvertent than deliberate sinners. This applies to rabbinic prohibitions.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanin challenges Abaye: the Mishnah forbids clapping, slapping, and dancing on Yom Tov, yet women do so and we say nothing.

Abaye counters: according to your reasoning, consider Rava's ruling that one should not sit at the entrance of an alleyway lest a vessel roll into the public domain, yet women do so and we say nothing.
Abaye resolves: leave Israel alone; it is better they be inadvertent sinners than deliberate ones, and the same applies to clapping and dancing.

items.text: Extension to Torah prohibitions
items.text_en: Extension to Torah prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially limits the principle to rabbinic laws, but then rejects this, citing Yom Kippur additions which are Torah law, yet people eat and drink until dark and we say nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially qualifies that this leniency applies only to rabbinic prohibitions, but then retracts and says even for Torah-level prohibitions (like Yom Kippur附加 time) we do not rebuke them, as people eat and drink until dark and we say nothing.
The Gemara rejects this limitation, citing that people eat and drink on Yom Kippur additions (a Torah law) until dark and we say nothing.

items.text: Rav Kahana's inference from the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's inference from the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana says the Mishnah's ruling that one may begin with a pile of straw implies that one may begin with a storehouse first, and attributes this to Rabbi Shimon who rejects muktzeh. The Gemara challenges with the second clause about wood, and resolves that it refers to cedar and pine, which are muktzeh due to financial loss, and even Rabbi Shimon agrees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana infers from the Mishnah's first clause that one may begin with a storehouse first, and attributes this to Rabbi Shimon who rejects muktzeh.
The Gemara objects that the second clause about wood in the muktzeh pile contradicts Rav Kahana's attribution, as it implies Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara resolves that the second clause refers to cedar and pine, which are muktzeh due to financial loss, and even Rabbi Shimon agrees.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Kahana's inference from the second clause
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Kahana's inference from the second clause
items.desc_en: Some teach Rav Kahana's statement on the second clause: one may not begin with a storehouse, attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda who holds muktzeh. The Gemara challenges with the first clause about straw, and resolves that it refers to spoiled straw, which is fit for clay, but the Gemara objects that it has thorns, making it unfit.

sub.desc_en: Some teach Rav Kahana's statement on the second clause: one may not begin with a storehouse, attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda who holds muktzeh.
The Gemara challenges: the first clause about straw implies Rabbi Shimon, who rejects muktzeh.
The Gemara resolves that the straw is spoiled, fit for clay, but the objection is raised that it has thorns, making it unfit.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not take wood from the sukkah itself on Yom Tov, but only from wood that is adjacent to it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not take wood from the sukkah itself on Yom Tov, but only from wood adjacent to it.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answers
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why taking from the sukkah is prohibited (due to dismantling a tent) and why adjacent wood is also prohibited. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that 'adjacent' means adjacent to the walls, while Rav Menashya suggests it refers to wood that is not adjacent to the walls, but rather to wood that is tied together (isuryata).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why taking wood from the sukkah itself is prohibited (due to dismantling a tent) and why taking from adjacent wood is also prohibited.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that 'adjacent' in the Mishnah means adjacent to the walls of the sukkah, not the sukkah itself.
Rav Menashya offers an alternative explanation: even if the wood is not adjacent to the walls, the baraita refers to wood that is tied together (איסורייתא).

items.text: Baraita with Rabbi Shimon's opinion and resolution
items.text_en: Baraita with Rabbi Shimon's opinion and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef before Rabbi Yochanan states that one may not take wood from the sukkah except from adjacent wood, and Rabbi Shimon permits it. The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's permission seems to contradict the prohibition of dismantling a tent. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the baraita deals with a fallen sukkah, and Rabbi Shimon follows his view that there is no muktzeh, as evidenced by a baraita about leftover oil in a lamp.

sub.text: Baraita taught by Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Baraita taught by Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one may not take wood from the sukkah except from adjacent wood, Rabbi Shimon permits it, and all agree that a sukkah built for the festival is prohibited during the festival unless a condition was stipulated.
The Gemara objects: how can Rabbi Shimon permit taking wood from the sukkah, since that involves dismantling a tent, which is prohibited?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: the baraita deals with a fallen sukkah, so the only concern is muktzeh, and Rabbi Shimon holds there is no muktzeh.
A supporting baraita is cited: leftover oil in a lamp or bowl is prohibited (muktzeh), but Rabbi Shimon permits it, consistent with his view.

items.text: Refining the case of the fallen sukkah
items.text_en: Refining the case of the fallen sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the comparison to the lamp case, noting that one anticipates the lamp going out but not the sukkah falling. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then clarifies that the case is a dilapidated sukkah, which one expected to fall from yesterday, so his mind was already on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of the lamp is not comparable, because one anticipates the lamp going out but does not anticipate the sukkah falling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by clarifying that the case involves a dilapidated sukkah, which one expected to fall from yesterday, so his mind was already on it.

items.text: Condition on the sukkah and its efficacy
items.text_en: Condition on the sukkah and its efficacy
items.desc_en: The baraita states that if one stipulated a condition on the sukkah, it is effective. The Gemara questions whether a condition can override the sanctity of the sukkah, citing Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Akiva that sukkah wood is forbidden for all seven days, as derived from the verse 'Chag HaSukkot shivat yamim laHashem'. Rav Menashya bar Rava distinguishes between a regular sukkah (where a condition works) and a sukkah of mitzvah (where it does not).

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that all agree the sukkah of the festival is forbidden, but if one stipulated a condition, it is effective.
The Gemara questions whether a condition can be effective for the sukkah of the festival.
Rav Sheshet in the name of Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'חג הסוכות שבעת ימים לה׳' that sukkah wood is consecrated to God for all seven days, implying a condition cannot override this sanctity.

Rav Menashya bar Rava resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between a regular sukkah (סוּכָּה דְעָלְמָא), where a condition works, and a sukkah of the mitzvah (סוּכָּה דְמִצְוָה), where it does not.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the sukkah of mitzvah
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the sukkah of mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Menashya's distinction with a baraita that allows a condition on decorations of a sukkah built according to halakha. Abaye and Rava explain that the condition works only when one says 'I do not separate from them during twilight', preventing sanctity from taking effect, but sukkah wood, which has sanctity, is set aside for all seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Menashya's assertion that a condition is ineffective for a sukkah of mitzvah by citing a baraita that permits a condition on decorations of a sukkah built according to halakha.

Abaye and Rava explain that the condition works only when one says 'I do not separate from them during twilight', preventing sanctity from taking effect, but sukkah wood, which has sanctity, is set aside for all seven days.

items.text: Comparison to etrogim and conclusion
items.text_en: Comparison to etrogim and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the sukkah case to a dispute between Rav and Rav Asi about etrogim designated for each day of Sukkot: Rav permits eating immediately after use, while Rav Asi requires waiting until the next day. The Gemara explains the difference: for etrogim, nights separate the days, making each day an independent mitzvah, whereas for the sukkah, nights do not separate the days, so all seven days are considered one long day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the sukkah case from the dispute between Rav and Rav Asi about etrogim designated for each day of Sukkot, where Rav permits eating immediately after use and Rav Asi requires waiting until the next day.

The Gemara answers that for etrogim, nights separate the days, making each day an independent mitzvah, whereas for the sukkah, nights do not separate the days, so all seven days are considered one long day.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may bring wood from the field only if it is gathered, but from a קרפף even if scattered. It then defines a קרפף according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may bring wood from the field only if gathered, but from a קרפף (enclosure) even if scattered, and defines a קרפף according to Rabbi Yehuda (near the city) and Rabbi Yosei (accessible via a gate, even within the Shabbat limit).

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution via a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution via a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that wood may only be brought from gathered wood in a קרפף, contradicting the Mishnah. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is a minority opinion, citing a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on scattered wood in fields and gathered wood in a קרפף, but disagree on scattered wood in a קרפף and gathered wood in fields.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that wood may only be brought from gathered wood in a קרפף, which contradicts the Mishnah's allowance of even scattered wood from a קרפף.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the Mishnah represents a minority opinion.

sub.text: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on scattered wood in fields (forbidden) and gathered wood in a קרפף (permitted), but disagree on scattered wood in a קרפף and gathered wood in fields.

items.text: Rava's ruling on cane and vine leaves
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on cane and vine leaves
items.desc_en: Rava rules that cane and vine leaves, even if gathered and placed, are considered scattered because wind scatters them, and are therefore forbidden. However, if a vessel was placed on them from yesterday, they are considered gathered and permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that cane and vine leaves, even if gathered and placed, are considered scattered because wind scatters them, and are therefore forbidden.
Rava adds that if a vessel was placed on them from yesterday, they are considered gathered and permitted.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry into the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry into the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the definition of קרפף: whether Rabbi Yehuda requires proximity to the city and a gate, and Rabbi Yosei adds that even within the Shabbat limit with a gate suffices; or whether Rabbi Yehuda requires only proximity, and Rabbi Yosei requires a gate even within the Shabbat limit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei: whether Rabbi Yehuda requires proximity to the city and a gate, and Rabbi Yosei adds that even within the Shabbat limit with a gate suffices.
The Gemara presents an alternative interpretation: Rabbi Yehuda requires only proximity, and Rabbi Yosei requires a gate even within the Shabbat limit.

items.text: Resolution of the inquiry and halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Resolution of the inquiry and halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves from the Mishnah's wording that Rabbi Yosei is lenient in two ways: he permits a קרפף with a gate even within the Shabbat limit, and he does not require proximity to the city. Rav Sala in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei's lenient opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the inquiry by proving from the Mishnah's wording that Rabbi Yosei is lenient in two ways: he permits a קרפף with a gate even within the Shabbat limit, and he does not require proximity to the city.

sub.text: Rav Sala in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Rav Sala in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: Rav Sala in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei's lenient opinion.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Restrictions on chopping wood
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Restrictions on chopping wood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not chop wood from beams or a beam that broke on Yom Tov, and may not use an axe, saw, or sickle, but only a special chopper (קופיץ).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the restrictions on chopping wood on Yom Tov: not from beams or a broken beam, and only with a special chopper (קופיץ).

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah about splitting wood
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the Mishnah about splitting wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction in the Mishnah: first it says one may not split wood at all, then it permits splitting with a kofitz. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it prohibits splitting from a beam that broke on Yom Tov, but permits splitting from one that broke before Yom Tov. A baraita supports this distinction, adding that the wood is not mukan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause prohibits splitting wood entirely, while the later clause permits it with a kofitz.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it prohibits splitting from a beam that broke on Yom Tov, but permits splitting from one that broke before Yom Tov.
A baraita supports this distinction, adding that the wood is not מוכן (prepared) for use on Yom Tov.

items.text: Distinction between male and female axes
items.text_en: Distinction between male and female axes
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Shelemya in the name of Rav states that the prohibition against using an axe (kardom) applies only to its female side (nakvut), but its male side (zachrut) is permitted. The Gemara questions this, noting that the Mishnah already permits a kofitz, and suggests that without this teaching one might think that using a kardom-kofitz combination would be entirely prohibited due to the forbidden side; the teaching clarifies that only the female side is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Shelemya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Shelemya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Shelemya in the name of Rav states that the Mishnah's prohibition of using a קרדום (axe) applies only to its female side (נקבות), but its male side (זכרות) is permitted.
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious, since the Mishnah already permits a קופיץ (hatchet), which is the male side of an axe.

The Gemara explains that without this teaching one might think that using a קרדום-קופיץ combination would be entirely prohibited due to the forbidden side; the teaching clarifies that only the female side is forbidden.

items.text: Alternative version of the teaching on axes
items.text_en: Alternative version of the teaching on axes
items.desc_en: An alternative version applies Rav's teaching to the end of the Mishnah: the kofitz is permitted only on its male side, but its female side is forbidden. The Gemara again questions this, noting that the Mishnah already prohibits a kardom, and explains that without this teaching one might think that a kofitz-kardom combination would be entirely permitted; the teaching clarifies that only the male side is permitted.

sub.desc_en: There is an alternative version that applies Rav's teaching to the end of the Mishnah: the blunt side of the קופיץ (hatchet) is permitted, but the notched side is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that this is also obvious, since the Mishnah explicitly prohibits a קרדום (axe).

The Gemara resolves that the teaching is necessary lest one think that a combined axe-hatchet would be entirely permitted due to the permitted side; the teaching clarifies that only the permitted side is allowed.
Explains that without this teaching one might think that a kofitz-kardom combination would be entirely permitted; the teaching clarifies that only the male side is permitted.

items.text: Debate about breaking open a sealed house on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Debate about breaking open a sealed house on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house full of produce collapses, one may take from the breach. Rabbi Meir adds that one may even create a breach initially. The Gemara questions how this is allowed, since it involves demolishing a tent. Rav Nechumi bar Adda in the name of Shmuel answers that it refers to a pile of loose bricks. Rav Nachman notes that such bricks are permitted for handling on Shabbat if they are set aside for sitting, but if they are arranged, they become muktzeh. Rabbi Zeira clarifies that Rabbi Meir's leniency applies only on Yom Tov, not Shabbat, and a baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house full of produce collapses, one may take from the breach, and Rabbi Meir adds that one may even create a breach initially.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir's leniency is allowed, since it involves demolishing a tent (אוהל).

sub.text: Rav Nechumi bar Adda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nechumi bar Adda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nechumi bar Adda in the name of Shmuel answers that the case involves a pile of loose bricks (אוירא דליבני), not a permanent structure.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Nachman's ruling that loose bricks set aside for sitting are permitted for handling on Shabbat, but if arranged, they become מוקצה (set aside).
Rabbi Zeira resolves that Rabbi Meir's leniency applies only on יום טוב (festival), not on שבת (Sabbath).
A baraita supports Rabbi Zeira's distinction, explicitly stating that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies on יום טוב but not on שבת.

items.text: Laws of seals on the ground and on vessels
items.text_en: Laws of seals on the ground and on vessels
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that for seals in the ground (karka), one may untie but not break or cut on Shabbat or Yom Tov; for seals on vessels, one may untie, break, or cut on both. An objection is raised from a baraita that permits breaking and cutting seals in the ground on Yom Tov. The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Meir's lenient view, while Shmuel follows the Sages. However, another baraita states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir regarding seals in the ground, which seems to contradict Shmuel's position.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that for seals attached to the ground one may only untie, but for seals on vessels one may untie, unravel, or cut, on both שבת (Sabbath) and יום טוב (festival day).
The Gemara raises an objection from a ברייתא (baraita) that permits unraveling and cutting seals in the ground on יום טוב (festival day), contradicting Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara answers that the ברייתא (baraita) follows the lenient view of רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir), while Shmuel rules like the Sages who disagree with him.
The Gemara questions whether the Sages actually disagree with רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) regarding seals in the ground.

A ברייתא (baraita) is cited stating that the Sages concede to רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) regarding seals in the ground, permitting unraveling and cutting on יום טוב (festival day), which appears to contradict Shmuel's position.

items.text: Baraita about seals on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Baraita about seals on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between seals in the ground and on vessels: on both Shabbat and Yom Tov one may loosen but not break or cut ground seals; on vessels, on Shabbat one may only loosen, but on Yom Tov one may loosen, break, or cut.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that on Shabbat and Yom Tov, ground seals may only be loosened, while vessel seals may be loosened on Shabbat but also broken or cut on Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution: Rabbi Nehemya's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution: Rabbi Nehemya's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the beginning of the baraita was resolved, but the end is difficult. It suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Nehemya, who holds that vessels may only be moved for their designated use. The Gemara objects that Rabbi Nehemya would prohibit even on Yom Tov, and questions whether he distinguishes between Shabbat and Yom Tov prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the beginning of the baraita was resolved, but the end remains difficult.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita follows Rabbi Nehemya, who holds that vessels may only be moved for their designated use.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Nehemya would prohibit even on Yom Tov, and questions whether he distinguishes between Shabbat and Yom Tov prohibitions.

items.text: Three conflicting baraitot about using vessels for fuel
items.text_en: Three conflicting baraitot about using vessels for fuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings three baraitot about using vessels or their fragments for fuel: one permits vessels but not fragments, one permits both, and one permits neither. It resolves the contradiction by attributing them to Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Nehemya respectively, noting that two of these are tannaitic disputes within Rabbi Nehemya's framework.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites three contradictory baraitot about using vessels or their fragments for fuel on Yom Tov.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing each baraita to a different Tanna: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Nehemya.
The Gemara notes that two of the baraitot represent a dispute between two Tannaim within Rabbi Nehemya's framework.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not trim a lamp (because it makes a vessel), make charcoal, or cut a wick on Yom Tov. Rabbi Yehuda permits cutting the wick with fire.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions on Yom Tov: trimming a lamp (because it makes a vessel), making charcoal, and cutting a wick; Rabbi Yehuda permits cutting the wick with fire.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the first clause (Rabbi Meir)
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the first clause (Rabbi Meir)
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests the Mishnah's first clause follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that a clay vessel becomes susceptible to impurity only when its work is completed. Abaye objects that Rabbi Meir's reasoning there (it can hold something) does not apply here (the trimmed piece can only hold small coins).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that a trimmed piece of a lamp is considered a vessel.
Rav Yosef identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a clay vessel becomes susceptible to impurity only when its work is completed.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Meir's reasoning there (the vessel can hold something) does not apply here, since the trimmed piece can only hold small coins.

items.text: Alternative identification: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok
items.text_en: Alternative identification: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok
items.desc_en: Some say Rav Yosef identified the Tanna as Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok, who rules that unfinished clay vessels (ilpasin hiraniiyot) are pure even when carrying a zav. Abaye again objects that the reasoning there (they can hold something) does not apply here (only small coins).

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef identified the Tanna as Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok, who rules that unfinished clay vessels (אלפסין חרניות) are pure even when carrying a zav.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok's reasoning there (the vessels can hold something) does not apply here, where the vessel can only hold small coins (פשיטי).

items.text: Baraita on trimming lamps and making ilpasin hiraniiyot
items.text_en: Baraita on trimming lamps and making ilpasin hiraniiyot
items.desc_en: A baraita repeats the prohibition on trimming a lamp and making ilpasin hiraniiyot on Yom Tov, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitting the latter. Rav Yehuda and Abaye explain that ilpasin hiraniiyot are 'field bowls' (large bowls used by field workers).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the prohibition on trimming a lamp and making ilpasin hiraniiyot on Yom Tov, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitting the latter.
The Gemara asks what the term 'hiraniiyot' means.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'hiraniiyot' means 'iraniiyot' (city bowls).
The Gemara further asks what 'iraniiyot' means.
Abaye explains that 'iraniiyot' are 'field bowls' (large bowls used by field workers).

items.text: Gemara on making charcoal and cutting the wick
items.text_en: Gemara on making charcoal and cutting the wick
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why making charcoal is prohibited (it is obviously useless for cooking). Rabbi Chiya explains it was only needed for giving to blacksmiths on that day. Rava clarifies it was permitted for sweating (to soften iron) before the decree. The Gemara then begins discussing cutting the wick, noting the difference between cutting with a knife (prohibited) and with fire (permitted by Rabbi Yehuda).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why making charcoal is prohibited on Yom Tov, since it is obviously useless for cooking.
Rabbi Chiya explains that the prohibition was only needed for giving charcoal to blacksmiths on that day.
Rava clarifies that it was permitted for sweating (to soften iron) before the decree, and the same applies here.
The Gemara transitions to discussing cutting the wick, noting the difference between cutting with a knife (prohibited) and with fire (permitted by Rabbi Yehuda).

items.text: Gemara's continuation on wick preparation
items.text_en: Gemara's continuation on wick preparation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that cutting a wick with fire is permitted because it is like preparing a utensil. Rabbi Chiya teaches that one may cut the wick between two lamps. Rav Nathan bar Abba quotes Rav that one may 'mochat' the wick, which Rav Chanina bar Shelemaya explains means removing the soot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that cutting a wick with fire is also preparing a utensil, just like cutting it with a knife.
Rabbi Chiya teaches a baraita that one may cut the wick with fire between two lamps, implying it is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Nathan bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba quotes Rav that one may 'mochat' the wick on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rav Chanina bar Shelemaya explaining Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemaya explaining Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemaya explains that 'mochat' means removing the soot, not cutting the wick.

items.text: Bar Kappara's six laws of wicks
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's six laws of wicks
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara enumerates six laws about wicks on Yom Tov: three stringencies (not to twist, not to singe, not to cut in two) and three leniencies (to crush by hand, to soak in oil, and to cut between two lamps).

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara enumerates six laws about wicks on Yom Tov: three stringencies (not to twist, not to singe, not to cut in two) and three leniencies (to crush by hand, to soak in oil, and to cut between two lamps).

items.text: Aggadic statements on charity and the wealthy of Babylonia
items.text_en: Aggadic statements on charity and the wealthy of Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba quotes Rav that the wealthy of Babylonia descend to Gehinnom because they did not support Shabbtai bar Marinos. The Gemara then discusses that one who does not have mercy is not from Abraham's seed. Rav Nathan bar Abba also quotes Rav that one who depends on others' table lives in darkness, and Rav Chisda adds that such a life is not life. A baraisa lists three whose lives are not lives: one who depends on his friend's table, one whose wife rules over him, and one who suffers bodily afflictions.

sub.text: Rav Nathan bar Abba citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba quotes Rav that the wealthy of Babylonia descend to Gehinnom, citing the incident where Shabbtai bar Marinos visited and they refused to support him.
Shabbtai bar Marinos explains that the wealthy lack mercy, proving they are not from Abraham's seed, as mercy is a sign of Abrahamic descent.

sub.text: Rav Nathan bar Abba citing Rav, with Rav Chisda's addition
sub.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba citing Rav, with Rav Chisda's addition
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Abba quotes Rav that one who depends on others' table lives in darkness, and Rav Chisda adds that such a life is not life.

A baraita lists three whose lives are not lives: one who depends on his friend's table, one whose wife rules over him, and one who suffers bodily afflictions, with an additional opinion including one who has only one garment, which the Tanna Kamma rejects as he can inspect it.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions: not to break a potsherd, not to cut paper for roasting fish, not to sweep an oven or range (but one may press down ashes), not to place two barrels to support a pot, not to support a pot with a stick or door, and not to lead an animal with a stick. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the prohibition of breaking a potsherd or cutting paper for roasting fish.
The Mishnah states the prohibition of sweeping an oven or range, but permits pressing down the ashes.

The Mishnah lists further prohibitions: not to place two barrels to support a pot, not to support a pot with a stick or door, and not to lead an animal with a stick, with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permitting the latter.

items.text: Gemara's reason for the first prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara's reason for the first prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one may not break a potsherd or cut paper, and answers that it is because one is thereby preparing a utensil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah prohibits breaking a potsherd or cutting paper on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that it is because one is thereby preparing a utensil (מתקן מנא).

items.text: Permissibility of sweeping an oven when necessary
items.text_en: Permissibility of sweeping an oven when necessary
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef taught before Rav Nachman that if one cannot bake without sweeping the oven, it is permitted. The Gemara relates that Rabbi Chiya told his wife to sweep the oven for fine bread, and Rava told his attendant to roast a goose and be careful of the soot. Ravina asked Rav Ashi about Rav Acha from Hutzal who had the oven swept for him, and Rav Ashi explained that they rely on the Euphrates clay, and it is only permitted if the oven was sealed from before Yom Tov. Ravina adds that ash is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not sweep an oven or stove on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef taught before Rav Nachman that if one cannot bake without sweeping the oven, it is permitted.
The Gemara relates that when a brick fell into Rabbi Chiya's oven on Yom Tov, he told his wife to sweep it because he wanted fine bread.
Rava told his attendant to roast a goose for him and to be careful of the soot, implying that sweeping to remove soot is permitted when necessary.
Ravina asked Rav Ashi about Rav Acha from Hutzal, for whom they would sweep the oven on Yom Tov.
Rav Ashi explained that they rely on the Euphrates clay, and it is only permitted if the oven was sealed from before Yom Tov.
Ravina adds that ash is permitted to be used on Yom Tov.

items.text: Discussion on placing barrels and stones for a seat
items.text_en: Discussion on placing barrels and stones for a seat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman permits moving stones for a toilet on Yom Tov. Rabba objects from the Mishnah that one may not place two barrels to support a pot, but Rav Nachman distinguishes because barrels create a tent. Rabba Zuta asks Rav Ashi about building a bench, which does not create a tent, and Rav Ashi explains that permanent building is prohibited by Torah, temporary building is rabbinically prohibited, but for honor (like a toilet) the rabbis did not decree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman permits moving stones designated for a toilet on Yom Tov.
Rabba objects from the Mishnah that one may not place two barrels to support a pot, implying a similar prohibition for stones.
Rav Nachman distinguishes because barrels create a tent (אוהל), which is prohibited, whereas stones for a toilet do not.
Rabba Zuta asks Rav Ashi whether building a bench (אצטבא) on Yom Tov, which does not create a tent, would be permitted.
Rav Ashi explains that permanent building is prohibited by Torah, temporary building is rabbinically prohibited, but for honor (like a toilet) the rabbis did not decree.

items.text: Rav Yehuda on arranging a bonfire
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda on arranging a bonfire
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that arranging a bonfire from top to bottom is permitted, but from bottom to top is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that arranging a bonfire from top to bottom is permitted, but from bottom to top is prohibited.

items.text: Prohibition of supporting a pot with a splinter or door
items.text_en: Prohibition of supporting a pot with a splinter or door
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not support a pot with a splinter or a door on Yom Tov, as wood is only designated for heating. The Gemara clarifies the text and notes that Rabbi Shimon permits it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that may not be supported with a splinter or a door on Yom Tov, then the Gemara corrects the text from 'בדלת' to 'וכן הדלת'.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states the prohibition of supporting a pot with a splinter or a door, because wood was only given for heating.
The baraita concludes that Rabbi Shimon permits supporting a pot with a splinter or a door on Yom Tov.

items.text: Leading an animal with a stick on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Leading an animal with a stick on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits leading an animal with a stick on Yom Tov, but Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permits it. The Gemara questions whether he follows his father's view that there is no מוקצה, and concludes that even Rabbi Shimon would agree here because it appears as if going to a market.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of leading an animal with a stick on Yom Tov, with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon permitting it.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon follows his father Rabbi Shimon's view that there is no מוקצה (set-aside) prohibition.
The Gemara answers that even Rabbi Shimon would agree here because leading with a stick appears as if going to a market (a weekday activity).

items.text: Dispute about using wood for roasting: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Dispute about using wood for roasting: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman forbids and Rav Sheshet permits using wood for roasting. The first version says the dispute is over dry wood, with all agreeing wet wood is forbidden. The second version reverses it, with the halakha concluding dry wood is permitted and wet wood forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the dispute: Rav Nachman forbids and Rav Sheshet permits using wood for roasting, with the first version stating all agree wet wood is forbidden and the dispute is over dry wood.

The gemara presents a second version of the dispute, reversing the positions: all agree dry wood is permitted, and the dispute is over wet wood, with the halakhic conclusion that dry wood is permitted and wet wood forbidden.

items.text: Rava's ruling about a woman entering a wood shed and a broken utensil
items.text_en: Rava's ruling about a woman entering a wood shed and a broken utensil
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman may not enter a wood shed to take a coal, and a broken coal is forbidden to burn on Yom Tov because one may burn vessels but not their broken pieces. The Gemara questions if Rava follows Rabbi Yehuda's view of מוקצה, and answers that in the case of a spoiled animal, one's mind was on it from before.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a woman may not enter a wood shed to take a coal, and a broken coal is forbidden to burn on Yom Tov because one may burn vessels but not their broken pieces.
The Gemara questions whether Rava's ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda's view of מוקצה (set-aside items).
The Gemara objects that Rava himself instructed his servant to throw spoiled innards to a cat, implying he does not hold of מוקצה.
The Gemara resolves that in the case of a spoiled animal, one's mind was on it from before Yom Tov, so it is not מוקצה.

items.text: Mishnah: Taking a splinter to pick teeth and gathering wood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Taking a splinter to pick teeth and gathering wood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter from before him to pick teeth and gathering wood from the courtyard to light, as everything in the courtyard is prepared. The Sages say one may only gather from before him. The Mishnah also lists prohibited methods of producing fire.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter from before him to pick teeth and gathering wood from the courtyard to light, as everything in the courtyard is prepared.
The Sages restrict gathering only from before him, rejecting the broader permission of the courtyard.
The Mishnah lists prohibited methods of producing fire on Yom Tov.

items.text: Beginning of Gemara on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of Gemara on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with Rav Yehuda's statement, introducing the discussion on the Mishnah's rulings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda introduces the Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that animal food does not have the status of 'fixing a vessel' (i.e., it is not subject to the prohibition of making a vessel on Yom Tov).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that animal food does not have the status of 'fixing a vessel' (i.e., it is not subject to the prohibition of making a vessel on Yom Tov).

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding wood for smelling
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding wood for smelling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rav Yehudah with a baraita that permits handling fragrant wood and rubbing it, but prohibits cutting it, with different penalties. Rav Yehudah resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to hard wood, and then reinterprets the baraita to distinguish between soft and hard wood.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges Rav Yehudah by citing a baraita that permits handling fragrant wood and rubbing it, but prohibits cutting it, with different penalties for different uses.
Rav Yehudah responds that the baraita must be referring to hard wood, questioning whether hard wood can be crushed by hand.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita to distinguish between soft wood (permitted to cut) and hard wood (prohibited to cut, with different penalties).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution of two conflicting baraitot
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution of two conflicting baraitot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda resolves a contradiction between two baraitot—one permitting cutting wood for smelling, the other prohibiting it—by attributing them to soft and hard wood respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Stam presents two conflicting baraitot: one permits cutting wood to smell it, the other prohibits it.
רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) in the name of רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient baraita to soft wood and the stringent one to hard wood.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects to the distinction between soft and hard wood, citing a Mishnah that permits breaking a barrel to eat figs, and a practice of Rav Yehudah giving out branches even though they could be used for axe handles, implying that hard wood is also permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects to the distinction between soft and hard wood, asking why hard wood should be forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's first proof
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's first proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites a Mishnah that permits breaking a barrel to eat figs, provided one does not intend to make a vessel, implying hard wood is also permitted.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's second proof
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's second proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites a practice of Rav Yehudah giving out branches even though they could be used for axe handles, implying hard wood is permitted.

items.text: Resolution by attributing to Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.text_en: Resolution by attributing to Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by attributing the lenient view (permitting cutting hard wood) to Rabbi Eliezer and the stringent view to the Sages, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter for toothpicking, while the Sages restrict it to animal feed, and both agree on liability for cutting for other purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Eliezer and the stringent view to the Sages, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter for toothpicking, while the Sages restrict it to animal feed, and both agree on liability for cutting for other purposes.

The Gemara explains the positions: Rabbi Eliezer's view in the baraita (liable for a sin-offering) corresponds to the lenient ruling in the earlier dispute, while the Sages' view (merely a שבות (rabbinic prohibition)) corresponds to the stringent ruling.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Eliezer and the barrel-breaking Mishnah
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Eliezer and the barrel-breaking Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer agrees with the Mishnah that permits breaking a barrel for figs, and Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah refers to a barrel that is already broken (מוסתקי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer disagrees with the Mishnah that permits breaking a barrel for figs.
Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah refers to a barrel that is already broken (מוסתקי), so Rabbi Eliezer would agree.

items.text: Gathering wood from the courtyard
items.text_en: Gathering wood from the courtyard
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may gather wood from the courtyard for fuel, provided one does not make piles, and Rabbi Shimon permits even that. The dispute is about whether the gathering appears to be for future use.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the basic rule: one may gather wood from the courtyard and light it, since everything in the courtyard is prepared (מוכן).
The baraita adds a condition: one may not make piles, to avoid the appearance of gathering for future use.
Rabbi Shimon permits making piles even on Yom Tov.
The gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon.

The gemara explains: one Sage (the Sages) holds that piling appears to be gathering for the next day, while the other (Rabbi Shimon) holds that the pot itself testifies that the wood is for immediate use.

items.text: Prohibition of producing fire on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Prohibition of producing fire on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one may not produce fire on Yom Tov because it creates something new (מוליד).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one may not produce fire on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that it is because producing fire creates something new (מוליד) on Yom Tov.

items.text: Prohibition of baking new tiles
items.text_en: Prohibition of baking new tiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the prohibition of baking new tiles on Yom Tov, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that it refers to new tiles, because one is making a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what prohibited act is being performed when one bakes tiles on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case involves new tiles, because baking them constitutes making a vessel (תיקון כלי).

items.text: Two explanations for the Mishnah's prohibition
items.text_en: Two explanations for the Mishnah's prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes two versions of the reason for the Mishnah's prohibition: one says it is because one must inspect the tiles, and another says it is because one must seal them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states one version of the Mishnah's reason: because one must inspect the tiles.
The Gemara presents an alternative version: because one must seal them.

items.text: Mishnah about a treifa animal and Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah about a treifa animal and Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an animal that was trampled or fell and then survived a day; it is kosher. Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai says in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonos that it requires inspection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an animal that was trampled or fell and survived a day, which is kosher.
