sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonos
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonos
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai states in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonos that such an animal requires inspection.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about slaughtering on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about slaughtering on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether one may slaughter such an animal on Yom Tov, questioning if we assume a defect on Yom Tov. Rabbi Zeira responds by citing a Mishnah about not whitening tiles for roasting, and the Gemara debates whether the reason is inspection or sealing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether one may slaughter an animal with a defect on Yom Tov, questioning if we assume the defect is present on Yom Tov.
Rabbi Zeira cites a Mishnah about not whitening tiles for roasting, and explains via Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan that the reason is the need to inspect the tiles.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the Mishnah's reason is actually the need to seal the tiles, not to inspect them.

items.text: Baraita about multiple people preparing a fire on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Baraita about multiple people preparing a fire on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if multiple people each perform a part of the cooking process, all are liable. Another baraita says only the last one is liable. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita refers to bringing fire initially, the second to adding fire at the end.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists six people who each perform a step in cooking (bringing fire, wood, pot, water, spices, stirring) and states that all are liable.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita that says only the last person is liable and all others are exempt.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita refers to bringing fire at the beginning (initial kindling), the second to adding fire at the end (final step).

items.text: Question about placing a pot and Resh Lakish's answer
items.text_en: Question about placing a pot and Resh Lakish's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what action is performed by the one who places the pot. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that we are dealing with a new pot, and the issue is related to whitening tiles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that all the other participants in the baraita perform a direct action, but what action does the one who places the pot perform?
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that we are dealing with a new pot, and the issue is related to whitening tiles (ליבון רעפים), which is prohibited on Yom Tov.

items.text: Baraita about new ovens and stoves on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Baraita about new ovens and stoves on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that new ovens and stoves are like other vessels that may be moved in the courtyard, but one may not anoint, plaster, or cool them to seal them. However, if done for baking, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that new ovens and stoves may be moved in the courtyard like other vessels, but one may not anoint, plaster, or cool them to seal them; if done for baking, it is permitted.

items.text: Baraitot about permitted and forbidden preparations on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Baraitot about permitted and forbidden preparations on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Several baraitot list activities: scalding and singeing animal parts is permitted, but plastering with clay or cutting with scissors is forbidden. Similarly, cutting vegetables with a special cutter is forbidden, but preparing certain tools and baking in an oven is permitted, except for a new oven. Blowing with bellows is forbidden but with a tube is permitted; splitting a reed for roasting is forbidden, but splitting a nut with a cloth is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing permitted and forbidden actions on Yom Tov: scalding and singeing animal parts is permitted, but plastering with clay or cutting with scissors is forbidden.
The baraita continues with additional rules: cutting vegetables with a special cutter is forbidden, but preparing certain tools and baking in an oven is permitted, except for a new oven.

The baraita concludes with further distinctions: blowing with bellows is forbidden but with a tube is permitted; splitting a reed for roasting is forbidden, but splitting a nut with a cloth is permitted.

items.text: Beginning of Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer on standing by the muktzeh
items.text_en: Beginning of Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer on standing by the muktzeh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins with Rabbi Eliezer's statement that a person may stand by the muktzeh (designated produce) on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's statement that a person may stand by the muktzeh (designated produce) on Yom Tov.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about designating produce on Shabbat eve of the Sabbatical year: Rabbi Eliezer permits a general declaration, while the Sages require a precise boundary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer permits a general declaration of intent on Shabbat eve of the Sabbatical year, while the Sages require a precise boundary designation.

items.text: Gemara's citation of parallel Mishnayot
items.text_en: Gemara's citation of parallel Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites two related Mishnayot: one about children who forgot to tithe figs stored before Shabbat, and another about figs brought through a courtyard for drying, which are exempt from tithes when eaten casually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites two Mishnayot: one about children who forgot to tithe figs stored before Shabbat, and another about figs brought through a courtyard for drying, which are exempt from tithes when eaten casually.

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether Shabbat establishes a fixed status for tithing (kovea' l'ma'aser) on produce whose processing is incomplete, based on the verse 'and you shall call Shabbat a delight'.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether Shabbat establishes a fixed status for tithing (קובעת למעשר) on produce whose processing is incomplete, based on the verse 'וקראת לשבת עונג' (and you shall call Shabbat a delight).

items.text: Rav Nachman's answer and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that Shabbat establishes a fixed status for both complete and incomplete produce. Rava objects by analogy to a courtyard, which only fixes status for complete produce. Rav Nachman insists that the tradition is clear that Shabbat fixes status for both.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that Shabbat establishes a fixed status for tithes (קובעת) both for produce whose processing is complete and for produce whose processing is incomplete.
Rava objects by analogy to a courtyard (חצר), which only fixes status for produce whose processing is complete, arguing that Shabbat should follow the same rule.
Rav Nachman insists that the tradition (תלמוד ערוך) is clear that Shabbat fixes status for both complete and incomplete produce, rejecting the analogy to a courtyard.

items.text: Mar Zutra's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra cites the Mishnah's ruling about Shabbat eve in the Sabbatical year, arguing that the restriction in non-Sabbatical years implies Shabbat establishes a fixed status for tithing.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra cites the Mishnah's ruling about Shabbat eve in the Sabbatical year, arguing that the restriction in non-Sabbatical years implies Shabbat establishes a fixed status for tithing.

items.text: Gemara's rejection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's rejection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Mar Zutra's proof, explaining that the Mishnah's case is unique because the person's declaration ('from here I will eat tomorrow') itself establishes the status, not Shabbat. The Gemara then clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that untithed produce is considered 'prepared' for Shabbat, so if one fixes it, it is fixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Mar Zutra's proof, explaining that the Mishnah's case is unique because the person's declaration ('from here I will eat tomorrow') itself establishes the status, not Shabbat.
The Gemara questions why Shabbat is mentioned at all, since the same rule would apply on a weekday.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that untithed produce is considered 'prepared' for Shabbat, so if one fixes it, it is fixed.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer from the Mishnah of olives
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer from the Mishnah of olives
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Eliezer holds Shabbat establishes a fixed status, citing a mishnah where he exempts from tithes when the surplus can be returned, implying that if surplus returns, there is no fixing. Rabbi Abahu explains the mishnah's distinction: in the first case, the vat is pure and the person impure, so the surplus cannot be returned; in the second, both are impure, so it can.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Eliezer's position by citing a mishnah where surplus olives can be returned, implying that when surplus returns, Shabbat does not establish a fixed status.
The Gemara cites the mishnah about taking olives from the vat, where Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between a pure vat (liable) and an impure vat (exempt because surplus can be returned).
Rabbi Abahu explains the mishnah's distinction: the first case involves a pure vat and an impure person, so the surplus cannot be returned.
Rabbi Abahu explains the second case: both vat and person are impure, so the surplus can be returned, leading to exemption.

items.text: Rejection of the analogy to the mishnah
items.text_en: Rejection of the analogy to the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy, arguing that in the mishnah on the daf, the produce is already in a state of being returned (מוחזרין ועומדין), so the comparison fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted analogy, arguing that in the mishnah the produce is already in a state of being returned (מוחזרין ועומדין), so the comparison fails.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's consistent position: Terumah and Shabbat establish
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's consistent position: Terumah and Shabbat establish
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains that Rabbi Eliezer consistently holds that terumah establishes a fixed status, and all the more so Shabbat, as taught in a baraita where he prohibits eating untithed produce even casually before the work is finished.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi defends Rabbi Eliezer's position by saying he consistently holds that terumah establishes a fixed status, and all the more so Shabbat, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids even casual eating of produce that was tithed before the work was finished, while the Sages permit it.

items.text: Proof from the mishnah's seifa and its rejection
items.text_en: Proof from the mishnah's seifa and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the seifa of the mishnah that Shabbat establishes, since the Sages require marking only on Shabbat eve of the Sabbatical year, implying that in other years Shabbat would forbid. The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the marking itself establishes the status, and the case teaches that untithed produce is prepared for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the seifa of the mishnah that Shabbat establishes, since the Sages require marking only on Shabbat eve of the Sabbatical year, implying that in other years Shabbat would forbid.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the marking itself establishes the status, and the case teaches that untithed produce is prepared for Shabbat.

items.text: Contradiction from the baraita of the cluster and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from the baraita of the cluster and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says one may finish eating a cluster when entering a courtyard or when Shabbat begins, contradicting the idea that Shabbat establishes. Rabbi Nathan resolves that Rabbi Eliezer meant to finish outside the courtyard or after Shabbat, not during.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says one may finish eating a cluster when entering a courtyard or when Shabbat begins, implying that Shabbat does not establish.
The Gemara cites the second case of the baraita where Shabbat begins and Rabbi Eliezer again says one may finish, reinforcing the contradiction.
Rabbi Nathan resolves that Rabbi Eliezer meant one should finish outside the courtyard or after Shabbat, not during, thus Shabbat does establish.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: None establish except for finished produce
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: None establish except for finished produce
items.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that Shabbat, terumah, courtyard, and purchase do not establish a fixed status except for produce whose work is finished. This excludes Hillel's view, who forbids even moving produce on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that Shabbat, terumah, courtyard, and purchase all establish a fixed status only for produce whose work is finished.
The gemara explains that the exclusion of Shabbat from establishing status is to reject Hillel's view, who forbids even moving produce on Shabbat.

items.text: Distinguishing the Mishnah from other tannaitic sources
items.text_en: Distinguishing the Mishnah from other tannaitic sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'in a courtyard' excludes Rabbi Yaakov's view, 'terumah' excludes Rabbi Eliezer's view, and 'purchase' excludes the case of exchanging produce. Three inferences are drawn from the purchase case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's word 'courtyard' excludes Rabbi Yaakov's view, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yaakov obligates maaser (tithe) on figs brought for drying in a courtyard, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda exempts.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's word 'terumah' excludes Rabbi Eliezer's view, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer forbids eating untithed produce on an a priori (לכתחילה) basis before the work is finished, while the Sages permit it.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's word 'purchase' refers to the case of buying figs from an am ha'aretz (an unlearned person), where one may eat them on an ad hoc basis and must tithe them as doubtfully tithed produce (דמאי).

The Gemara infers three principles from the purchase case: purchase only establishes maaser (tithe) liability for produce whose work is finished, most amei ha'aretz (unlearned people) do tithe, and one must tithe doubtfully tithed produce (דמאי) even for unfinished produce.

The Gemara excludes the case of exchanging produce with a friend, citing a baraita where one who exchanges for eating is liable for maaser (tithe) but for drying is exempt, with Rabbi Yehuda distinguishing between eating (liable) and drying (exempt).

items.text: Return to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase 'הדרן עלך המביא', indicating the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new one with the phrase 'הדרן עלך המביא'.

items.text: Mishnah: Moving fruit through a skylight
items.text_en: Mishnah: Moving fruit through a skylight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may move fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov but not on Shabbat, and discusses covering fruit and placing vessels under a leak.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may move fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov but not on Shabbat, and permits covering fruit with vessels against a leak and placing a vessel under a leak on Shabbat.

items.text: Variant readings of the verb in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Variant readings of the verb in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses different versions of the verb in the Mishnah: 'משילין', 'משחילין', 'משירין', 'משחירין', and 'מנשירין'. Each is justified by a biblical or tannaitic source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Yehuda and Rav Natan transmitted variant readings of the Mishnah's verb: one taught 'משילין' and the other taught 'משחילין'.
Mar Zutra justifies both readings: 'משילין' is supported by the verse 'כי ישל זיתך' (Deut 24:20), and 'משחילין' is supported by the tannaitic terms 'השחול והכסול' (a limping animal).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that three further variant readings — 'משירין', 'משחירין', and 'מנשירין' — are also not mistaken.
The reading 'משירין' is supported by Rabbi Yishmael's baraita about a nazirite causing hair to fall out (משיר), and 'משחירין' is supported by a baraita about a barber's 'שחור' (blackening tool).

The reading 'מנשירין' is supported by a baraita about a person whose garments fell off (נשרו) in water, and alternatively by the definition of gleanings (לקט) as that which falls (הנושר) during harvest.

items.text: Determining the limit for moving fruit
items.text_en: Determining the limit for moving fruit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much fruit may be moved through the skylight. Rabbi Zeira cites Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan, comparing it to the case of clearing four or five baskets for guests. The Gemara raises three possible distinctions between that case and this one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much fruit may be moved through a skylight on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan answers that the limit is like the case of clearing four or five baskets for guests or to prevent neglect of the study hall.
The Gemara objects that the case of clearing baskets is different because there is concern for neglect of the study hall, which does not apply here.

Alternatively, the Gemara objects that on Shabbat, which is stringent, one will not come to treat it lightly, but on Yom Tov, which is lighter, one might come to treat it lightly, so the leniency may not apply.
Alternatively, the Gemara objects that in the basket case there is no financial loss, but here there is financial loss, so even a large amount should be permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question: Comparing the case of the storehouse
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Comparing the case of the storehouse
items.desc_en: The Gemara recalls a Mishnah about not emptying an entire storehouse on Shabbat, and Shmuel's explanation that one must not finish it all lest he come to smooth out depressions. It then asks: what about Yom Tov?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalls the Mishnah about not emptying a storehouse on Shabbat and Shmuel's explanation, then asks whether the same restriction applies on Yom Tov.

items.text: First possible distinction: Severity of Shabbat vs. Yom Tov
items.text_en: First possible distinction: Severity of Shabbat vs. Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the leniency applies because Shabbat is stringent, while Yom Tov is light and thus permitted, or because the concern of neglecting the study hall applies on Shabbat but not on Yom Tov, making Yom Tov even more lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible distinction: perhaps the leniency of moving fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov is because Shabbat is stringent (חמיר) and thus forbidden, but Yom Tov is light (קיל) and therefore permitted.
The Gemara offers a second possibility: the prohibition on Shabbat is due to neglect of the study hall (ביטול בית המדרש), and since Yom Tov has no such concern, it is all the more lenient.

items.text: Second case: Moving fruit from roof to roof
items.text_en: Second case: Moving fruit from roof to roof
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah allowing fruit to be lowered through a skylight on Yom Tov, but Rav Nachman limits this to the same roof, not from roof to roof. A baraita supports this. The Gemara then asks about Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that allows lowering fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov.
Rav Nachman limits the Mishnah's permission to moving fruit within the same roof, not from roof to roof.
A baraita supports Rav Nachman's ruling, stating that one may not move items from roof to roof even when the roofs are level.

items.text: Two possible distinctions for the roof case
items.text_en: Two possible distinctions for the roof case
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes two distinctions: first, that Yom Tov is light and might lead to disrespect, while Shabbat is stringent and won't; second, that here there is loss of fruit, so it is permitted, but on Shabbat there is no loss, so it is even more permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the rule is for the roof case, proposing two possible distinctions.
The Gemara suggests that on Shabbat, which is stringent, one would not come to treat it lightly, so it is permitted.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that since here there is loss of fruit, it is permitted, and on Shabbat where there is no loss, it is even more permitted.

items.text: Third case: Lowering fruit via rope or ladder
items.text_en: Third case: Lowering fruit via rope or ladder
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah forbidding lowering fruit via rope or ladder on Yom Tov, and asks about Shabbat. It considers two distinctions: one based on neglect of the study hall, the other on loss of fruit. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that forbids lowering fruit through windows with a rope or by ladder on Yom Tov.
The Gemara asks what the law would be on Shabbat regarding this same action.
The Gemara suggests that on Yom Tov it is forbidden because there is no neglect of the study hall, but on Shabbat, where there is such neglect, it would be permitted.
The Gemara alternatively proposes that here, where there is loss of fruit, one might say it is permitted, but there (in the earlier case) where there is no loss, it would certainly be forbidden.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Covering fruits and the opinion of Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Covering fruits and the opinion of Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cover fruits with vessels. Ulla says even a pile of bricks may be covered. Rabbi Yitzchak limits it to fruits that are fit for use, consistent with his view that a vessel may only be moved for something that is itself movable on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cover fruits with vessels.
Ulla says that even a pile of bricks may be covered.
Rabbi Yitzchak limits the covering to fruits that are fit for use.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling is consistent with his general principle that a vessel may only be moved for something that is itself movable on Shabbat.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah: Only fruits, not bricks
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah: Only fruits, not bricks
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla: the Mishnah says 'cover fruits,' implying only fruits, not bricks. It answers that the same applies even to bricks, but the Mishnah mentions fruits because the first clause discussed fruits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's ruling by citing the Mishnah that says 'cover fruits,' implying only fruits, not bricks.
The Gemara answers that the same rule applies even to bricks, but the Mishnah mentions fruits because the first clause discussed fruits.

items.text: Jugs of wine and oil: Dealing with tevel
items.text_en: Jugs of wine and oil: Dealing with tevel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah also mentions covering jugs of wine and oil. The Gemara explains this refers to untithed produce (tevel), which is not yet fit. It justifies the separate mention: one might think only great loss is considered, but the Mishnah teaches that even small loss is considered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's mention of jugs of wine and oil and asks what case is being addressed.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with untithed produce (טבל), which is not yet fit for use.
The Gemara provides supporting reasoning: if the jugs contained permitted wine and oil, they would already be covered by the earlier mention of fruits.
The Gemara resolves that the separate mention of jugs was necessary to teach that even a small loss (הפסד מועט) is considered, not only a great loss.

items.text: Placing a vessel under a leak
items.text_en: Placing a vessel under a leak
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat. The Gemara clarifies this refers to a leak that is fit for use (e.g., the water is drinkable).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat, and the Gemara clarifies this refers to a leak that is fit for use (e.g., the water is drinkable).

items.text: Spreading a mat over bricks
items.text_en: Spreading a mat over bricks
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one may spread a mat over bricks on Shabbat, because the bricks are leftover from building and can be used for sitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may spread a mat over bricks on Shabbat because the bricks are leftover from building and suitable for sitting.

items.text: Spreading a mat over stones
items.text_en: Spreading a mat over stones
items.desc_en: Another baraita: one may spread a mat over stones on Shabbat, referring to sharp stones fit for use in the toilet.

sub.desc_en: The baraita permits spreading a mat over stones on Shabbat, specifying that these are sharp stones fit for use in the toilet.

items.text: Spreading a mat over a beehive
items.text_en: Spreading a mat over a beehive
items.desc_en: A baraita permits spreading a mat over a beehive on Shabbat to protect from sun or rain, provided one does not intend to trap the bees. The Gemara notes this is because the hive contains honey.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that permits spreading a mat over a beehive on Shabbat to protect from sun or rain, provided one does not intend to trap the bees, and explains that this is permitted because the hive contains honey.

items.text: Question about rainy season and the two honeycombs
items.text_en: Question about rainy season and the two honeycombs
items.desc_en: Rav Ukva from Meishan asks Rav Ashi: in the rainy season, there is no honey, so what permits covering? The answer: it refers to the two honeycombs that hold the hive together. But they are muktzeh! The Gemara answers: if one designated them for use.

sub.text: Rav Ukva from Meishan's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Ukva from Meishan's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Ukva from Meishan asks Rav Ashi: in the rainy season, when there is no honey, what permits covering the beehive?
Rav Ashi answers that the permission applies to the two honeycombs that hold the hive together.
The Gemara objects that those two honeycombs are מוקצה (set aside and forbidden for use).
The Gemara resolves that the case is where one designated them for use, removing their מוקצה status.

items.text: Challenge: Why not mention designation in the baraita?
items.text_en: Challenge: Why not mention designation in the baraita?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if designation is required, why doesn't the baraita state it explicitly? It answers that the baraita means: even if one designated them, he still must not intend to trap.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if designation is required, why doesn't the baraita state it explicitly? It argues that the baraita should have distinguished between designated and non-designated honeycombs.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means: even if one designated them, he still must not intend to trap.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's first part (muktzeh) follows Rabbi Yehuda, but the condition 'not intending to trap' follows Rabbi Shimon. It resolves that the entire baraita is Rabbi Yehuda, and the case involves a hole in the hive, so trapping is inevitable (פסיק רישיה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the baraita can be consistent: its first part follows רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) who holds מוקצה (muktzeh), but its condition 'provided he does not intend to trap' follows רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) who permits an unintentional act.

The Gemara objects that the baraita cannot follow רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon), because אביי (Abaye) and רבא (Rava) both rule that even רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) concedes in a case of 'פסיק רישיה ולא ימות' (an inevitable consequence).

The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita follows רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), and the case involves a hive with a hole (כווי), so covering does not inevitably trap the bees, and the condition 'provided he does not intend to trap' is consistent with רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda).

items.text: Clarification of the trap prohibition
items.text_en: Clarification of the trap prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the earlier statement: the concern is that one might make a trap (מצודה). It clarifies that even if the animal is not of the same species, it is still prohibited, and the teaching is necessary to prevent a mistaken leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition is against making a trap (מצודה), and the teaching is necessary to prevent a mistaken leniency for animals not of the same species.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'in the summer because of the heat and in the rainy season because of the rain' refers to the months of Nisan and Tishrei, when both heat and rain are possible, and honey is available.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'in the summer because of the heat and in the rainy season because of the rain' refers to the months of Nisan and Tishrei, when both heat and rain are possible, and honey is available.

items.text: Placing a vessel under a leak on Shabbat
items.text_en: Placing a vessel under a leak on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat. A Tosefta adds that if the vessel becomes full, one may pour it out and repeat, without concern.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat.
A Tosefta adds that if the vessel becomes full, one may pour it out and repeat, without concern.

items.text: Abaye's leak and the ruling of Rabbah
items.text_en: Abaye's leak and the ruling of Rabbah
items.desc_en: Abaye's mill was leaking. He came before Rabbah, who told him to bring his bed there to make it like a 'graaf shel rei' (a vessel for waste) and then remove it. Abaye questioned whether one may initially create a graaf shel rei, and before the issue was resolved, the mill collapsed, leading Abaye to acknowledge Rabbah's wisdom.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Abaye's mill was leaking, and Rabbah instructed him to bring his bed there to make it like a גרף של רעי (a vessel for waste) and then remove it.
Abaye questioned whether one may create a גרף של רעי (a vessel for waste) לכתחילה (as an initial, intentional act).
Before the issue was resolved, the mill collapsed, leading Abaye to acknowledge Rabbah's wisdom.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on graaf shel rei and similar vessels
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on graaf shel rei and similar vessels
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a graaf shel rei (vessel for waste) and an avit shel mei raglayim (vessel for urine) may be taken out to the garbage dump, and when returning it, one may put water in it and bring it back.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a vessel for waste (גרף של רעי) and a vessel for urine (עביט של מי רגלים) may be taken out to the garbage dump, and when returning it, one may put water in it and bring it back.

items.text: Clarification and proof regarding graaf shel rei
items.text_en: Clarification and proof regarding graaf shel rei
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought that graaf shel rei may only be moved when attached to another vessel, but not alone. A proof is brought from Rav Ashi's case of a mouse found in a spice shop, where he instructed to take it by its tail and remove it, showing that even alone it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a graaf shel rei (chamber pot) may only be moved when attached to another vessel, but not alone.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rav Ashi's case
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rav Ashi's case
sub.desc_en: A proof is brought from Rav Ashi's case of a mouse found in a spice shop, where he instructed to take it by its tail and remove it, showing that even alone it is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Activities forbidden on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Activities forbidden on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all activities for which one is liable on Shabbat due to shevut (rabbinic rest), reshut (permitted but not for mitzvah), or mitzvah (a commandment) are also forbidden on Yom Tov. It lists examples: climbing a tree, riding an animal, swimming, clapping, etc. (shevut); judging, betrothing, chalitzah, yibbum (reshut); consecrating, evaluating, etc. (mitzvah). The only difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat is the preparation of food.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all activities for which one is liable on Shabbat due to shevut, reshut, or mitzvah are also forbidden on Yom Tov.
The Mishnah lists the activities forbidden due to shevut: climbing a tree, riding an animal, swimming, clapping, slapping, and dancing.
The Mishnah lists the activities forbidden due to reshut: judging, betrothing, performing חליצה (chalitzah), and performing יבום (yibbum).
The Mishnah lists the activities forbidden due to mitzvah: consecrating, evaluating, devoting, and separating תרומה (terumah) and מעשר (maaser).
The Mishnah concludes that all these are prohibited on Yom Tov, and the only difference between Yom Tov and Shabbat is the preparation of food (אוכל נפש).

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for the prohibitions
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for the prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasons for each prohibition: climbing a tree lest one pluck; riding lest one go beyond the techum (or cut a branch); swimming lest one make a float; clapping lest one repair a musical instrument. For reshut activities like judging and betrothing, the Gemara questions why they are not considered mitzvot, and answers that they are only forbidden when there is a more qualified person available.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prohibition of climbing a tree is a גזירה (decree) lest one pluck a branch.
The Gemara initially explains that riding is forbidden lest one go beyond the techum (Sabbath boundary), and then questions whether this implies that techumin are biblical.
The Gemara revises the explanation: the prohibition is a גזירה (decree) lest one cut a branch for a riding crop.
The Gemara explains that swimming is forbidden lest one make a float (a vessel for swimmers).
The Gemara explains that clapping, slapping, and dancing are forbidden lest one repair a musical instrument.
The Gemara questions why judging is classified as reshut (optional), since it is a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara answers that judging is forbidden only when there is a more qualified person available to judge.

items.text: Clarification of the case of a man with a wife and children
items.text_en: Clarification of the case of a man with a wife and children
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of a man with a wife and children is not about performing a mitzvah, because if there is an older brother, the mitzvah of yibbum falls on him. The reason for the prohibition is a decree lest one write.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a man with a wife and children is prohibited from performing yibbum (levirate marriage), since it is a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara answers that the case is unnecessary for a mitzvah because if there is an older brother, the מצוה (commandment) of yibbum falls on him.
The Gemara concludes that the reason for all these prohibitions is a גזירה (decree) lest one write on Yom Tov.

items.text: Activities prohibited due to the decree of buying and selling
items.text_en: Activities prohibited due to the decree of buying and selling
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists activities prohibited on Yom Tov due to a decree lest one come to buy and sell, including consecration, valuations, and declarations of herem. It then discusses the case of separating terumot and ma'asrot, clarifying that the prohibition applies only to fruits that became obligated yesterday, but for fruits that become obligated today, one may separate and give to the priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists activities prohibited on Yom Tov due to a decree lest one come to buy and sell: consecration, valuations, and declarations of herem.
The Gemara questions why separating terumot and ma'asrot is listed, as it seems obvious that it is prohibited.
Rav Yosef explains that the prohibition applies only to giving the separated portions to the priest on the same day.
The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition applies only to fruits that became obligated yesterday, but for fruits that become obligated today, one may separate and give to the priest.

items.text: Distinction between shevut of permission and shevut of mitzvah
items.text_en: Distinction between shevut of permission and shevut of mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why these activities are prohibited only due to permission or mitzvah but not due to shevut. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the mishnah is speaking in a 'not necessary' style: not only pure shevut is prohibited, but even shevut of permission, and not only shevut of permission, but even shevut of mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why these activities are categorized only under permission or mitzvah but not under the prohibition of shevut (rest).
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the mishnah uses a 'not necessary' style: not only pure shevut is forbidden, but even shevut of permission, and not only shevut of permission, but even shevut of mitzvah.

items.text: Contradiction between mishnayot and resolution by Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Contradiction between mishnayot and resolution by Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the mishnah prohibits these activities on Yom Tov, but another mishnah permits lowering fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov. Rav Yosef resolves that the first mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer and the second follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the mishnah prohibits these activities on Yom Tov, but another mishnah permits lowering fruit through a skylight on Yom Tov.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the first mishnah to Rabbi Eliezer and the second to Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Supporting baraita: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an animal and its offspring that fell into a pit. Rabbi Eliezer permits raising the first to slaughter it, and providing sustenance for the second. Rabbi Yehoshua permits raising the first without slaughtering it, then raising the second through a ruse, and then slaughtering either.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of an animal and its offspring that fell into a pit, and cites Rabbi Eliezer's position: one may raise the first to slaughter it, and provide sustenance for the second in place so it does not die.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua's position: one may raise the first without slaughtering it, then use a ruse to raise the second, and then slaughter either one.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to Rav Yosef's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rav Yosef's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's attribution: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's leniency there is only because sustenance is possible, but here where it is not possible, he would prohibit. Alternatively, perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency there is only because a ruse is possible, but here where it is not possible, he would prohibit.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's resolution by suggesting that Rabbi Eliezer's leniency in the baraita applies only where sustenance is possible, but here where it is not, he would prohibit.
Abaye offers an alternative challenge: perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency applies only where a ruse is possible, but here where it is not, he would prohibit.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative resolution: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative resolution: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction differently: the first mishnah follows Beit Shammai, who prohibit taking out a child, lulav, or Torah scroll to the public domain, and the second follows Beit Hillel, who permit. The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai's prohibition applies only to taking out but not to mere moving, but concludes that moving is necessary for taking out.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by attributing the first mishnah to Beit Shammai, who prohibit taking out a child, lulav, or Torah scroll to the public domain, and the second to Beit Hillel, who permit.
The Gemara objects that Beit Shammai's prohibition may apply only to taking out (הוצאה) but not to mere moving (טלטול) within the domain.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that moving (טלטול) is inherently necessary for taking out (הוצאה), so Beit Shammai's prohibition logically extends to moving as well.

items.text: Mishnah: laws of techum for animals and vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: laws of techum for animals and vessels
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that an animal and vessels follow the techum of their owner. If one entrusts his animal to his son or shepherd, it follows the owner's techum. Vessels designated for a particular brother follow his techum; undesignated vessels follow the place where they are taken. A borrowed vessel follows the borrower's techum if borrowed before Yom Tov, but the lender's if borrowed on Yom Tov. Similarly, a woman who borrowed spices, water, or salt for her dough — these follow the techum of both; Rabbi Yehuda exempts water because it has no substance.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating the general principle that an animal and vessels follow the techum of their owner, and that an animal entrusted to a son or shepherd also follows the owner's techum.
The mishnah adds that vessels designated for a particular brother follow his techum, while undesignated vessels follow the place where they are taken.
The mishnah concludes with the rule for borrowed vessels and borrowed spices, water, and salt for dough, noting that Rabbi Yehuda exempts water because it has no substance.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Dosa on animal following the buyer
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Dosa on animal following the buyer
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Dosa's (or Abba Shaul's) ruling that an animal purchased on Erev Yom Tov, even if delivered on Yom Tov, follows the buyer's techum. Similarly, an animal given to a shepherd follows the shepherd's techum.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Dosa's (or Abba Shaul's) ruling that an animal purchased on Erev Yom Tov follows the buyer's techum, and an animal given to a shepherd follows the shepherd's techum.

items.text: Resolution: one shepherd vs. two shepherds
items.text_en: Resolution: one shepherd vs. two shepherds
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Dosa and the Mishnah by distinguishing between one shepherd (where the animal follows the shepherd) and two shepherds (where it follows the owner). This is supported by the Mishnah's phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one shepherd (where the animal follows the shepherd) and two shepherds (where it follows the owner), citing the Mishnah's phrasing as support.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Dosa. The Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yochanan also rules like a stam Mishnah which says animals follow the owner. The Gemara answers by invoking the same distinction between one and two shepherds.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Dosa.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, noting he also rules like a stam Mishnah that says animals follow the owner's domain.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by invoking the earlier distinction between one shepherd and two shepherds.

items.text: Baraita on a shared cloak
items.text_en: Baraita on a shared cloak
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses two partners who borrowed a cloak, one for morning and one for evening, and made different eiruvin. Each may only walk to the other's techum, and if they limited the techum, the cloak cannot be moved.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces two partners who borrowed a shared cloak, one for morning study and one for evening feasting.
The baraita details that each partner made a different eiruv (one north, one south), and each may only walk to the other's techum.
The baraita concludes that if the partners limited the techum, the cloak may not be moved from its place.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute on shared barrel and animal
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute on shared barrel and animal
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about a jointly purchased barrel and animal: Rav permits the barrel but forbids the animal; Shmuel forbids both. The Gemara questions Rav's logic, and Rav's silence suggests a difficulty. The issue involves bereira and techumin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav permits a jointly purchased barrel but forbids the animal, while Shmuel forbids both.

The Gemara questions Rav's logic: if he holds יֵשׁ בְּרֵירָה (retroactive clarification is valid), the animal should be permitted; if he holds אֵין בְּרֵירָה (no retroactive clarification), the barrel should also be forbidden.

The Gemara answers that Rav holds יֵשׁ בְּרֵירָה, but the animal is different because its owners' techumin (Sabbath boundaries) intermingle; Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object that if the sages were not concerned for מוקצה (set-aside), why are they concerned for techumin? Rav remains silent.

items.text: Rabbi Hoshaya and Rabbi Yochanan on bereira
items.text_en: Rabbi Hoshaya and Rabbi Yochanan on bereira
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rabbi Hoshaya says yesh bereira, Rabbi Yochanan says ein bereira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ruling is regarding bereira (retroactive designation).
Rabbi Hoshaya asserts that bereira (retroactive designation) is valid.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that bereira (retroactive designation) is invalid.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Hoshaya from Ohalot
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Hoshaya from Ohalot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Hoshaya's view from a Mishnah in Ohalot about a corpse in a house with many doors. Rabbi Hoshaya explains that bereira applies only lehaba (future), not lemafre'a (retroactively).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Hoshaya's position that there is bereira (retroactive designation) by citing a Mishnah in Ohalot about a corpse in a house with many doors, where the doors' status depends on prior intent.
The Mishnah records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding when the intent to remove the corpse through a specific door must be formed.
Rabbi Hoshaya explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies only לכאן ולהבא (from now onward), not למפרע (retroactively), thus bereira is affirmed only for future designation, not past.

items.text: Switch: Rabbi Hoshaya says ein bereira, Rabbi Yochanan says yesh
items.text_en: Switch: Rabbi Hoshaya says ein bereira, Rabbi Yochanan says yesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara reverses the earlier attribution: Rabbi Hoshaya actually holds ein bereira, and Rabbi Yochanan holds yesh bereira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reverses the earlier attribution, stating that Rabbi Hoshaya holds אֵין בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation is invalid) and Rabbi Yochanan holds יֵשׁ בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation is valid).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from Yovel and eiruv
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan from Yovel and eiruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view from a ruling about brothers dividing inheritance (they are purchasers and return in Yovel) and from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says one cannot stipulate on two directions for eiruv. This suggests Rabbi Yochanan may hold ein bereira even derabanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position on bereira by citing Rav Asi's statement that Rabbi Yochanan ruled brothers who divide inheritance are purchasers and must return property in Yovel, implying no retroactive clarification.
The Gemara proposes a distinction: Rabbi Yochanan rejects bereira only for Torah law (דאורייתא) but accepts it for rabbinic law (דרבנן).

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one cannot stipulate on two directions for eiruv, showing that even in rabbinic law (eiruv) bereira is rejected, contradicting the proposed distinction.

items.text: Gemara's question on bereirah and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on bereirah and Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between certain cases, suggesting that the principle of bereirah is not accepted. Rabbi Yochanan then states that a wise man has already arrived, implying that he does not accept bereirah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between certain cases, suggesting that the principle of בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation) is not accepted.
Rabbi Yochanan states that a wise man has already arrived, implying that he does not accept the principle of בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation).

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Oshaya distinguishes between Torah and rabbinic law
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Oshaya distinguishes between Torah and rabbinic law
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Oshaya does not accept bereirah in Torah law but does accept it in rabbinic law, thus reconciling the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Oshaya does not accept bereirah (retroactive designation) in Torah law (דאורייתא) but does accept it in rabbinic law (דרבנן), reconciling the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches that the halakhah follows Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches that the halakhah follows Rabbi Oshaya's position.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a fattened ox and a shepherd's ox
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a fattened ox and a shepherd's ox
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that a fattened ox (belonging to a group) follows the feet of all people, while a shepherd's ox follows the feet of that city.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a fattened ox follows the feet of all people, while a shepherd's ox follows the feet of that city.

items.text: Borrowing a vessel before Yom Tov
items.text_en: Borrowing a vessel before Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one borrows a vessel before Yom Tov but receives it on Yom Tov, teaching that it follows the borrower's feet, supporting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of borrowing a vessel before Yom Tov but receiving it on Yom Tov, noting that the obvious ruling is clarified by the specific scenario where the vessel was not handed over until Yom Tov.
The Gemara explains that the teaching is necessary to counter the assumption that the borrower does not acquire possession, and it concludes that the vessel follows the borrower's feet.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explicit statement on borrowing
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explicit statement on borrowing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explicitly rules that a vessel borrowed before Yom Tov, even if given on Yom Tov, follows the borrower's feet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's explicit ruling that a vessel borrowed before Yom Tov, even if delivered on Yom Tov, follows the borrower's domain (רגלי השואל).

items.text: Borrowing on Yom Tov itself
items.text_en: Borrowing on Yom Tov itself
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one borrows on Yom Tov, teaching that it follows the lender's feet, even if the borrower is accustomed to borrowing from him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: borrowing on Yom Tov itself follows the lender's feet.
The Gemara asks why this rule is not obvious.

The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary for a case where the borrower is accustomed to borrowing from this lender, lest one think the borrower's feet control; the lender might find another borrower, so the borrower's feet do not apply.

items.text: Women borrowing and Rabbi Abba's arrival
items.text_en: Women borrowing and Rabbi Abba's arrival
items.desc_en: The Gemara extends the same rule to women borrowing from each other. When Rabbi Abba ascended, he found Rabbi Yochanan and others discussing why water and salt should not nullify the dough, and he responded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends the rule of borrowing to women, and introduces Rabbi Abba's wish to say something acceptable upon his ascent.
Rabbi Abba finds Rabbi Yochanan and others sitting and discussing why water and salt should not nullify the dough.
Rabbi Abba responds to the question posed by Rabbi Yochanan and the others.

items.text: Opening anecdote: the case of mixed wheat
items.text_en: Opening anecdote: the case of mixed wheat
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one se'ah of wheat became mixed with ten se'ah of a friend's wheat. The owner of the majority may eat it, and the Sages laughed at this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one se'ah of wheat became mixed with ten se'ah of a friend's wheat, and the Sages laughed at the ruling that the owner of the majority may eat it.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's defense of the Sages' laughter
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's defense of the Sages' laughter
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya explains that the Sages laughed because the case of wheat mixed with barley is nullified (since it is a different species), but wheat mixed with wheat, according to the Rabbis, is also nullified, so the ruling is obvious.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya defends the Sages' laughter, explaining that while the original case involved wheat mixed with barley (a different species that becomes nullified), the parallel case of wheat mixed with wheat is also nullified according to the Rabbis, making the ruling obvious.

items.text: Rav Safra's objection: monetary loss
items.text_en: Rav Safra's objection: monetary loss
items.desc_en: Rav Safra objects, citing Rav Chiya Ktospa'ah's ruling that one who separates stones from a friend's granary must pay for the wheat, implying that the friend lost a measure. Here too, the owner lost a measure, so the mixture should not be permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra objects to the laughter, citing Rav Chiya Ktospa'ah's ruling that one who removes stones from a friend's granary must pay for the wheat, implying a loss of a measure.
Rav Safra infers that the owner lost a measure of wheat, and here too the owner lost a measure, so the mixture should not be permitted.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: claimable vs. unclaimable money
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: claimable vs. unclaimable money
items.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the master distinguishes between money that has claimants (like a friend's wheat) and money that has no claimants (like ownerless property).

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the master distinguishes between money that has claimants (like a friend's wheat) and money that has no claimants (like ownerless property).

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on neveilah and shechutah
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on neveilah and shechutah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Chisda's ruling that neveilah (carrion) is nullified in shechutah (slaughtered meat) because shechutah cannot become neveilah, but shechutah is not nullified in neveilah because neveilah can become shechutah. This is applied to the case: if the wheat has owners, it is not nullified, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's teaching about ownerless objects acquiring a dwelling place shows that even ownerless objects are treated as if they have owners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye by citing Rav Chisda's ruling that neveilah (carrion) is nullified in shechutah (slaughtered meat) because shechutah cannot become neveilah.
Rav Chisda's ruling continues: shechutah is not nullified in neveilah because neveilah can become shechutah, establishing a parallel to the wheat case.

The Gemara objects that if the wheat has owners it is not nullified, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's teaching about ownerless objects acquiring a dwelling place shows that even ownerless objects are treated as if they have owners.

items.text: Distinction between prohibition and monetary law
items.text_en: Distinction between prohibition and monetary law
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that one cannot compare prohibition (issura) to monetary law (mamona): in prohibition, nullification applies, but in monetary law, it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that one cannot compare prohibition (איסורא) to monetary law (ממונא): in prohibition, nullification applies, but in monetary law, it does not.

items.text: Reason for the distinction: Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Reason for the distinction: Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason. Abaye says it is a decree lest one make a partnership dough. Rava says that spices are for flavor, and flavor is not nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the ruling that spices are not nullified.
Abaye explains that the decree is a גזירה (rabbinic safeguard) lest one make a partnership dough (עיסה בשותפות) to circumvent the prohibition of cooking on Yom Tov for a weekday.
Rava explains that spices are used for flavor (טעמא), and flavor is not nullified (בטל) in a mixture, so the prohibition remains.

items.text: Rav Ashi's principle and resolution of contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's principle and resolution of contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the reason for the earlier ruling is that the mixture is a 'davar sheyesh lo matirin' which is not nullified even in a thousand. The Gemara then resolves contradictions between two baraitot about Rabbi Yehuda's view on salt and water being nullified, distinguishing between Sodomite salt and Istrokanite salt, and between thick and thin porridge.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the earlier ruling is because the mixture is a דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מַתִּירִין (an item that will become permitted later), which is not nullified even in a thousand parts.
The Gemara questions a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda exempts water from nullification but not salt, yet a baraita says Rabbi Yehuda rules that both water and salt are nullified in dough and in a pot.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Sodomite salt (which is valuable and not nullified) and Istrokanite salt (which is common and nullified).
The Gemara raises another contradiction: a baraita says Rabbi Yehuda rules that water and salt are nullified in dough but not in a pot because of its gravy.
The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between thick porridge (עָבָה), where the salt is nullified, and thin porridge (רַכָּה), where it is not.

items.text: Mishnah: The coal and the flame
items.text_en: Mishnah: The coal and the flame
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a coal follows the status of its owner for carrying on Shabbat, while a flame is permitted everywhere. A consecrated coal has me'ilah, but a flame does not. One who carries out a coal to the public domain is liable, but for a flame he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a coal and a flame regarding Shabbat boundaries, consecrated property, and liability for carrying out.

items.text: Gemara: Five laws of the coal and distinction between idolatry and hekdesh
items.text_en: Gemara: Five laws of the coal and distinction between idolatry and hekdesh
items.desc_en: A baraita lists five laws about the coal, including the additional law regarding a coal of idolatry. The Gemara asks why a flame of idolatry is permitted while a flame of hekdesh is forbidden, and answers that since idolatry is repulsive, people distance themselves from it, so the Sages did not decree, but for hekdesh they did.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists five laws about the coal, including the additional law regarding a coal of idolatry.
The Gemara asks why a flame of idolatry is permitted while a flame of hekdesh is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that since idolatry is repulsive, people distance themselves from it, so the Sages did not decree, but for hekdesh they did.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction about carrying out a flame and resolutions
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction about carrying out a flame and resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah (exempt for flame) and a baraita (liable for any flame). Rav Sheshet answers that the baraita refers to carrying a flame on a piece of wood. The Gemara objects that the wood itself should be liable, but it is resolved if the wood is less than the minimum shiur. Abaye offers another answer: the flame was kindled on a potsherd with oil, and the potsherd is less than the shiur. Finally, the Gemara explains that the Mishnah's exemption applies when one merely wafts the flame into the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah exempts one who carries a flame into the public domain, but a baraita holds one liable for any flame.
Rav Sheshet answers that the baraita refers to carrying a flame on a piece of wood, which is a separate object.
The Gemara objects that the wood itself should be a separate liability, but it is resolved if the wood is less than the minimum shiur (size) for liability.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the minimum shiur for carrying wood is the amount needed to cook a light egg, supporting that a smaller piece is exempt.
Abaye offers another answer: the flame was kindled on a potsherd (חספא) coated with oil, so the flame is on a vessel.
The Gemara objects that the potsherd itself should be liable, but it is resolved if the potsherd is less than the minimum shiur.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the minimum shiur for a potsherd is the amount to place between window panes, per Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's exemption: it applies when one merely wafts (אַדְּיֵיהּ אַדּוֹיֵי) the flame into the public domain without carrying a physical object.

items.text: Mishnah: The well and its status for carrying
items.text_en: Mishnah: The well and its status for carrying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a well belonging to an individual follows the individual's status for carrying on Shabbat; a well of the townspeople follows their status; and a well of the Babylonian exiles follows the status of the one who draws water from it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a well belonging to an individual follows the individual's status for carrying on Shabbat; a well of the townspeople follows their status; and a well of the Babylonian exiles follows the status of the one who draws water from it.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction about rivers and resolution, and dispute about the well of Babylonian exiles
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction about rivers and resolution, and dispute about the well of Babylonian exiles
items.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between the Mishnah (well of an individual follows his status) and a baraita (rivers and springs are like everyone's feet). The answer is that the Mishnah deals with collected water. Then there is a dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet about a well of Babylonian exiles: Rav Nachman says it follows the one for whom the water was drawn, Rav Sheshet says it follows the drawer. The Gemara explains they argue whether the well is ownerless or partnership property. Rava then attempts to refute Rav Nachman from a baraita about a herem.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's ruling that an individual's well follows his feet and a baraita stating that rivers and springs are like everyone's feet.
Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah deals with collected water, and Rabbi Chiya bar Avin cites Shmuel in support.

The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet regarding a well of Babylonian exiles: Rav Nachman says it follows the one for whom the water was drawn, Rav Sheshet says it follows the drawer.
The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether the well is considered ownerless (הפקר) or partnership property (שותפי).

sub.text: Rava's attempted refutation of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava's attempted refutation of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava attempts to refute Rav Nachman by citing a baraita about a herem (חרם) that restricts the one who is subject to the vow.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Vows of prohibition and the categories of public property
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Vows of prohibition and the categories of public property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'you are hereby חרם to me,' the vow is binding. If two say 'I am upon you and you upon me,' both are forbidden to each other but permitted to use items designated for עולי בבל (the returnees from Babylon) and forbidden to use items of that city. The Mishnah then lists what belongs to עולי בבל and what belongs to the city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a vow of חרם (ban) is binding, and that two people who mutually vow are forbidden to each other but permitted to use items of עולי בבל (returnees from Babylon) and forbidden to use items of that city.
The Mishnah lists the items belonging to עולי בבל (the returnees from Babylon) and those belonging to the city.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is the well permitted if it is shared?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is the well permitted if it is shared?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that the well (בור של אמצע הדרך) is permitted to both parties. If the well is jointly owned, why is it permitted? The Mishnah elsewhere states that partners who vowed not to benefit from each other are forbidden to enter the courtyard to bathe in the well. The Gemara answers that the case here is about drawing water, not bathing, and each draws from his own share.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the well is permitted if it is jointly owned, citing a baraita that forbids partners who vowed against each other from entering the courtyard to bathe in the well.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case involves drawing water (למלאות), not bathing, and each partner draws from his own share, so it is permitted.

items.text: Debate about ברירה: Rav Nachman's position challenged
items.text_en: Debate about ברירה: Rav Nachman's position challenged
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's assumption that there is retroactive designation (ברירה). It cites a Mishnah about brothers who are partners: when they are liable for the kolbon (half-shekel), they are exempt from animal tithe, and vice versa. Rav Anan says this applies only if they divided different types (e.g., goats against lambs), but if they divided like against like, one can say 'this is his share from the beginning.' Rav Nachman disagrees and says even in that case, there is no retroactive designation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's assumption that there is retroactive designation (ברירה) by citing a Mishnah about brothers who are partners, where liability for the kolbon (half-shekel) and animal tithe are mutually exclusive.

Rav Anan limits the Mishnah's exemption from animal tithe to cases where brothers divided different types (e.g., goats against lambs); but if they divided like against like, one can invoke retroactive designation (ברירה) to say 'this is his share from the beginning.'
Rav Nachman rejects retroactive designation (ברירה) even when brothers divided like against like, asserting that one cannot say 'this is his share from the beginning.'

items.text: Resolution: The well is ownerless, and the dispute is about acquiring a found object for another
items.text_en: Resolution: The well is ownerless, and the dispute is about acquiring a found object for another
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that everyone agrees the well is ownerless (הפקר). The dispute between the earlier authorities is actually about whether one can acquire a found object on behalf of another (מגביה מציאה לחבירו). One opinion holds that the finder acquires it for the other, and the other holds that he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by asserting that all agree the well is ownerless (הפקר), and the disagreement is about whether one can acquire a found object on behalf of another (מגביה מציאה לחבירו).

items.text: Mishnah: Produce in another city and the law of עירוב
items.text_en: Mishnah: Produce in another city and the law of עירוב
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person's produce is in another city and the residents of that city made an עירוב (to bring the produce to him), they may not bring it to him. But if he himself made an עירוב, his produce is like him (and may be brought).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's produce is in another city and the residents of that city made an עירוב (eruv) to bring it to him, they may not bring it; but if he himself made the eruv, his produce is like him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one invited guests on Yom Tov, the guests may not take portions home unless the host granted them ownership of the portions before Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that guests invited on Yom Tov may not take portions home unless the host granted them ownership before Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara's dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on deposited produce
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on deposited produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav says deposited produce follows the techum of the bailee, Shmuel says it follows the depositor. It connects this to a Tannaitic dispute about liability for an ox, and each Amora defends his position even according to the opposing Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav says deposited produce follows the techum of the bailee, Shmuel says it follows the depositor.

The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel follow their respective positions in a Tannaitic dispute about liability for an ox, citing Rav Huna's ruling that Rav follows the Sages and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav defends his position even according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, distinguishing that Rabbi only exempts the bailee when he did not accept explicit guardianship, but here the bailee accepted it.

Shmuel defends his position even according to the Sages, distinguishing that the Sages only impose liability on the bailee because the owner is content for his ox to be in the bailee's domain, but here the owner would not want his produce in the bailee's domain.

items.text: Challenges from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenges from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's view from the Mishnah: if the host designated a corner for the guests, the portions follow the host. It also challenges Rav's view from the Mishnah about guests, and resolves that designation via another is like a designated corner, or alternatively, 'zikkah' is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's view from the Mishnah: if the host set an עירוב (Shabbat boundary merger), his produce follows him; but if Shmuel holds that deposited produce follows the depositor, how does the host's עירוב help?
Rav Huna (or the school of Rav) answers that the case is where the host designated a specific corner for the guest's produce, making it like the guest's own domain.
The Gemara challenges Rav's view from the Mishnah about guests: if Rav holds that deposited produce follows the bailee, why can't guests take portions unless the host designated them before Yom Tov?
The Gemara answers that designation via another is like designating a corner, so the portions follow the guest's domain.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves that the case of explicit designation (זיכה) is different from mere deposit.

items.text: Story of Rav Hana bar Chanilai and the hanging meat
items.text_en: Story of Rav Hana bar Chanilai and the hanging meat
items.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Chanilai hung meat on a doorpost. Rav Huna ruled: if you hung it, take it; if others hung it for you, do not take it. The Gemara questions this based on Rav's and Shmuel's principles, and explains that Rav Hana was a great man preoccupied with his studies, so he might forget.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Chanilai hung meat on a doorpost; Rav Huna ruled that if he hung it himself he may take it, but if others hung it for him he may not.

The Gemara objects: if Rav Hana hung it himself, why may he take it? Rav (Rav Huna's teacher) holds that deposited items follow the depositor's domain, so the meat should be restricted to Rav Hana's own techum; the Gemara answers that the doorpost is like a designated corner (קרן זווית), making it the owner's property.

sub.text: Rav Hillel's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Hillel's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Hillel objects to Rav Ashi: if others hung it for him he may not take it? But Shmuel rules that a fattened ox follows everyone's domain, implying the meat should be permitted.
Ravina objects to Rav Ashi: if others hung it for him he may not take it? But Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Dosa, who permits carrying items belonging to others on Yom Tov.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's objection to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Rav Kahana: if others hung it for him he may not take it? But the Mishnah teaches that an animal and vessels follow the owners' domain, so the meat should be permitted.

The Gemara resolves: Rav Hana bar Chanilai was a great man preoccupied with his studies, so Rav Huna meant that if he hung it himself he has a sign and will not forget, but if others hung it for him he might forget and violate the techum.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Desert vs. domesticated animals
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Desert vs. domesticated animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not water and slaughter desert animals on Yom Tov, but may do so for domesticated ones. Desert animals are those that lodge in the fields; domesticated ones lodge in the city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not water and slaughter desert animals on Yom Tov, but may do so for domesticated ones, defining desert animals as those that lodge in the fields and domesticated ones as those that lodge in the city.

items.text: Gemara on the second Mishnah and Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Gemara on the second Mishnah and Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the order of watering then slaughtering to avoid damage to the hide. It then defines desert and domesticated animals according to the Sages and Rabbi, and questions whether Rabbi holds of 'muktzeh', citing a case about dates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both watering and slaughtering, and answers that it teaches the practical order: one should water the animal first to prevent damage to the hide.
A baraita defines desert and domesticated animals according to the Sages and Rabbi, with Rabbi holding that only animals that never enter settled areas are considered desert animals.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi holds of מוקצה (set-aside), citing a case where Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi asked Rabbi about dates and Rabbi replied that there is no מוקצה for Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Initial challenge
items.text_en: Initial challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges a previous statement by noting that only dried figs and raisins are exempt from the prohibition of preparing, implying a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement by pointing out that the Mishnah exempts only dried figs and raisins from the prohibition of preparing, implying a contradiction with the earlier ruling.

items.text: First two answers
items.text_en: First two answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes two possible answers: either these items are comparable to dried figs and raisins, or the statement was made according to Rabbi Shimon's view but the speaker does not hold it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers two resolutions: first, that these items are comparable to dried figs and raisins; second, that the statement was said in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's view, though the speaker does not hold it.
The Gemara proposes the second answer: the statement was made according to Rabbi Shimon's view (לדבריו דרבי שמעון), but the speaker himself does not hold that view.

items.text: Third answer and dialogue
items.text_en: Third answer and dialogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third answer: the statement was made according to the Rabbis' view, and then presents a dialogue where Rabbi Shimon tells the Rabbis that for him there is no מוקצה, but they should concede regarding animals that go out and graze, to which the Rabbis respond that they are desert animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third resolution: the statement was said to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning, conceding that for himself there is no מוקצה (set-aside), but for them he argues that animals that go out to pasture on Passover and enter the first watering are domesticated, though the Rabbis replied that they are desert animals.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon's argument to the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's argument to the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon tells the Rabbis that for him there is no מוקצה (set-aside prohibition), but they should concede regarding animals that go out and graze during Passover and enter at the first rain, that they are domesticated.
The Rabbis respond that those animals are desert animals (not domesticated), so they are subject to מוקצה.
